nodes.title: HTML
nodes.short: Tim Berners-Lee's tagged-text format for web pages, from CERN in 1989 to 1991. HTML says what is on a page; CSS says how it looks and JavaScript what it does.
nodes.long: Tim Berners-Lee made HTML at CERN between 1989 and 1991 along with the URL and HTTP, the three small inventions behind the Web. HTML, HyperText Markup Language, is tagged text for pages with links: headings, paragraphs, links and forms. The web software had its general release on CERN machines on 17 May 1991, and after NCSA's Mosaic put images inline in 1993 the format spread with browsers. In a page, HTML gives the structure, CSS the appearance and JavaScript the behavior, joined by the DOM, the browser's in-memory tree of the page. The W3C's strict XML-based XHTML 2 was dropped when its working group's charter lapsed at the end of 2009. The WHATWG's backward-compatible HTML5 became a W3C Recommendation in October 2014, and since 2019 the WHATWG living standard has been the single specification.

refs.label: W3C: A Little History of the World Wide Web

nodes.title: Python
nodes.short: Guido van Rossum's readable language. Today the most-used language, thanks to data science, AI and scripting.
nodes.long: Python uses indentation instead of braces and ships a large standard library. The 2008 move to Python 3 took a decade. Its scientific stack (NumPy, pandas, PyTorch) made it the default language of data science and AI.
nodes.sleeper: Python was a hobby language in 1991. Today it is the number one language for AI, data and teaching.

code.text:
total = sum(range(1, 11))
print(total)  # 55

nodes.title: Java
nodes.short: Sun's 'write once, run anywhere' language: compiled to bytecode and run on a virtual machine with garbage collection.
nodes.long: James Gosling's team released Java in 1995. The JVM made enterprise software portable and spawned Kotlin, Scala and Android's app ecosystem. Oracle acquired Sun in 2010 and Java now ships a new version every six months.

nodes.title: JavaScript
nodes.short: Written in ten days for Netscape in 1995; now the language of every web page and, via Node.js, many servers.
nodes.long: Brendan Eich created JavaScript for Netscape Navigator. Standardized as ECMAScript, it grew with the V8 engine (2008), Node.js (2009), and frameworks such as React. TypeScript (2012) adds static types and now outranks it in many surveys.

nodes.title: PHP
nodes.short: Rasmus Lerdorf's 1994 CGI toolkit that became the web's default server-side language. It runs 69.8 percent of sites with a detectable server language.
nodes.long: Rasmus Lerdorf created PHP in 1994 as a set of Common Gateway Interface programs written in C, called Personal Home Page Tools, originally to track visits to his online resume. The source was released in June 1995. In 1997 Andi Gutmans and Zeev Suraski rewrote the parser for an e-commerce project, and the name became the recursive acronym PHP: Hypertext Preprocessor; the Zend Engine and PHP 4 followed in May 2000. Cheap hosting and WordPress, written in PHP and first released in 2003, carried it. W3Techs reports PHP on 69.8 percent of sites with a detectable server-side language and WordPress on 40.2 percent of all websites. PHP 7 (2015) was up to twice as fast as PHP 5.6, and PHP 8.5 arrived on 20 November 2025.
nodes.sleeper: PHP started as a personal toy and still runs most of the visible web server layer. New-project share is slipping, though: TIOBE ranked it 7th in 2016 and 14th in 2026, and JetBrains lists it among languages in long-term decline.

nodes.title: C#
nodes.short: Microsoft's answer to Java, led by Anders Hejlsberg since 2000. It kept evolving (generics, LINQ, async/await, records) and now runs on Linux and macOS too.
nodes.long: Anders Hejlsberg, who wrote the compiler that became Turbo Pascal and was chief architect of Delphi at Borland, has led C# at Microsoft since 2000. C# 1.0 shipped with Visual Studio .NET 2002 and, in Microsoft's words, looked a lot like Java. It is statically typed, class-based and garbage collected, compiled to an intermediate language for the Common Language Runtime. It then kept adding features: generics (2005), LINQ and lambdas (2007), async/await (2012), nullable reference types (2019), records (2020) and extension members in C# 14 (November 2025). Microsoft open-sourced the server-side .NET stack on 12 November 2014, and .NET Core 1.0 (June 2016) ran on Linux and macOS. Standardized as ECMA-334, C# was TIOBE's language of the year for 2023 and 2025 and ranks fifth in September 2026 at 4.22 percent.
nodes.sleeper: C# did not exist before 2000, and its first form was Windows-only. Since 2014 it has been open source and cross-platform, unified as one .NET since 2020, with a new language version every November.

refs.label: Microsoft Learn: the history of C#

nodes.title: Go
nodes.short: Google's language from Griesemer, Pike and Thompson: C-like syntax, garbage collection, goroutines and channels, fast builds. Public in 2009, version 1.0 in 2012.
nodes.long: Robert Griesemer, Rob Pike and Ken Thompson began sketching Go on a whiteboard at Google on 21 September 2007. It became a public open-source project on 10 November 2009, and Go 1.0 shipped on 28 March 2012. The designers were frustrated by the complexity of building large software with the languages and build systems they had, they wanted first-class support for concurrency on multicore chips, and they wanted automatic memory management. Go's FAQ describes it as mostly in the C family for basic syntax, with declarations and packages from the Pascal, Modula and Oberon family and concurrency ideas from languages inspired by Hoare's CSP. It offers goroutines (cheap threads scheduled by the runtime), channels, garbage collection, interfaces, fast compilation and single static binaries. Generics arrived in Go 1.18 in 2022.
nodes.sleeper: Go is what some of Unix's creators designed after decades of C: garbage collected, with indexes checked at run time. An out-of-range index stops the program with a panic instead of silently corrupting memory.

nodes.title: Rust
nodes.short: A systems language that prevents memory errors at compile time through ownership, without a garbage collector.
nodes.long: Graydon Hoare started Rust at Mozilla; version 1.0 shipped in 2015. Its borrow checker rejects code with dangling pointers and data races. Rust now appears in the Linux kernel, Android, Windows and Chromium.

nodes.title: APL
nodes.short: Kenneth Iverson's notation of single-symbol array operations: a whole computation fits on one line with no loops, and Dyalog still sells it.
nodes.long: APL began in about 1956 as Kenneth Iverson's mathematical notation for describing algorithms, first used in 1957 to communicate a complete system design, and his book A Programming Language appeared in 1962. IBM implemented it on System/360 as APL\360, which was running in the fall of 1966, the year this map uses. Functions are single symbols that act on whole arrays, so the sum of 1 to 5 is +/⍳5, and the design was shaped by the 88-character set of the IBM 1050 terminal. The Computer History Museum says APL was widely used in scientific, financial and actuarial work. Edsger Dijkstra called it a mistake carried through to perfection in 1975. Dyalog Ltd still sells and supports it, but TIOBE does not list APL in its top 100.
nodes.sleeper: APL's symbol keyboard looked strange in 1990, and the array-at-a-time idea it started now runs through MATLAB, R, Julia and NumPy. The family continues as J and K, and K sits under the kdb+ database.

nodes.title: Simula
nodes.short: A Norwegian simulation language. Simula 67 introduced classes, objects, inheritance and virtual methods, the core of later object-oriented languages.
nodes.long: Ole-Johan Dahl and Kristen Nygaard designed Simula at the Norwegian Computing Center in Oslo between 1962 and 1967. Simula I, built on ALGOL 60, began as a language for describing and simulating systems; they then realized its ideas applied to programming in general and designed Simula 67. It had classes and objects, subclasses, virtual methods, coroutines and automatic memory management with garbage collection. The idea of prefixing, the origin of inheritance, came to them in December 1966. ACM's 2001 Turing Award citation credits them with ideas fundamental to object-oriented programming, and both Alan Kay and Bjarne Stroustrup name Simula as an inspiration. It never became widely used, and TIOBE does not list it in its top 100.

nodes.title: Regular Expressions
nodes.short: A compact pattern language for text. Ken Thompson's 1968 paper made it fast; grep, Lex, Perl, JavaScript and SQL all use it. Backtracking engines can blow up.
nodes.long: A regular expression is a compact pattern for text, such as (\d{4})-(\d{2})-(\d{2}), which splits 2026-10-01 into 2026, 10 and 01. Ken Thompson's 1968 CACM paper turned them into fast matchers, the grep tool, named for the ed command g/re/p, appeared in Unix in 1973, and Lex (1975) turns a table of regular expressions into a scanner built on a finite automaton. The catch is the engine's strategy. In 2007 Russ Cox reported that Perl needed over sixty seconds to match a 29-character string that a Thompson automaton matched in twenty microseconds, because many engines backtrack and can take exponential time. In Node v22, the pattern /^(a+)+$/ against a run of a's ending in b took 42 ms at 24 characters and 679 ms at 28, about four times longer for every two characters added.

refs.label: Cox, Regular Expression Matching Can Be Simple And Fast

nodes.title: Smalltalk
nodes.short: Alan Kay's group at Xerox PARC built the first dynamic object-oriented language: everything is an object, and computation is messages sent to objects.
nodes.long: Smalltalk came from Alan Kay's Learning Research Group at Xerox PARC, with Dan Ingalls implementing it and Adele Goldberg a leading contributor. In September 1972 Kay bet that the "most powerful language in the world" could be defined in a page of code; the versions ran from Smalltalk-71 through -72, -74 and -76, which added inheritance, to Smalltalk-80, which reached a wide audience through the August 1981 issue of BYTE. Everything is an object, programs send messages, typing is dynamic, memory is garbage collected, and the language came with an integrated environment of debugger, editor and windows on the Alto. Objective-C's additions to C are mostly based on Smalltalk, and Ruby says that like Smalltalk everything in it is an object. Squeak and Pharo continue it, and Pharo 13.1.0 (June 2025) is the latest release.
nodes.sleeper: In the late 1980s Smalltalk was the model of object-oriented programming. C++ and Java made Simula-style classes mainstream instead, and Kay says later Smalltalks backslid towards Simula. It survives in Squeak, Pharo, Cincom Smalltalk and the GemStone/S database.

refs.label: Kay, The Early History of Smalltalk (HOPL-II)

nodes.title: ML and Standard ML
nodes.short: Robin Milner's 1970s Edinburgh language that introduced type inference and polymorphism. Its datatypes and pattern matching now appear in Rust, Swift and Java.
nodes.long: ML began as the metalanguage, hence the name, of the LCF theorem-proving system that Robin Milner and his group built at Edinburgh from 1973 to 1978. Milner wanted a type discipline that combined the flexibility of a typeless language with the security of compile-time checking. The result lets the compiler work out types for you, called type inference, and lets one function work on many types, called polymorphism. His 1978 paper proved that well-typed programs cannot go wrong. Datatypes with pattern matching reached ML through the languages NPL and HOPE, and Standard ML became its standardized form. The most popular use of Standard ML has been writing compilers, and it also underlies proof assistants such as HOL and Isabelle; TIOBE lists ML only in its 51 to 100 band.
nodes.sleeper: Almost nobody writes ML now, yet its ideas won. Type inference and generics reached mainstream languages from the mid-2000s, and pattern matching arrived in C# 9 (2020), Python 3.10 (2021) and Java 21 (2023).

refs.label: MacQueen, Harper and Reppy, The History of Standard ML
Milner, A Theory of Type Polymorphism in Programming (1978)

nodes.title: C Basics: Syntax and Structure
nodes.short: How to read C: main and functions, headers and the preprocessor, separate compilation and linking, fixed-size types, arrays, zero-terminated strings and pointers.
nodes.long: A C program is a set of functions, and execution starts at main. Lines beginning with # go to the preprocessor: #include <stdio.h> pastes in a header of declarations, and #define N 5 substitutes text before the compiler proper runs. Each .c file is compiled alone into an object file and the linker joins the files, resolving names across them, so forgetting one gives the classic undefined-reference error. Integer sizes are not fixed by the language: int is typically 32 bits, and long is 4 bytes on 64-bit Windows but 8 on 64-bit Linux and macOS. Arrays have a fixed size, start at index 0 and carry no length or bounds check. There is no string type, only char arrays ending in a zero byte. A pointer holds an address, and an array name in an expression becomes a pointer to its first element, so a[2] means *(a + 2). Heap memory comes from malloc and must be released exactly once with free.
nodes.sleeper: C itself still checks nothing at run time, but compilers help far more than in 1990: clang warns when sizeof is applied to an array parameter, and sanitizers abort a program that writes past the end of an array.

refs.label: Ritchie, The Development of the C Language

nodes.title: The C Programming Language (K&R)
nodes.short: Kernighan and Ritchie's 'white book' of 1978. It served as C's reference for over ten years, until ANSI C; the second edition (1988) described ANSI C.
nodes.long: The C Programming Language by Brian Kernighan and Dennis Ritchie, published in 1978 and known as the white book or simply K&R, was written mostly by Kernighan, with Ritchie writing the reference manual in Appendix A and the chapter on interfacing with Unix. It served as the language reference until a formal standard was adopted more than ten years later, and the dialect it describes is called K&R C. Between 1973 and 1980 C had gained unsigned, long, union and enumeration types. A K&R function definition lists parameter names first and declares their types afterward, and that style has now been removed from the language. The second edition appeared in 1988 and described ANSI C. Stroustrup notes that every example in it is also a C++ program.

refs.label: Ritchie, The Development of the C Language

nodes.title: Unix Shell and Bash
nodes.short: A shell is the command line and a small language for chaining programs with pipes. From the 1979 Bourne shell to bash, it remains everyday glue.
nodes.long: A Unix shell is the program you type commands into and also a scripting language that joins other programs. Dennis Ritchie wrote that it was crucial that the shell was a user-level program, not part of the operating system, and that the pipe, in Unix from 1972 thanks to Doug McIlroy's persistence, was among the most admired contributions of Unix. The Thompson shell of 1971 came first. The Bourne shell, introduced with Seventh Edition Unix in 1979, gave scripts real control structures and borrowed ALGOL 68-style reversed keywords, fi and esac, to close blocks. Bash, the GNU Bourne-Again SHell, was first released in 1989 and is at version 5.3. macOS has used zsh as its default login shell since 10.15. In Stack Overflow's 2025 survey 48.7 percent of respondents used Bash or shell.
nodes.sleeper: Shell scripts are now the glue of build, deployment and AI-agent tooling. GitHub's Octoverse 2025 called shell scripts (up 324 percent) the fastest riser in new AI-related repositories.

refs.label: Ritchie, The Evolution of the Unix Time-sharing System

nodes.title: Ada
nodes.short: The Pentagon's strongly typed language with packages and built-in tasking, designed 1977 to 1983. Its mandate largely failed; it endures in safety-critical code.
nodes.long: Ada was designed from 1977 to 1983, by a team led by Jean Ichbiah at Honeywell Bull, for the US Department of Defense, to replace more than 450 languages then in use. It is strongly typed, with packages, built-in tasking for concurrency and range-checked types: assigning 101 to an integer declared to range from 0 to 100 stops the program with a constraint error. A 1983 policy mandated Ada for new mission-critical software, with waivers; a 1987 directive prescribed it for most procurements; and the mandate was effectively removed in 1997. A 1997 National Research Council review judged the requirement helpful for custom weapons and command software but often counterproductive where commercial software was strong. Ada lives on in avionics, rail, space and medical systems, and in SPARK, a subset that adds formal proof. Ada 2012 added contracts, and the current standard is Ada 2022.
nodes.sleeper: TIOBE ranked Ada 17th in September 2026 (0.85 percent) and said it is showing renewed strength, up from 31st on the 2021 twelve-month average. Its stronghold is certified safety-critical code.

refs.label: National Research Council, Ada and Beyond (1997)

nodes.title: MATLAB
nodes.short: Cleve Moler's MATrix LABoratory, commercialized in 1984. Matrices are the native type, so loops that need nested loops in Fortran become single statements.
nodes.long: Cleve Moler wrote the first MATLAB in the late 1970s at the University of New Mexico so his students could use the LINPACK and EISPACK packages without writing Fortran. Its only data type was the matrix, it had 80 functions, and adding one meant editing the Fortran source and recompiling. After IBM announced its PC in August 1981, Jack Little and Steve Bangert reprogrammed it in C and added M-files, toolboxes and graphics, and the three founded The MathWorks in 1984. Moler says that things needing doubly or triply nested loops in Fortran, C or Java become single statements in MATLAB. It ships twice a year, with R2026b dated 24 September 2026, and TIOBE ranks it 27th. The free GNU Octave runs most of the same syntax.

nodes.title: Objective-C
nodes.short: C with Smalltalk-style messaging, from Brad Cox and Tom Love in the early 1980s. It became the language of NeXT, then of Mac OS X and iOS, until Swift.
nodes.long: Brad Cox and Tom Love created Objective-C in the early 1980s at their company Productivity Products International, after meeting Smalltalk at ITT in 1981; Cox first wrote a C preprocessor to add Smalltalk-like abilities. The result is a strict superset of C with Smalltalk-style message passing: you do not call a method, you send a message, written in square brackets, and a dynamic runtime decides what to do with it. NeXT licensed Objective-C in 1988 and extended GCC to compile it, Apple acquired NeXT in 1996 and made it the language of Mac OS X (Cocoa) and then iOS, and at WWDC 2014 Apple introduced Swift, described as Objective-C without the C. TIOBE named Objective-C its Programming Language of the Year in 2011 and 2012, during the iPhone boom, and ranked it 19th in September 2026.
nodes.sleeper: In 1990 Objective-C was a niche NeXT language. After Apple bought NeXT it became the language of Mac OS X and iOS until Swift took over, though TIOBE still ranks it 19th (up from 29th a year earlier).

code.text:
// Square brackets send a message to an object
[array addObject:[NSString stringWithFormat:@"Hello, %@", name]];

nodes.title: Erlang
nodes.short: Ericsson's language for telephone switches: swarms of tiny isolated processes that pass messages, restart independently and can be upgraded while running.
nodes.long: Joe Armstrong began Erlang in 1986 at Ericsson's Computer Science Laboratory as an experiment to add concurrent processes to Prolog, since the best method for programming plain old telephony seemed to be a Prolog variant with parallel processes. By 1990 it was a language in its own right, with message passing and failure detection. Ericsson's AXD301 switch, first delivered in 1998, had over 1.7 million lines of Erlang by 2003, which Armstrong called probably the largest system ever written in a functional style. In February 1998 Ericsson banned Erlang for new products, and in December 1998 it released Erlang and the OTP libraries as open source. The much-quoted nine nines of reliability is an undocumented vendor claim, as Armstrong's own thesis notes.
nodes.sleeper: Erlang began as proprietary telecom technology. Open source since December 1998, its default limit today is 1,048,576 simultaneous processes, and Elixir and Gleam run on the same virtual machine.

code.text:
%% Erlang, run as an escript: sum of the squares of the odd numbers 1 to 10
main(_) -> io:format("~p~n", [lists:sum([X * X || X <- lists:seq(1, 10), X rem 2 =:= 1])]).
%% prints 165

refs.label: Armstrong, Making reliable distributed systems in the presence of software errors

nodes.title: Perl
nodes.short: Larry Wall's 1987 text-processing and scripting language, the early web's CGI workhorse. Still released yearly, but down from TIOBE's top 10 to 23rd.
nodes.long: Larry Wall released Perl 1.000 on 18 December 1987, a general-purpose Unix scripting language that, in its own FAQ's words, derives from C and to a lesser extent from sed, awk and the Unix shell. Perl 5.000 arrived in October 1994, CPAN, the Comprehensive Perl Archive Network, was set up in October 1995, and Perl was widely used for CGI scripts on the mid-1990s web. In July 2000 Wall announced the effort to write Perl 6; its first official specification came in December 2015, and in 2019 it was renamed Raku, a separate language in the same family. Perl 5 kept shipping, with 5.44.0 on 15 July 2026. TIOBE ranks Perl 23rd in September 2026, down from 10th in 2016, and W3Techs finds it on 0.1 percent of sites.
nodes.sleeper: Perl was the glue language of the early web and of system administration. TIOBE's September 2026 headline said Perl and Ruby had left its top 20, and 3.8 percent of Stack Overflow 2025 respondents still use it.

refs.label: perldoc: perlhist, the Perl history records

nodes.title: ANSI C (C89/C90)
nodes.short: The first C standard, ANSI X3.159-1989, adopted by ISO as C90. It codified existing practice and made one big change: function prototypes, borrowed from C++.
nodes.long: ANSI formed the X3J11 committee in the summer of 1983, at the urging of Doug McIlroy. It reported at the end of 1989, and ISO accepted the result as ISO/IEC 9899:1990, which is why the language is called both C89 and C90. The committee was cautious and conservative, and its stated goal was a clear, consistent and unambiguous standard that codifies the common, existing definition of C. Ritchie says it introduced only one genuinely important change: putting the types of a function's parameters into its signature, in a syntax borrowed from C++. These function prototypes let the compiler check every call. Amendment 1 in 1995 added wide-character support, and the second edition of K&R, published in 1988, described the language as it was being standardized.
nodes.sleeper: C89 is probably the C you remember: comments only as /* */, declarations at the top of a block, int main() and char * strings. The standard has since been revised in 1999, 2011, 2018 and 2024.

refs.label: Ritchie, The Development of the C Language

nodes.title: Visual Basic
nodes.short: Microsoft's drag-and-drop BASIC for Windows, released in May 1991. Classic VB ended with VB6 in 1998, and the .NET version is frozen by policy.
nodes.long: Visual Basic 1.0 was released for Windows in May 1991 at a trade show in Atlanta. According to secondary accounts, Alan Cooper's company Tripod built a drag-and-drop form generator that Microsoft contracted under the code name Ruby, and Microsoft combined it with an embedded BASIC engine. You drew the controls on a form and attached BASIC code to events such as a button click, the visual, event-driven style that Delphi and, later, C# with Windows Forms shared. VB6 arrived in 1998 and mainstream support ended in 2005; Microsoft still supports the VB6 runtime for the lifetime of each Windows version, but not the IDE. Visual Basic .NET followed in 2002. Microsoft's strategy page now says Visual Basic will keep a stable design, adopt a consumption-only approach, avoid new syntax and not be extended to new workloads.

code.text:
' Runs when the user clicks the button named Command1
Private Sub Command1_Click()
    Label1.Caption = "Hello, world"
End Sub

refs.label: Microsoft Learn, Visual Basic language strategy
Microsoft Learn, Support statement for Visual Basic 6.0

nodes.title: R
nodes.short: A statistics language by Ihaka and Gentleman, announced in 1993 and modeled on S. Its CRAN archive holds more than 25,000 packages.
nodes.long: Ihaka wrote that R began as an experiment in using the methods of Lisp implementors to build a small testbed for a statistical environment, and that early on the team chose an S-like syntax. R is in effect a different implementation of S, the Bell Laboratories statistics language of John Chambers and colleagues. Binaries went to Statlib with a small announcement on the s-news mailing list in August 1993, and the source was released under the GNU GPL in June 1995. A statistical model takes one line, as in the sample below. CRAN, the package archive, listed 25,284 packages on 1 October 2026. TIOBE ranks R 9th in September 2026, up from 13th a year earlier, and 4.9 percent of Stack Overflow 2025 respondents use it.

code.text:
# R: a linear regression in one line
print(coef(lm(mpg ~ wt, data = mtcars)))
# prints (Intercept) 37.285126 and wt -5.344472

refs.label: Ihaka, R: Past and Future History

nodes.title: Templates and the STL
nodes.short: Templates let C++ code work for any type. Alexander Stepanov's Standard Template Library, accepted in 1994, supplied generic containers, iterators and algorithms.
nodes.long: Templates, accepted by the C++ committee in 1990 and first shipped in Cfront 3.0 in October 1991, let one function or class definition work for many types. The Standard Template Library (STL), designed by Alexander Stepanov, then at HP Labs, applied them to containers, iterators and algorithms, so that an algorithm such as max_element is written once and works on many container types. Stroustrup learned of it in late 1993, found it very odd, even ugly and verbose, then judged it met all but one of his twelve criteria for a container library; the committee accepted it in 1994 and it joined the 1998 standard. Templates had a cost: a small mistake could produce spectacularly long and unhelpful error messages, which concepts in C++20 largely fixed. The export keyword, meant to allow separate compilation of templates, was standardized in 1998, implemented by one vendor, and later dropped.
nodes.sleeper: In 1990 C++ had no standard library to speak of. The STL arrived in 1994 and the first ISO standard in 1998, so containers such as vector and algorithms such as sort are now ordinary parts of the language.

refs.label: Stroustrup, Evolving a language in and for the real world: C++ 1991-2006

nodes.title: Delphi
nodes.short: Borland's visual Object Pascal for Windows, released 14 February 1995 with Anders Hejlsberg as chief architect. Now Embarcadero's RAD Studio, still maintained.
nodes.long: Delphi 1.0 was released on 14 February 1995 as the successor to Turbo Pascal for Windows, with Anders Hejlsberg as chief architect. It let developers build Windows interfaces visually in Object Pascal, a descendant of Wirth's Pascal with classes, constructors and destructors, properties and method pointers. Its Visual Component Library, VCL, supported rapid application development, and Delphi kept a loyal Windows line-of-business base. Hejlsberg left Borland for Microsoft in 1996, and Embarcadero acquired the product line in 2008. RAD Studio 13.2, announced in September 2026, targets Windows, macOS, iOS, Android and Linux, with VCL for Windows and FireMonkey for cross-platform interfaces. TIOBE ranked Delphi/Object Pascal 13th in September 2026, and 2.5% of Stack Overflow's 2025 respondents said they use it. Free Pascal and Lazarus are open-source implementations.

nodes.title: Ruby
nodes.short: Yukihiro Matsumoto's 1995 language, designed to feel natural to write. Rails brought it a large audience from 2004; it is now mature rather than growing.
nodes.long: Yukihiro Matsumoto, known as Matz, released Ruby publicly in 1995, blending parts of Perl, Smalltalk, Eiffel, Ada and Lisp. The official site says he tried to make Ruby natural, not simple, and that like Smalltalk everything in Ruby is an object, with blocks, iterators and meta-classes. The Rails framework, extracted by David Heinemeier Hansson from Basecamp and first released in July 2004, made Ruby a web favorite on the principles of programmer happiness and convention over configuration. Ruby 4.0.0 shipped on 25 December 2025 with the new ZJIT compiler, and a major release arrives each December. The decline is relative: TIOBE ranked Ruby 12th in 2016 and 22nd in 2026, Stack Overflow 2025 usage is 6.4 percent, and RedMonk still ranks it 9th.
nodes.sleeper: Rails (2004) set the pattern for convention-based web frameworks. On 27 July 2026 W3Techs reported that JavaScript had overtaken Ruby as the second most used server-side language, behind PHP.

nodes.title: CSS
nodes.short: Cascading Style Sheets describe how a page looks: layout, fonts and colors. Dating from 1994 to 1996, CSS separates appearance from HTML's structure.
nodes.long: CSS, Cascading Style Sheets, says how a web page looks, with layout, fonts and colors, while HTML says what is on it and JavaScript what it does; its origins date to 1994 to 1996. Ethan Marcotte's May 2010 article in A List Apart joined flexible grids and CSS media queries into responsive design, so one page adapts from phone to desktop, and Bootstrap spread the idea in 2011. When WebAssembly became a W3C Recommendation on 5 December 2019, the W3C called it the fourth language for the Web, after HTML, CSS and JavaScript. RedMonk's January 2026 ranking places CSS 7th, tied with C++, and Stack Overflow's 2025 survey counts HTML and CSS together at 61.9 percent of respondents and 66.6 percent of people learning to code.

refs.label: Marcotte, Responsive Web Design (A List Apart)
W3C: WebAssembly becomes a W3C Recommendation

nodes.title: PowerShell
nodes.short: Microsoft's shell and scripting language. Jeffrey Snover's 2002 design passes .NET objects through pipes instead of text; it went open source in 2016.
nodes.long: PowerShell began as Jeffrey Snover's Monad Manifesto of 8 August 2002, which argued that integrating tools through text requires clumsy, lossy, imprecise text manipulation utilities and proposed building administrative automation on the .NET platform. PowerShell 1.0 appeared on 14 November 2006. It keeps the pipe, but what flows through it are .NET objects, not lines of text. Microsoft open-sourced it on 18 August 2016, and cross-platform PowerShell now runs on Windows, Linux and macOS, while Windows PowerShell 5.1 is supported through Windows support channels. PowerShell 7.6.6, a long-term-support release, shipped on 8 September 2026. In Stack Overflow's 2025 survey 23.2 percent of respondents used it, RedMonk ranks it 17th and TIOBE ranks it 32nd.
nodes.sleeper: If you remember DOS batch files, PowerShell is what Windows administrators use instead. It pipes .NET objects rather than text, and since 2016 it also runs on Linux and macOS.

nodes.title: Clojure
nodes.short: Rich Hickey's Lisp for the Java virtual machine, built around immutable data structures and designed for concurrency.
nodes.long: Clojure is a Lisp that runs on the Java virtual machine and calls Java libraries directly. Its rationale page describes it as a Lisp for functional programming, symbiotic with an established platform and designed for concurrency: Clojure is the language and the JVM is the platform. Its data structures are immutable and persistent, so adding an item to a vector yields a new vector and leaves the old one unchanged, and it offers software transactional memory and agents for shared state. Rich Hickey designed it, and it appeared around 2007. Clojure stays small: Compiler Explorer offers version 1.12.3, and TIOBE lists it only in the unranked 51 to 100 band.

code.text:
;; Clojure: vectors are persistent, so conj returns a new vector
(def v [1 2 3])
(def w (conj v 4))
(println v w)   ; prints [1 2 3] [1 2 3 4]

nodes.title: C++11 and Modern C++
nodes.short: The 2011 revision that modernized C++: auto, lambdas, move semantics, smart pointers and a threading memory model. New standards have come every three years since.
nodes.long: C++11, approved by ISO on 12 August 2011, is the second major version of C++ and, according to cppreference, the most important update since C++98; it was called C++0x because it was expected before 2010. It added auto and decltype, lambda expressions, rvalue references and move semantics, constexpr, nullptr, range-based for loops, variadic templates, override and final, a multithreaded memory model, and a library that absorbed much of TR1 and Boost, including threads and smart pointers. Smart pointers such as unique_ptr, which replaced the old auto_ptr (removed in C++17), tie the release of memory to scope, the RAII idiom. New versions then came every three years: C++14, C++17, C++20 with concepts, modules, coroutines and ranges, C++23 and C++26. Herb Sutter, an advocate, calls C++11 the last big and impactful release before C++26.

refs.label: Sutter, C++26 is done: trip report, March 2026

nodes.title: Kotlin
nodes.short: JetBrains' concise, safer language for the Java virtual machine. Google made Android Kotlin-first in 2019, and Kotlin became its default language.
nodes.long: JetBrains started Kotlin in 2010, kept it open source from early on and released version 1.0 on 15 February 2016, billing it as a pragmatic language for the JVM and Android that combines object-oriented and functional features and focuses on interoperability, safety, clarity and tooling. Google announced official Android support on 17 May 2017 and said at Google I/O 2019 that Android development would be increasingly Kotlin-first; Android's site claims over 60 percent of professional Android developers use it. Classes are closed to inheritance by default. Kotlin Multiplatform was declared stable in November 2023, and Kotlin 2.0 (May 2024) brought the K2 compiler. Stack Overflow 2025 usage is 10.8 percent, RedMonk ranks Kotlin 14th, and TIOBE ranks it 26th.
nodes.sleeper: Java held Android until Kotlin. Since Google's 2019 Kotlin-first stance it is the default for new Android code, and with Kotlin Multiplatform it also targets iOS and the server.

refs.label: Android Developers Blog: Android Announces Support for Kotlin

nodes.title: Julia
nodes.short: A 2012 language built so scientists need not prototype in a slow language and rewrite in a fast one. TIOBE says it is fast but has not broken through.
nodes.long: Julia was announced on 14 February 2012 with a blunt rationale: because we are greedy. Its creators were power Matlab users and Lisp hackers who wanted the speed of C with the dynamism of Ruby, true macros like Lisp and familiar mathematical notation like Matlab. Their paper says Julia questions the idea that high-level dynamic programs have to be slow and that one must prototype in one language and then rewrite in another for speed or deployment, the two-language problem. Julia picks a method by the types of its arguments, called multiple dispatch. Version 1.0 appeared on 8 August 2018. In September 2026 TIOBE ranks Julia 21st at 0.74 percent, noting that it first entered the top 20 in summer 2023 and that it is fast, but there are faster languages.

code.text:
# Julia: multiple dispatch picks a method by argument type
f(x::Int) = "int"
f(x::Float64) = "float"
println(f(1), " ", f(1.0)); println([1, 2, 3] .^ 2)   # prints int float, then [1, 4, 9]

refs.label: Bezanson et al., Julia: A Fresh Approach to Numerical Computing

nodes.title: Swift
nodes.short: Apple's compiled, memory-safe language that displaced Objective-C. Chris Lattner began it in 2010; it was announced in June 2014 and open-sourced in December 2015.
nodes.long: Chris Lattner started work on Swift at Apple in July 2010, building much of the basic language in secrecy until others joined in late 2011. Apple announced it on 2 June 2014 and launched the open-source project and Swift.org on 3 December 2015, with a Linux port. Swift is compiled and statically typed, and its book says variables are always initialized, array indices and integer overflow are checked, optionals make nil handling explicit, and memory is managed automatically by reference counting, not by a tracing collector. Swift 5 made the binary interface stable on Apple platforms in 2019. Swift 6.3 (March 2026) added an official Android SDK, and 6.4 (September 2026) improved WebAssembly and embedded use. TIOBE ranks Swift 18th, up from 25th a year earlier, and RedMonk ranks it 11th.
nodes.sleeper: If you knew Apple's languages from the Mac and NeXT era, the one to know now is Swift. It replaced Objective-C as the main language for Apple platforms and also targets Linux, Windows, Android, WebAssembly and embedded systems.

nodes.title: Zig
nodes.short: Andrew Kelley's C-like language with compile-time execution (comptime), explicit allocators and a built-in C compiler. Announced in 2016, still pre-1.0 in 2026.
nodes.long: Andrew Kelley first announced Zig on 8 February 2016, and the nonprofit Zig Software Foundation funds it. It keeps C's explicitness and adds compile-time execution: ziglang.org promises no hidden control flow, no hidden memory allocations, and no preprocessor or macros, so code that allocates must be handed an allocator. Errors are values returned to the caller, and a defer statement releases a resource when its scope ends. A Zig download also works as a zero-dependency C and C++ compiler, zig cc, built on Clang, that cross-compiles out of the box. The current release, 0.16.0 of 13 April 2026, is still pre-1.0 and changes its APIs between releases. Adopters include TigerBeetle, a financial database, and Ghostty, a terminal emulator.
nodes.sleeper: Bun, a flagship Zig project from 2021, moved to Rust in 2026. Its creator, who works at Anthropic after Anthropic bought Bun, cited memory bugs but said other Zig users do not have them.

nodes.title: Syntax Tour: One Task, Many Languages
nodes.short: The same small task, summing the squares of the odd numbers from 1 to 10, shown in about forty languages. Almost all were run on real compilers; the answer is 165.
nodes.long: One task makes the differences between languages visible: sum the squares of the odd numbers from 1 to 10, which is 1 + 9 + 25 + 49 + 81 = 165. It was written in about forty languages, and nearly all were executed on 30 September and 1 October 2026 using Compiler Explorer, Try It Online and Node.js. C, Pascal, Ada, COBOL, BASIC and Go use loops and mutable variables. Functional languages chain filter, map and sum, and mainstream languages now offer the same pipeline: Java, C#, Rust, Swift, Kotlin, Python and JavaScript. Prolog collects the solutions of a query, APL, J and K state the whole computation on arrays with no loop, and SQL describes the rows wanted. A COBOL program declares in advance how many digits a number may hold, with a picture clause such as PIC 9(5); only Smalltalk and Mathematica were written from documentation and not run.

code.text:
Python:   print(sum(x * x for x in range(1, 11) if x % 2 == 1))
Haskell:  main = print (sum [x * x | x <- [1 .. 10], odd x])
Clojure:  (println (->> (range 1 11) (filter odd?) (map #(* % %)) (reduce +)))
Elixir:   IO.puts(1..10 |> Enum.filter(&(rem(&1, 2) == 1)) |> Enum.map(&(&1 * &1)) |> Enum.sum())
Julia:    println(sum(x^2 for x in 1:10 if isodd(x)))
Swift:    print((1...10).filter { $0 % 2 == 1 }.map { $0 * $0 }.reduce(0, +))
APL:      ⎕←+/×⍨(2|⍳10)/⍳10
J:        echo +/ *: (#~ 2&|) 1+i.10
(each prints 165)

nodes.title: Plankalkül
nodes.short: Konrad Zuse's 1945 'Plan Calculus', designed on paper with data types down to single bits and 49 pages of chess algorithms. It stayed unpublished until 1972.
nodes.long: Plankalkül was designed by Konrad Zuse in 1945, after Allied bombs had destroyed most of his relay computers and he had moved the surviving machine to the village of Hinterstein. Knuth and Trabb Pardo say it arose purely as desk work, with no machine in view that could run its programs. Its data types ran all the way down to the bit level, with single bits, compound types, arrays and lists, a richness that did not enter programming languages again until the late 1950s, and the manuscript included 49 pages of algorithms for playing chess. Zuse's 1945 manuscript lay unpublished until 1972, with only brief excerpts printed in 1948 and 1959, so it influenced almost no one. The Computer History Museum calls it the first algorithmic programming language.

refs.label: Knuth and Trabb Pardo, The Early Development of Programming Languages (1976)
Computer History Museum, Timeline of Software and Languages

nodes.title: Short Code
nodes.short: The first high-level notation actually implemented: an interpreter for coded math formulas, suggested by John Mauchly in 1949 for the BINAC and UNIVAC.
nodes.long: Short Code was an interpreter that let a user write mathematical formulas in a coded form instead of machine instructions. John Mauchly suggested it in 1949, William Schmitt coded it for the BINAC that year and recoded it for the UNIVAC in late 1950, and J. Robert Logan revised it in January 1952. Knuth and Trabb Pardo call it the first high-level language actually to be implemented. Its write-up claimed that any mathematical equation could be evaluated by the mere expedient of writing it down, that the need for special programming had been eliminated, and that it gave a speed ratio of at least fifty to one against manual methods. That is an early case of the over-promising that later 'automatic programming' efforts repeated, and the lack of published detail suggests Short Code was not an instant success.

refs.label: Knuth and Trabb Pardo, The Early Development of Programming Languages (1976)

nodes.title: Autocode
nodes.short: Alick Glennie's 1952 formula translator for the Manchester Mark 1, credited by Knuth and Trabb Pardo as the first compiler. Brooker's cleaner one came in 1955.
nodes.long: Autocode was written by Alick Glennie at the Royal Armament Research Establishment, Fort Halstead, for the Manchester Mark 1 in 1952. It translated formulas written in a notation of the user's choosing into Mark 1 machine code. Knuth and Trabb Pardo chose to credit Glennie with the first compiler, even though Grace Hopper's A-0 was completed first, because his system really turned algebraic statements into machine language, and they call him the unsung hero. His own reasoning was that the best notation for programs is the usual mathematical notation, because it is already known. R. A. Brooker's Mark 1 Autocode, implemented in 1955, was nearly machine-independent, spared users the work of scaling numbers and managing the two-level store, and was heavily used.

refs.label: Knuth and Trabb Pardo, The Early Development of Programming Languages (1976)

nodes.title: Speedcoding
nodes.short: John Backus's group at IBM made the 701 behave as if it had floating point and index registers. Speedcoding (1953) was easy to use but slow and memory-hungry.
nodes.long: Speedcoding was a software layer built by John Backus's group at IBM, started in January 1953 and described in a manual dated 10 September 1953. The IBM 701 had no floating-point arithmetic and no index registers, so Speedcoding made it act as though it had both: users wrote numbers in decimal floating-point notation, the system converted between decimal and binary, and it handled address modification so that one part of a program could modify another instruction. It consumed scarce memory, leaving 714 words of electrostatic storage for the user's program and data, yet it greatly reduced the time needed to write a program. Backus said programming in machine code was a pretty lousy business. His next project, a compiler for the 704, took a different route, because the 704 had built-in floating point and index registers, which was all Speedcoding was meant to supply.

refs.label: IBM Speedcoding System for the 701, manual 24-6059-0

nodes.title: PL/I
nodes.short: IBM and SHARE's 1963 attempt at one language for business, science and systems work. It never displaced FORTRAN or COBOL, but Multics was written in it.
nodes.long: PL/I (Programming Language One) was designed in 1963 by a committee drawn from IBM and SHARE, the IBM users' group, and announced in 1964. It was meant to serve business, scientific and systems programming, and it drew on FORTRAN for syntax, ALGOL 60 for block structure and COBOL for record structures. Its size was the problem. Dijkstra compared using it to flying a plane with 7000 buttons, switches and handles in the cockpit, and the author of the Multics PL/I compiler warned in 1969 that compilers were far harder to build than most implementors assumed. For years the only important implementations were IBM's own and the one for Multics, whose operating system was written in EPL, a large subset of PL/I. PL/I never displaced FORTRAN or COBOL, a standard appeared in 1976, and IBM still sells Enterprise PL/I for z/OS.
nodes.sleeper: IBM no longer offers a PL/I compiler for Windows or AIX. The language survives on z/OS mainframes, and TIOBE lists it only among the languages ranked 51 to 100.

nodes.title: BCPL
nodes.short: Martin Richards's simple, typeless language (designed 1966, first run in 1967), the ancestor of B and C. C++ later revived its // comments.
nodes.long: Martin Richards designed BCPL in 1966 as a research student at Cambridge, influenced by the committee-designed CPL, and first implemented it in spring 1967 while at MIT. It is simple and typeless: it has only one kind of value, the machine word. BCPL was used for the OS6 operating system at Oxford and for parts of Xerox PARC's Alto work, and Bell Labs people knew it because the MIT CTSS system on which Richards worked was used to develop Multics. Its file-inclusion mechanism, like PL/I's, was a model for C's #include. Ken Thompson squeezed BCPL into 8K bytes of memory to make B, and Dennis Ritchie turned B into C. In 1993 Ritchie noted that C++ had resurrected the BCPL comment convention, the // comment.

refs.label: Ritchie, The Development of the C Language

nodes.title: B
nodes.short: Ken Thompson's 1969-70 stripped-down BCPL for the first Unix on a PDP-7. It had a single data type, the word, and was reworked into C by Dennis Ritchie.
nodes.long: After Bell Labs withdrew from the Multics project in 1969, Ken Thompson's group wanted a comfortable computing environment, and Unix began on a little-used PDP-7 minicomputer. Doug McIlroy quickly re-created the TMG compiler-writing language there, which challenged Thompson to provide a systems programming language; after a rapidly scuttled attempt at Fortran he wrote B. Ritchie summarized it as BCPL squeezed into 8K bytes of memory and filtered through Thompson's brain, or C without types. B had one data type, the word, and its documents describe it as intended for primarily non-numeric work such as system programming, with a small, unrestrictive syntax that is easy to compile. The byte-addressed PDP-11 exposed its weaknesses, so in 1971 Ritchie added a character type and wrote a compiler that emitted machine code. That version, NB for new B, grew into C.

refs.label: Ritchie, The Development of the C Language

nodes.title: Forth
nodes.short: Charles Moore's stack-based, extensible, interactive language: operands first, operator last, and new words that extend the language. A niche in firmware.
nodes.long: Forth is a stack-based language: you write the operands first and the operator last, so 2 3 + 4 * leaves 20 on the stack, and you define new words that become part of the language. Charles Moore wrote orbit programs at the Smithsonian Astrophysical Observatory and built a simple interpreter to read cards that controlled the program, so that he did not have to recompile it; he co-founded FORTH, Inc. in 1971. ANSI Forth dates from 1994, the same year Sun's Open Boot evolved into Open Firmware (IEEE 1275), the predominant boot-level plug-and-play firmware on non-Intel PCI systems from Apple, IBM and others as well as Sun. Forth has stayed a niche language for embedded systems and boot firmware and is not in TIOBE's top 100.

code.text:
: sumsq  0  10 1 do  i 2 mod if  i dup * +  then  loop ;
sumsq . cr   \ prints 165 (sum of the squares of the odd numbers 1 to 9)

nodes.title: C Structs, Unions and Function Pointers
nodes.short: How C groups data and passes behavior: structs with padding, unions that overlay bytes, enums, and function pointers, the callback tool behind qsort.
nodes.long: A struct groups named fields in declaration order; you reach a field with a dot, or through a pointer with an arrow, so e->id is shorthand for (*e).id. The compiler may insert padding to align fields: a struct holding a 16-byte name, a 4-byte int and two doubles takes 40 bytes rather than 36, because 4 bytes of padding follow the int. A union overlays its members on the same bytes, so the bit pattern of the float 1.0 can be read back as the integer 0x3f800000, and an enum names integer constants. Ritchie wanted structs partly to describe a Unix directory entry, and that need led to the rule that array names turn into pointers. A function pointer holds the address of code and is how C does callbacks: the library's qsort sorts any array by calling a comparison function you supply, and the same technique, built by hand, is what C++ virtual functions later automated.

refs.label: Ritchie, The Development of the C Language

nodes.title: Scheme
nodes.short: A small, clean Lisp dialect from MIT. Brendan Eich was recruited in 1995 to put Scheme in the browser, and its first-class functions ended up in JavaScript.
nodes.long: Scheme is a compact dialect of Lisp described at MIT by Sussman and Steele in 1975 (MIT AI Memo 349). Like Lisp it writes programs as nested parenthesized lists and treats functions as ordinary values. Its best-known influence runs through JavaScript. Brendan Eich says Netscape recruited him with the promise of doing Scheme in the browser; management then required the language to look like Java, which ruled Scheme out, but he kept Scheme-style first-class functions as one of the main ingredients. The sample below, run under the Guile implementation, filters, squares and sums a list. TIOBE lists Scheme only in its unranked 51 to 100 band in September 2026.

code.text:
;; Scheme (GNU Guile); filter and iota come from SRFI-1
(use-modules (srfi srfi-1))
(display (apply + (map (lambda (x) (* x x)) (filter odd? (iota 10 1)))))
;; prints 165

nodes.title: AWK
nodes.short: A Bell Labs text-processing language from 1977, named for Aho, Weinberger and Kernighan. Like grep and sed, it is a filter built to sit in a Unix pipe.
nodes.long: AWK was created at Bell Labs by Alfred Aho, Peter Weinberger and Brian Kernighan, and first appeared in 1977; its name comes from their surnames. It is a data-driven language for text processing, and like sed and grep it is a filter, designed to be composed with the pipe that Unix gained in 1972 at Doug McIlroy's urging. The Unix text tools grep, sed and awk all came out of Bell Labs between 1973 and 1977. AWK is also one of the ancestors of Perl, whose own FAQ says the language derives to a lesser extent from sed, awk and the Unix shell.

nodes.title: Modula-2 and Oberon
nodes.short: Niklaus Wirth's successors to Pascal: Modula-2 (designed from 1978), built on modules, and Oberon (1987), a minimal language and system. Influential, little used.
nodes.long: Niklaus Wirth followed Pascal with Modula-2, designed in 1978 to 1980 at ETH Zurich and published in 1979 by his own account, and with Oberon in 1987. Their main contribution was the module: a separately compiled unit that hides its internals and exports a defined interface. Wirth said modularization was the principal idea behind Modula-2, motivated by Xerox's Mesa, itself a descendant of Pascal, and that Ada adopted the idea as well. He also led construction of the Lilith workstation (1980) and the Ceres workstations at ETH, and his web page still lists Project Oberon, 2013 Edition. Go's own FAQ credits the Pascal, Modula and Oberon family for its declarations and packages. Neither language appears in TIOBE's September 2026 top 100, although GCC includes a Modula-2 front end.

refs.label: Niklaus Wirth, ETH Zurich home page
Wirth, A Brief History of Software Engineering (2008)

nodes.title: Fourth-Generation Languages
nodes.short: A 1980s marketing label for high-level application tools that promised software without programmers. They did not end programming, but some of their tools survived.
nodes.long: Fourth-generation languages, called 4GLs, were high-level tools that vendors in the 1980s promoted as ending the need for programmers, and James Martin's 1982 book Application Development Without Programmers is the emblematic title. The 4GL and 5GL labels were buzzwords of the 1980s and 1990s, and a 2017 Computerwoche article called 4GL a rather vague term used mainly for marketing. In 1994 Bill Curtis said of structured programming, CASE and the third to fifth generation languages that many of the promised technologies had not been delivered. What lasted were domain tools used alongside programmers, among them SQL, spreadsheets, report writers and scripting. The label itself is dead, and low-code platforms now trace their roots back to 4GLs and the rapid-application-development tools of the 1990s.
nodes.sleeper: The 4GL label is gone, but the promise returns each decade: rapid application development in the 1990s, low-code platforms from 2014, AI coding assistants now. Each wave widened who could build software without removing professional developers.

nodes.title: Common Lisp
nodes.short: The large, standardized member of the Lisp family. It took shape in the 1980s and became an ANSI standard in 1994; the Lisp family is a niche today.
nodes.long: McCarthy wrote in 1979 that no organization had ever tried to propagate Lisp and that there had never been an attempt to agree on a standard. Common Lisp, which took shape in the 1980s, is the large, standardized member of the family, and ANSI approved a standard for it in 1994. It keeps Lisp's parenthesized prefix syntax and adds a big library: the sum of the squares of the odd numbers from 1 to 10 combines loop, remove-if-not, mapcar, lambda and reduce, and prints 165 under GNU CLISP. TIOBE ranks Lisp 43rd in September 2026 at 0.42 percent, and the Stack Overflow 2025 survey found 2.4 percent of respondents using it.

refs.label: McCarthy, History of Lisp: beyond LISP 1.5

nodes.title: Eiffel
nodes.short: Bertrand Meyer's object-oriented language built around Design by Contract: preconditions, postconditions and class invariants that are checked as the program runs.
nodes.long: Eiffel is an object-oriented language designed by Bertrand Meyer and tied to Design by Contract, a method in which the expected behavior of every component is explicitly defined, checked and enforced. A precondition is what a caller must guarantee, a postcondition is what the routine promises in return, and a class invariant must always hold. Meyer's 1992 article 'Applying Design by Contract' in IEEE Computer argued that reliability matters even more in object-oriented programming than elsewhere and showed how to cut bugs by building components on carefully designed contracts. The idea spread: Ada 2012 added a Pre aspect, and C++26 has contract assertions. Ritchie listed Eiffel among the languages that treat C as a portable assembly language, compiling to it. Eiffel itself is niche and is not in TIOBE's top 100.

code.text:
half (x: INTEGER): INTEGER
    require
        even: x \\ 2 = 0
    do
        Result := x // 2
    ensure
        exact: Result * 2 = x
    end

refs.label: Meyer, Applying Design by Contract, IEEE Computer, October 1992

nodes.title: Mathematica
nodes.short: Wolfram's commercial system for symbolic and numeric mathematics, first released in June 1988. Its language works by rewriting expressions according to rules.
nodes.long: Wolfram's revision history lists Mathematica 1.0 as the initial release in June 1988 and Mathematica 15 in June 2026, with 15.0.1 following in July 2026. It is a commercial symbolic and numeric system whose language rewrites expressions by rules. Function calls use square brackets: the sum of the squares of the odd numbers from 1 to 10 is written Total[Select[Range[10], OddQ]^2], which should give 165. Stephen Wolfram describes a notebook as an interactive document that freely mixes code, results, graphics, text and everything else. Jack Dongarra's linear-algebra libraries are incorporated into Mathematica, as they are into MATLAB, Maple, GNU Octave, R and SciPy. TIOBE does not list Mathematica in its top 100.

nodes.title: J and K
nodes.short: Descendants of APL. J, by Iverson and Roger Hui, appeared in 1990 and uses plain ASCII; K, by Arthur Whitney, is proprietary and underlies the kdb+ database.
nodes.long: J was designed by Kenneth Iverson and Roger Hui and first appeared in 1990; it is now free software under the GPLv3, and J9.7 was released on 14 April 2026. K was designed by Arthur Whitney, first appeared in 1993 and is proprietary, sold by KX Systems; it underlies the kdb+ column database. Both keep APL's idea that one expression operates on a whole array, but their programs use ordinary ASCII characters, as in the samples below, which list the primes up to 20 in J and average five numbers in K without a loop. In TIOBE's September 2026 list neither J nor K is ranked, though Q, the language of kdb+, appears in the unranked 51 to 100 band.

code.text:
NB. J: primes up to 20 prints 2 3 5 7 11 13 17 19
echo (#~ 1&p:) 1+i.20
/ K (the oK interpreter): mean of 3 1 4 1 5 prints 2.8
{(+/x)%#x}3 1 4 1 5

nodes.title: Lua
nodes.short: A small embeddable scripting language from Brazil's Tecgraf, created in 1993. Games from World of Warcraft to Roblox's Luau use it as an extension language.
nodes.long: Lua was created in 1993 at Tecgraf, a group at PUC-Rio in Brazil, by Roberto Ierusalimschy, Luiz Henrique de Figueiredo and Waldemar Celes. It grew out of two in-house data-description languages, DEL and Sol, built for Petrobras engineering programs, and its name is Portuguese for moon. The authors explain that from 1977 to 1992 Brazil's market reserve put strong trade barriers on computer hardware and software, so Tecgraf's clients could not buy customized software from abroad and Tecgraf built its own tools. Lua is dynamically typed, garbage collected, MIT-licensed and designed to be embedded in a host program. Adobe Photoshop Lightroom, World of Warcraft and Angry Birds use it, and lua.org calls it the leading scripting language in games. Stack Overflow 2025 usage is 9.2 percent and TIOBE ranks it 31st.

refs.label: Ierusalimschy et al., The Evolution of Lua (HOPL III)

nodes.title: OCaml
nodes.short: INRIA's ML dialect that added objects and a fast native compiler. OCaml 5.0 (2022) rewrote the runtime to allow shared-memory parallelism.
nodes.long: OCaml is the French branch of the ML family. Xavier Leroy designed Caml Light, a bytecode interpreter written in C, in 1990 and 1991, and Objective Caml followed in 1996 as the first language to combine the full power of object-oriented programming with an ML-style polymorphic type system and type inference. Caml originally stood for Categorical Abstract Machine Language, and the official name became OCaml in 2011. OCaml 5.0, released in 2022, was a complete rewrite of the language runtime that removed the global garbage-collector lock and added effect handlers, which makes shared-memory parallelism possible. TIOBE ranks OCaml 38th in September 2026 at 0.43 percent, with Caml itself 28th, and 1.2 percent of Stack Overflow 2025 respondents use it.

code.text:
(* OCaml: a variant type and pattern matching *)
type shape = Square of int | Rect of int * int
let area = function
  | Square s -> s * s
  | Rect (w, h) -> w * h
let () = print_int (area (Square 3) + area (Rect (2, 4)))   (* prints 17 *)

nodes.title: ECMAScript
nodes.short: The standard behind JavaScript (ECMA-262), first published in 1997. After the failed ES4, yearly editions since ES2015 turned it into an engineered language.
nodes.long: ECMAScript is the standard that defines JavaScript, published as ECMA-262 by Ecma International and developed by its committee TC39. The 1st edition came in June 1997, the 2nd in August 1998 and the 3rd in December 1999; a 4th edition was never published. The 5th followed in December 2009, 5.1 in June 2011 and the 6th, ES2015, in June 2015, with a new edition every June since: ES2025 was the 16th and ES2026 the 17th. The ES4 split, in which TC39 divided between backers of ES4 and ES3.1, ended at a July 2008 meeting in Oslo with Harmony, which shelved packages, namespaces and early binding. ES2015 added classes, modules, iterators, generators, arrow functions, let and const. TC39 now moves proposals through stages.

code.text:
// JavaScript (Node.js v22): arrow functions arrived with ES2015
console.log(Array.from({length: 10}, (_, i) => i + 1).filter(x => x % 2 === 1).map(x => x * x).reduce((a, b) => a + b, 0));   // prints 165

nodes.title: C99, C11, C23 and C2y
nodes.short: C's later standards: C99, C11, C17, C23 (published 2024) and C2y in draft. They add bool, fixed-width integers, threads, nullptr, constexpr and #embed.
nodes.long: C99 (December 1999) added _Bool, long long, fixed-width integers in stdint.h, restrict, compound literals, variable length arrays and designated initializers, borrowed inline, // comments and declarations inside for from C++, and removed implicit int. C11 (December 2011) added a thread-aware memory model with threads.h and stdatomic.h, _Generic and static assertions, removed gets, and made variable length arrays optional. C17 fixed defects and added no major features. C23 (ISO/IEC 9899:2024) made bool, true and false keywords, added nullptr, constexpr, typeof, auto type inference, #embed, bit-precise integers and attributes, made two's complement the only signed representation, and removed K&R-style definitions. C2y is in draft (N3886, May 2026), with named loops, if declarations, case ranges and _Countof among its additions, while defer is a separate technical specification.

nodes.title: F#
nodes.short: Microsoft's functional-first language for .NET, released near-silently in 2002. Its asynchronous workflows later shaped async/await in C#.
nodes.long: Don Syme's history describes F# as one of several responses by advocates of strongly typed functional programming to the object-oriented tidal wave of the mid-1990s. Microsoft began internal projects in 1997 that became .NET and C#, which led to .NET generics in 1998 and to F# in 2002, and the first release was made near-silently on 4 June 2002. F# runs on the .NET runtime. Its asynchronous workflows, seeded around a 2007 visit to EPFL, were still influencing C# years later in async/await (C# 5.0) and async sequences (C# 8.0). F# remains small: Stack Overflow's 2025 survey found 1.3 percent of respondents using it, and TIOBE lists it only in the 51 to 100 band.

code.text:
// F#: filter, map and sum chained with the pipe operator
[ 1 .. 10 ] |> List.filter (fun x -> x % 2 = 1) |> List.map (fun x -> x * x) |> List.sum |> printfn "%d"   // prints 165

refs.label: Syme, The Early History of F# (HOPL IV)

nodes.title: Scala
nodes.short: A Java-platform language from EPFL that fuses object-oriented and functional styles. Few developers use it as their main language, yet it tops salary rankings.
nodes.long: Scala is a language for the Java platform that fuses object-oriented and functional programming. It came from Martin Odersky's group at EPFL, with a first release in 2004. Its homepage shows immutable collections, derived JSON codecs, Scala.js and pattern matching on enums. Scala 3 shipped on 14 May 2021 after eight years of work and 28,000 commits, and Scala 3.9.0 is both the latest and the long-term-support release in September 2026, maintained by the Scala Center at EPFL and VirtusLab with support from JetBrains. In JetBrains' 2025 survey only 2 percent of developers use Scala as a primary language, yet it leads the salary ranking at 38 percent of top-paid developers. TIOBE ranks it 44th.

nodes.title: Dart
nodes.short: Google's language, announced in 2011 as a structured alternative to JavaScript, dropped from Chrome plans in 2015, then found a second life as Flutter's language.
nodes.long: Lars Bak announced Dart on 10 October 2011 as a class-based, optionally typed language for web applications, running on a native virtual machine or compiled to JavaScript. His earlier work included Beta, Self, Strongtalk, Sun's HotSpot, OOVM Smalltalk and V8. On 25 March 2015 Bak and Kasper Lund wrote that the team had decided not to integrate the Dart VM into Chrome and would focus on compiling Dart to JavaScript. The language then found its audience in Flutter, Google's open-source framework for building apps for several platforms from a single codebase, which reached 1.0 on 4 December 2018. Stack Overflow 2025 usage is 5.9 percent, RedMonk placed Dart 18th in January 2026, ahead of Rust, and TIOBE ranks it 41st.

refs.label: Dart team: Dart for the entire web (2015)
Google Code Blog: Dart, a language for structured web programming (2011)

nodes.title: Elixir
nodes.short: A modern language on the Erlang virtual machine, with a pipe operator and Erlang's fault tolerance. Stack Overflow's 2025 survey rated it among the most admired.
nodes.long: Elixir runs on the Erlang virtual machine and describes itself as built on decades of Erlang reliability and fault tolerance. José Valim created it around 2011. Its pipe operator, written |>, feeds the result of one call into the next, which is how the sample below chains filter, map and sum. Its site lists Discord, Adobe, Apple, Spotify, Supabase, the BBC, Change.org, PagerDuty and Royal Bank of Canada among users, though that is a marketing list, not an audit. Elixir v1.20 came out on 3 June 2026, and its packages come from Hex, which listed 26,315 packages on 30 September 2026. In Stack Overflow's 2025 survey 2.7 percent of respondents used Elixir, and 65.9 percent of its users wanted to keep using it, the third-highest score among languages.

code.text:
# Elixir: the pipe operator |> feeds each result into the next call
IO.puts(1..10 |> Enum.filter(&(rem(&1, 2) == 1)) |> Enum.map(&(&1 * &1)) |> Enum.sum())   # prints 165

nodes.title: SPARK
nodes.short: A proof-oriented dialect of Ada. Its GNATprove tool can prove programs free of run-time errors; users include aircraft engines, air-traffic systems and railways.
nodes.long: SPARK began at the University of Southampton in 1987, with Bernard Carré and Trevor Jennings and sponsorship from the UK Ministry of Defence, and was later associated with Praxis Critical Systems, which became Altran Praxis. AdaCore describes SPARK as a dialect of Ada that removes the Ada features leading to undefined behavior and extends Ada's support for formal specification. Its GNATprove tool proves the absence of run-time errors using the provers CVC4, Z3 and Alt-Ergo. Uses listed include Rolls-Royce Trent engines, the Eurofighter Typhoon, the UK iFACTS air-traffic system and rail signaling, and AdaCore's home page promotes an NVIDIA case study on security-critical software. SPARK is the proof-oriented survivor of the Ada effort that began with a Pentagon mandate in 1983.

nodes.title: Carbon
nodes.short: Google's experimental C++ successor, announced in 2022: C++ interoperability with safer fundamentals. Its own README says it is not ready for use.
nodes.long: Chandler Carruth of Google announced Carbon at CppNorth in Toronto on 19 July 2022 as a C++ successor. Its README calls it an experimental successor to C++ that is fast and works with C++, with safer fundamentals and an incremental path toward a memory-safe subset, and it states plainly that Carbon is not ready for use. It even tells developers who can use Go, Swift, Kotlin or Rust to do so instead. The roadmap lists potential goals of a working 0.1 language for evaluation in 2026, a finished 0.2 language in 2027 to 2028, and a 1.0 release beyond 2028. No source reviewed shows that the 0.1 milestone had shipped by the end of September 2026. Carbon is one of several attempts to move C++ codebases forward without rewriting them.

nodes.title: cppfront (Cpp2)
nodes.short: Herb Sutter's experimental compiler from 'Cpp2', a cleaner syntax, to ordinary C++. A personal experiment to test ideas for ISO C++, not a successor language.
nodes.long: cppfront is a compiler from an experimental syntax that Herb Sutter calls Cpp2 to today's C++ (Cpp1), written to prove out concepts and prototype features that can also be proposed for ISO C++. Its README says it aims to help evolve C++ itself, not to be a C++ successor. Sutter introduced it in a CppCon 2022 talk, and the latest GitHub release is v0.8.1 of 31 January 2025. Cpp2 keeps C++ semantics but changes the syntax: names come first, and one grammar covers every declaration. In a July 2026 status summary Sutter called it his personal experiment, said he deliberately did not support it as a production compiler, and said he was now concentrating on getting its features, such as metaclasses and call-site bounds checking, into ISO C++.

nodes.title: Mojo
nodes.short: Modular's Python-flavored language for AI and GPU code, from Chris Lattner. Mojo 1.0 shipped on 11 August 2026; the compiler was open-sourced a week later.
nodes.long: Mojo comes from Modular Inc., founded by Chris Lattner and Tim Davis. Lattner was earlier the architect of LLVM, Clang and Swift. Mojo was first publicly testable in May 2023, its standard library was open-sourced in March 2024, Mojo 1.0.0 was released on 11 August 2026, and the compiler was open-sourced under Apache 2.0 on 18 August 2026. Its website calls it the systems language for the AI era: Python-like syntax with static types and ownership rules, GPU kernels written in the same language with no CUDA or separate language, and Python interoperability. Secondary sources report that the original aim of being a full superset of Python has been abandoned or postponed indefinitely. It targets AI and GPU kernels rather than operating systems, runs on Linux and macOS, and was not in TIOBE's top 50 in September 2026.

code.text:
def main():
    print("Hello, world!")

nodes.title: Gleam
nodes.short: A typed functional language for the Erlang virtual machine, at 1.0 since March 2024. Stack Overflow's 2025 survey ranked it the second most admired language.
nodes.long: Gleam is a typed functional language that runs on the Erlang virtual machine, so it can share the platform's lightweight processes and the Hex package ecosystem with Elixir and Erlang. It reached version 1.0 in March 2024. In Stack Overflow's 2025 survey it was the second most admired language at 70.8 percent, behind Rust at 72.4 percent and ahead of Elixir and Zig, although that survey reports no usage figure for it. A 2026 review of new languages groups Gleam with Mojo, Zig and Carbon as promising but unproven, and found no adoption data for any of them.

nodes.title: C++26
nodes.short: The 2026 C++ standard, technically complete in March 2026: reflection, contracts, a hardened standard library, and no undefined behavior for uninitialized reads.
nodes.long: On 28 March 2026, at a meeting in London Croydon, the ISO committee completed the technical work on C++26. The plenary vote to ship it was 114 in favor, 12 opposed and 3 abstaining, with the opposition mainly over contracts. Its headline features are static reflection (P2996), contracts (P2900), a hardened standard library that bounds-checks common operations on vector, span and string, and erroneous behavior, which means that reading an uninitialized local variable is no longer undefined behavior. It also adds std::execution, #embed and pack indexing, among much else. At the end of September 2026 isocpp.org still named C++23 as the current standard and no source confirmed ISO publication of C++26. GCC 16 implements reflection and contracts, while Clang's status page listed them as not yet implemented.
nodes.sleeper: C++ now gets a new standard every three years, and its answer to memory-safety criticism is hardening, not a new language. Sutter cites Apple and Google deployments of a bounds-checked standard library at about 0.3 percent average cost.

refs.label: Sutter, C++26 is done: trip report, March 2026

nodes.title: Core Programming Concepts
nodes.short: Variables, types, arrays, functions, objects, memory and concurrency: the vocabulary every language shares.
nodes.long: Once you know these ideas, a new language is mostly a new spelling. They fall into how data is named and stored, how code is organized, and how programs run at the same time.

nodes.title: Memory Management
nodes.short: How a program gets memory and gives it back: by hand, by counting, by a collector, by compiler-checked ownership, or by freeing a whole region at once.
nodes.long: Every program must decide when borrowed memory can be given back. Five answers exist: the programmer says so, as with C's malloc and free; a counter on each object says so, as in Python and Swift; a collector finds what is unreachable, as in Lisp from 1958 to 1960 and later Java; the compiler proves it from ownership rules, as in Rust; or a whole region is released at once, as with arenas. The history is a steady shift of work from the programmer to the machine, driven by the cost of memory bugs more than by speed. Chromium reports that about 70 percent of its serious security bugs are memory-safety problems.
nodes.sleeper: Automatic memory management is no longer exotic: Java made garbage collection normal in the 1990s, and Rust now offers a third path with no collector and no manual freeing. CISA's December 2023 call for memory-safe roadmaps shows the choice has become policy.

nodes.title: Type Systems
nodes.short: The rules a language uses to reject meaningless operations, such as adding a number to a customer record, either before the program runs or while it runs.
nodes.long: A type system is the set of rules a language uses to stop meaningless operations. Static languages check the rules before the program runs, dynamic languages check them as it runs, and many languages now mix the two. Robin Milner's 1978 paper proved that in a well-designed static system, well-typed programs cannot go wrong. Type inference and generics came out of ML in the 1970s and reached mainstream languages from the mid-2000s, and null is now being designed out. The evidence that static typing prevents defects is real but modest: the cleanest study found that about 15 percent of already-public JavaScript bugs could have been caught by a type checker.
nodes.sleeper: TypeScript 1.0 (April 2014) put optional types on JavaScript, and by GitHub's own contributor count it was the most used language there in August 2025. TIOBE, using a different measure, ranks it 39th.

refs.label: Milner, A Theory of Type Polymorphism in Programming (1978)
Gao, Bird and Barr, To Type or Not to Type (ICSE 2017)

nodes.title: Concurrency and Parallelism
nodes.short: Doing several things in overlapping time. Threads and locks, actors, channels and async/await are the main ways to structure it, and none has won outright.
nodes.long: Concurrency means structuring a program as several activities in progress at once, while parallelism means using several processors at the same instant. The models differ on whether activities share memory, as threads and locks do, exchange only messages, as Erlang's actors and Go's channels do, or take turns on one thread, as async/await does. Shared memory brings deadlocks and race conditions. Herb Sutter's 2005 essay "The Free Lunch Is Over" argued that clock speeds had stopped rising, so only concurrent programs would keep getting faster, and Amdahl's law limits the gain. No single model has won.
nodes.sleeper: Before about 2003 programs got faster whenever the clock did. Chips now add cores instead, so concurrency is the main route to speed, and CPython 3.14 (2025) officially supports a free-threaded build.

nodes.title: Array
nodes.short: A numbered row of values stored side by side in memory, accessed by index. Index zero comes first.
nodes.long: Arrays make lookup by position instantaneous because the address is start plus index times size. Dynamic arrays (Python lists, JavaScript arrays, C++ vectors) grow automatically. Matrices are arrays of arrays.

nodes.title: Data Types
nodes.short: Integers, floating-point numbers, characters and strings: how bits in memory are read as values, and why each language reads them differently.
nodes.long: A data type tells the machine how to read the bits stored in a variable. FORTRAN, as described in 1957, decided the type from the first letter of a name: names starting with I to N were integers and the rest were floating-point. Languages still differ in their defaults. C uses fixed-width integers, Python integers can grow without limit, and JavaScript has one 64-bit floating-point Number type for ordinary numbers. Text is the hardest case: the string "héllo" followed by a smiley emoji is 11 bytes in UTF-8, 8 UTF-16 code units and 7 Unicode code points, so even asking for its length needs a definition.
nodes.sleeper: Text is now almost always UTF-8, used by 99.1 percent of websites whose encoding is known (W3Techs). The code pages of the 1980s are gone, and floating point follows one standard, IEEE 754.

code.text:
s = "héllo 😀"
print(len(s))                            # 7 code points
print(len(s.encode("utf-8")))            # 11 bytes
print(len(s.encode("utf-16-le")) // 2)   # 8 UTF-16 code units

refs.label: Backus et al., The FORTRAN Automatic Coding System (1957)
Spolsky, The Absolute Minimum About Unicode and Character Sets

nodes.title: Functions and Subroutines
nodes.short: A named, reusable block of steps with inputs and a result. Subroutine libraries came first, and today functions are values you can pass around.
nodes.long: A function packages steps under a name, takes parameters and returns a result. The idea predates high-level languages: EDSAC at Cambridge had a subroutine library, and the first programming textbook (1951) built its teaching on it. ALGOL 60 distinguished value parameters from call by name, and in 1973 Hoare lamented that the name parameter was the default. Lisp (1958) made functions values that can be passed and returned. Languages differ on whether a parameter is a copy or a reference to the caller's object, and on how a function reports failure. Python evaluates a default argument once, when the function is defined, so a default list is shared between calls, and Go functions can return several values.
nodes.sleeper: Functions are now ordinary values. You can store one in a variable, pass it to another function and return it, which is how callbacks, map and filter work in Python, JavaScript, Java and C++.

code.text:
def add(x, acc=[]):
    acc.append(x)
    return acc
