nodes.sleeper: Eventual consistency, as Werner Vogels explained it, means replicas converge if updates stop. With N replicas, W of them acknowledging each write and R of them consulted on each read, a system where W + R <= N can return stale data.

refs.label: Kleppmann, Please stop calling databases CP or AP (2015)

nodes.title: XML
nodes.short: Extensible Markup Language: nested, named tags for structured data. It ruled enterprise data exchange in the late 1990s before JSON took over the web.
nodes.long: XML is a text format built from nested, named tags, such as a person element containing a name element. Work began in 1996, and XML 1.0 became a W3C Recommendation on 10 February 1998. The specification describes it as a subset of SGML whose goal is to let generic SGML be served, received and processed on the web the way HTML is. XML dominated enterprise data exchange and spawned XML databases, but for web APIs it was overtaken: Michael Stonebraker and Andrew Pavlo write that JSON has since overtaken XML as the standard for web data exchange. SQL absorbed the format as well, with XML support in SQL:2003 and a dedicated Part 14, SQL/XML, in 2006.

code.text:
import xml.etree.ElementTree as ET
doc = ET.fromstring('<people><person id="1"><name>Ada</name></person><person id="2"><name>Alan</name></person></people>')
print([(p.get("id"), p.findtext("name")) for p in doc])   # [('1', 'Ada'), ('2', 'Alan')]

refs.label: W3C: Extensible Markup Language (XML) 1.0, Fifth Edition

nodes.title: SQLite
nodes.short: A whole SQL database in one file. Probably the most widely deployed database in the world.
nodes.long: D. Richard Hipp's SQLite is built into phones, browsers and countless applications. It needs no server, which makes it ideal for local data and testing.

nodes.title: Object-Relational Mapping
nodes.short: Libraries that convert between database rows and the objects of your language. They save boilerplate but bring the impedance mismatch and the N+1 query trap.
nodes.long: Object-relational mapping (ORM) converts data between a relational database and the objects of an object-oriented language. The difficulty is the object-relational impedance mismatch: objects form graphs that reference each other, while relational data are rows in tables linked by reversible joins. Martin Fowler named the Active Record pattern in 2003, the basis of Ruby on Rails' ActiveRecord. Hibernate for Java was released on 23 May 2001, SQLAlchemy for Python on 14 February 2006, and Entity Framework for .NET on 11 August 2008, to a vote of no confidence signed by at least a thousand developers. Fowler defended ORMs in 2012; Michael Stonebraker and Andrew Pavlo call them a vital tool for prototyping that often costs the ability to push logic into the database. The classic trap is N+1: one query for 7 creators plus one per creator for their languages made 8 statements instead of 1.

code.text:
from sqlalchemy import create_engine, select          # pip install sqlalchemy
from sqlalchemy.orm import DeclarativeBase, Mapped, mapped_column, Session
class Base(DeclarativeBase): pass
class Language(Base):                                  # one class per table, one object per row
    __tablename__ = "languages"
    id: Mapped[int] = mapped_column(primary_key=True)
    name: Mapped[str]
    year: Mapped[int]
engine = create_engine("sqlite://"); Base.metadata.create_all(engine)
with Session(engine) as s:
    s.add_all([Language(name="C", year=1972), Language(name="Python", year=1991)]); s.commit()
    print([lang.name for lang in s.scalars(select(Language).where(Language.year > 1980))])   # ['Python']

nodes.title: MapReduce and Hadoop
nodes.short: Google's 2004 model for processing huge data sets on clusters of cheap machines, and its open-source clone Hadoop. Oversold as a database, now mostly legacy.
nodes.long: In 2004 Jeffrey Dean and Sanjay Ghemawat of Google described MapReduce: users write a map function that turns key-value pairs into intermediate pairs and a reduce function that merges all values sharing a key, and the system runs the work in parallel across a cluster of commodity machines. Google reported upwards of a thousand MapReduce jobs a day. Doug Cutting and Mike Cafarella built Hadoop from Google's file system and MapReduce papers, naming it after the toy elephant of Cutting's son, and Yahoo, Facebook and others adopted it. In January 2008 David DeWitt and Michael Stonebraker called MapReduce a major step backwards. The Hadoop market cratered in the 2010s: Google said in 2014 that MapReduce had no place in its stack, Cloudera and Hortonworks merged in 2019, and MapR sold its technology to HPE.
nodes.sleeper: MapReduce programs were once the way to analyze big data. Parquet, ORC and Spark outlived them, and what Hadoop left behind is shared storage, open file formats and data lakes.

code.text:
from collections import defaultdict
docs = ["to be or not to be", "to see or not to see"]
pairs = [(w, 1) for d in docs for w in d.split()]       # map: emit (word, 1) for every word
groups = defaultdict(list)
for w, n in pairs: groups[w].append(n)                  # shuffle: gather the values for each key
print({w: sum(ns) for w, ns in groups.items()})         # reduce: sum each group
# {'to': 4, 'be': 2, 'or': 2, 'not': 2, 'see': 2}

refs.label: Dean and Ghemawat, MapReduce: Simplified Data Processing on Large Clusters (2004)
DeWitt and Stonebraker, MapReduce: A major step backwards (2008)

nodes.title: MongoDB
nodes.short: The best-known document database, storing JSON-like documents. Early defaults could lose data; it later added multi-document transactions and SQL.
nodes.long: MongoDB stores documents, which are hierarchies of field and value pairs kept in a JSON-like binary form called BSON, instead of rows in tables. The company 10gen began developing it in 2007 as part of a planned platform-as-a-service product, released it on 11 February 2009 and was renamed MongoDB Inc. in 2013. Multi-document ACID transactions arrived in version 4.0, and the license changed from AGPL to the Server Side Public License in November 2018. Its early reputation suffered from lost data: in a 2013 Jepsen test of version 2.4, 2,381 of 5,700 acknowledged writes disappeared after a network partition, and a 2020 test of version 4.2.6 found it could lose data by default and failed to preserve snapshot isolation. Current documentation says the default write concern is majority.
nodes.sleeper: Defaults decide what a database promises. MongoDB's early defaults did not check that writes succeeded, and later ones accepted a single node's acknowledgement, so the Jepsen reports became a lesson: web-scale claims need independent testing.

nodes.title: NoSQL
nodes.short: Key-value, document and wide-column stores built for web scale. Useful tools, not a replacement for SQL.
nodes.long: Google's Bigtable (2006) and Amazon's Dynamo (2007) inspired MongoDB, Cassandra and Redis. The hype that NoSQL would replace SQL faded as relational systems added scale and flexibility.

nodes.title: Redis
nodes.short: An in-memory data structure store whose values can be strings, lists, sets or hashes. Its 2024 license change led to the Valkey fork.
nodes.long: Redis was created by Salvatore Sanfilippo and first released on 26 February 2009. It keeps its data in memory and stores not just strings but lists, sets, hashes and other structures under each key, which makes it a popular cache and a source of fast counters. Memcached, first released in 2003 as a distributed memory cache for dynamic websites, was its older neighbor. On 20 March 2024 Redis moved from the BSD license to dual source-available licenses, and on 28 March the Linux Foundation announced Valkey, a BSD-licensed fork of Redis 7.2.4 backed by AWS, Google Cloud, Oracle, Ericsson and Snap. In May 2025 Redis added the OSI-approved AGPLv3 as a further option, and its chief executive wrote that the 2024 change had hurt the relationship with the community.

code.text:
> SET session:42 "ada" EX 3600       (store a value that expires after an hour)
OK
> GET session:42
"ada"
> INCR page:hits                     (atomic counter)
(integer) 1

nodes.title: DuckDB
nodes.short: An embedded analytical SQL database that runs inside your program, with no server, and can query CSV and Parquet files in place.
nodes.long: DuckDB is an in-process analytical SQL database developed by Mark Raasveldt and Hannes Mühleisen at CWI in the Netherlands. The first commit dates from July 2018 and the first release from 2019, so sources differ on the year; version 1.0.0 followed on 3 June 2024, under the MIT license. Its documentation says SQLite is the world's most widely deployed database and that DuckDB adopted the ideas of simplicity and in-process operation, with no external dependencies. DuckDB is aimed at analytical queries that scan large tables, and it can read CSV and Parquet files directly without loading them first. Michael Stonebraker and Andrew Pavlo credit its rising popularity to processing local and cloud files in place.
nodes.sleeper: Embedded used to mean a small file-based system such as dBase. DuckDB brings the idea to analytics: install a library, point SQL at a Parquet file, and query it with no server and no loading step.

code.text:
import duckdb                                      # pip install duckdb
with open("sales.csv", "w") as f: f.write("region,total
east,10
west,5
east,7
")
print(duckdb.sql("SELECT region, sum(total) AS total FROM 'sales.csv' GROUP BY region ORDER BY region"))   # east 17, west 5

refs.label: Raasveldt and Mühleisen, DuckDB: an Embeddable Analytical Database (SIGMOD 2019)

nodes.title: Vector Database
nodes.short: A database that stores embeddings, lists of numbers from a machine-learning model, and finds the closest ones. PostgreSQL and others absorbed it within a year.
nodes.long: A vector database stores embeddings, which are lists of hundreds or thousands of numbers produced by a machine-learning model so that similar items get nearby vectors, and finds the records closest to a query vector. Exact search over millions of vectors is too slow, so these systems use approximate nearest-neighbor indexes such as the Hierarchical Navigable Small World (HNSW) graph. After ChatGPT made large language models mainstream in late 2022, it took less than a year for several relational databases to add vector search, according to Michael Stonebraker and Andrew Pavlo; the pgvector extension adds it to PostgreSQL. Specialist products include Pinecone, Milvus and Weaviate, yet in DB-Engines' September 2026 vector ranking Elasticsearch, OpenSearch and Couchbase score above Pinecone and Milvus. Whether vector databases will last as a separate category is contested.
nodes.sleeper: In 1990 a database matched exact values or text. Search by meaning through embeddings is new since about 2019, and Stonebraker and Pavlo predict it will end up as a feature of relational systems rather than a separate product.

refs.label: Stonebraker and Pavlo, What Goes Around Comes Around... And Around... (2024)

nodes.title: Stack and Queue
nodes.short: Last-in, first-out and first-in, first-out collections. Function calls use a stack, while print spoolers and message brokers use queues.
nodes.long: A stack hands back the most recently added item first (last in, first out), and a queue hands back the oldest first (first in, first out). Stacks entered the literature in 1946, when Alan Turing used the terms bury and unbury for calling and returning from subroutines. Konrad Zuse's Z4 already had a two-level stack in 1945, and Friedrich Bauer and Klaus Samelson filed a German patent in 1957 that named the idea Keller, meaning cellar. Every function call pushes a frame onto the machine's call stack, which is why runaway recursion ends in a stack overflow. A Python list is a poor queue, since removing the first item shifts all the rest: draining 100,000 items took 0.21 seconds that way against 0.0023 seconds with a deque.

code.text:
from collections import deque
stack = []; stack.append("a"); stack.append("b")
print(stack.pop())                  # b  (last in, first out)
queue = deque(); queue.append("a"); queue.append("b")
print(queue.popleft())              # a  (first in, first out; list.pop(0) would be O(n))

nodes.title: Linked List
nodes.short: Elements that each hold a value and the address of the next one. Invented for early AI programs, and now rarely the best default.
nodes.long: A linked list stores each element in a node that holds a value and the address of the next node, so the elements can sit anywhere in memory. Allen Newell, Cliff Shaw and Herbert Simon first implemented the idea in 1955 and 1956 as the main data structure of their Information Processing Language, which they used for early artificial-intelligence programs such as the Logic Theory Machine. Lisp's cons cell, a pair of fields historically named car and cdr, is the basis of a simple singly linked list. Inserting after a node you already hold is cheap, but reaching the 1,000th element means following 1,000 links, and each node is usually a separate allocation in memory.
nodes.sleeper: Caches changed the advice. In Stroustrup's experiment, vectors beat linked lists even for insertions into a sorted sequence, where lists should win on paper, so his 2014 recommendation is to use vector by default.

code.text:
class Node:
    def __init__(self, value, next=None): self.value, self.next = value, next
head = Node(1, Node(2, Node(3)))       # 1 -> 2 -> 3
n = head
while n:
    print(n.value)                     # prints 1, 2, 3
    n = n.next

nodes.title: Graph (Data Structure)
nodes.short: Points joined by lines: road maps, friendships, web links, dependencies. Stored as adjacency lists or matrices and explored breadth-first or depth-first.
nodes.long: A graph is a set of points, called vertices or nodes, joined by lines called edges. Road maps, friendships, web links and the dependencies between software packages are all graphs. Two layouts are standard: an adjacency list, where each vertex stores a list of its neighbors, and an adjacency matrix, where rows are source vertices and columns are destination vertices. Breadth-first search finds the path with the fewest hops in an unweighted graph by visiting neighbors in queue order. SQL can do the same job with a recursive query over a table of edges, and graph databases such as Neo4j store the edges directly. No single date marks the start of graphs in programming, so the year on the map is approximate.

nodes.title: Binary Search Tree
nodes.short: A tree where smaller keys go left and larger keys go right, so each comparison discards a share of the keys if the tree stays balanced.
nodes.long: In a binary search tree each node has a left subtree of smaller keys and a right subtree of larger keys. A search starts at the root and goes left or right at each step, so a balanced tree of n keys needs about log n comparisons, while a tree built from already sorted input degenerates into a list and needs n. An in-order walk, which visits the left subtree, then the node, then the right subtree, returns the keys in sorted order. Related trees solve neighboring problems: the trie for prefix lookups such as autocomplete, the heap for a priority queue, and the B-tree that databases use for indexes. No single inventor or date is documented for the plain search tree, so the year on the map is approximate.

nodes.title: CODASYL Network Model
nodes.short: Records linked into named sets by chains of pointers, which programs navigate one record at a time. Bachman's IDS was its main technical input.
nodes.long: The CODASYL network model, defined by the Data Base Task Group of the committee that also gave the world COBOL, links records into named sets with chains of pointers. A program navigates by commands such as find the first employee in this department's set, then get the next one. Its first report, "COBOL extensions to handle data bases", appeared in January 1968, with further reports through 1969, and Charles Bachman's Integrated Data Store from General Electric was the main technical input. Implementations included Cullinet's IDMS, Honeywell's IDS/2, HP's Image and Univac's DMS-1100. Navigational programming depended on maintained currency indicators and was intrinsically procedural; during the 1980s it was eclipsed by declarative query languages, which offered better programmer productivity and a higher level of data independence.

code.text:
# pseudocode in the navigational style, not any product's syntax
get department with name = 'Sales'
get first employee in set department-employees
until end-of-set do
    process employee
    get next employee in set department-employees

nodes.title: CSV
nodes.short: Comma-separated values: plain text with one record per line. It has no types and no real standard, and still carries data between almost everything.
nodes.long: A CSV file holds one record per line, with fields separated by commas and often a header line naming the columns. Wikipedia reports that IBM's Fortran compiler under OS/360 supported comma-separated list-directed input and output in 1972, and the format was in wide use long before anyone wrote it down. RFC 4180, published in 2005, admits that the format has never been formally documented and registers the text/csv media type. Its rules: a field containing a comma, a line break or a double quote must be wrapped in double quotes, and a quote inside a quoted field is written twice. Every spreadsheet, language and database can read and write CSV, which is why it survives. The costs are that everything is text with no types, and that the character encoding is unspecified.

code.text:
import csv, io
text = 'region,units,price\n"Cambridge, UK",3,9.5\n'   # the first field contains a comma
for row in csv.DictReader(io.StringIO(text)):
    print(row["region"], int(row["units"]) * float(row["price"]))   # Cambridge, UK 28.5

refs.label: RFC 4180: Common Format and MIME Type for CSV Files

nodes.title: Ingres and QUEL
nodes.short: Berkeley's relational database project and its query language, QUEL. QUEL lost to SQL, but Ingres led to Sybase, SQL Server and PostgreSQL.
nodes.long: Ingres was a relational database built at UC Berkeley by Michael Stonebraker, Eugene Wong and colleagues. Jim Gray recalled that around 1972 Stonebraker got a grant for a geographic query system, and that it quickly turned into a relational database; some sources date the start to 1973. The project ran from the early 1970s to 1985 and used its own language, QUEL, which was considered truer to Codd's relational algebra than SQL, though SQL was easier to parse and less intimidating. Ingres spawned Sybase, Microsoft SQL Server and NonStop SQL, and Stonebraker's later POSTGRES project became PostgreSQL. Gray noted that some Ingres people felt the project lost ground by fighting SQL instead of embracing it, and when ANSI chose SQL over QUEL in 1986, Ingres became less competitive until it also offered SQL.

refs.label: The 1995 SQL Reunion: Teradata and the Ingres family

nodes.title: Data Warehouse
nodes.short: A central database that collects data from operational systems for reporting and analysis. Teradata was the archetype; cloud column stores now dominate.
nodes.long: A data warehouse gathers data from a company's operational systems into one central database for reporting. Teradata is the archetype: formed in 1979 by Caltech researchers and Citibank, it shipped its first parallel SQL engine around 1984 and in 1992 delivered the first system over a terabyte, for Walmart. Michael Stonebraker and Andrew Pavlo date the warehouse market from the mid-1990s, with retailers such as Walmart and Ralph Kimball's star schema, and say that all vendors active in it have converted from row stores to column stores. Cloud warehouses followed: BigQuery was announced in May 2010, Amazon Redshift reached general release on 15 February 2013, and Snowflake, founded in 2012, went public in September 2020 and raised $3.4 billion.

refs.label: Stonebraker and Pavlo, What Goes Around Comes Around... And Around... (2024)

nodes.title: Informix
nodes.short: A major commercial relational database of the late 1980s and 1990s, founded in 1980. IBM bought it in 2001, and HCLSoftware has developed it since 2017.
nodes.long: Roger Sippl founded Relational Database Systems, Inc. in 1980, and the company was later renamed Informix Corporation. Sippl said later that he was unaware of Edgar Codd's work when he began designing the query language. In the late 1980s and early 1990s Informix was one of the commercial database servers a company could choose, alongside Oracle and Sybase. IBM acquired Informix Software in 2001, and since April 2017 HCLSoftware has developed the product. It survives as a niche system, one of the commercial vendors that lost ground to Oracle, Db2, SQL Server and later the cloud.

nodes.title: Database Machines
nodes.short: Special-purpose hardware built to speed up databases. Britton-Lee's IDM/500 (1981) was the first product, and the approach failed commercially in the 1980s.
nodes.long: In the 1980s several vendors tried to speed up databases with custom hardware. Britton-Lee, a spin-off from Ingres, released the first commercial accelerator, the IDM/500, in 1981, and Jim Gray's 1995 account describes it as a database machine with an accelerator. Teradata's custom Y-net sorting network was later dropped for a software-only solution. Michael Stonebraker and Andrew Pavlo write that all other custom hardware acceleration of the 1980s failed, that FPGA and GPU databases repeated the pattern and remain mostly niche, and that custom hardware will succeed only at the large cloud vendors, with examples such as Redshift AQUA.

refs.label: The 1995 SQL Reunion: Teradata and the Ingres family
Stonebraker and Pavlo, What Goes Around Comes Around... And Around... (2024)

nodes.title: IBM Db2
nodes.short: IBM's flagship relational database, announced in June 1983 and built on System R's ideas. It sat beside IMS inside IBM, and customers often had to choose.
nodes.long: IBM's System R-derived products were System/38 (1979), SQL/DS (1981) and Db2 (1983). IBM Database 2 Release 1 was announced on 7 June 1983; Roger Miller recalled shipping it to six customers in November 1982 and to eighteen by March 1983, before the announcement widened it to dozens. IBM was slow to commit, which the reunion transcript attributes to internal politics, competing projects and the IMS franchise. One participant described a love-hate relationship with the folks in the tower next door, since a customer often came in saying they had to choose between IMS and Db2, and Bruce Lindsay remarked that IBM will not attack its own products, even when they are weak. SQL/DS had been built from System R's code at IBM's Endicott lab. Db2 remains in use across the IBM ecosystem and ranked ninth on DB-Engines in September 2026.

nodes.title: SQL Standard (ISO/IEC 9075)
nodes.short: SQL became an ANSI standard in 1986 and an ISO standard in 1987, and has been revised through SQL:2023. No implementation follows it fully.
nodes.long: SQL became an ANSI standard in 1986 (SQL-86, adopted as FIPS PUB 127) and an ISO standard in 1987, and is maintained as ISO/IEC 9075. NIST certified compliance until 1996, and since then vendors self-certify. Later revisions added integrity constraints (SQL-89), a major overhaul (SQL-92), recursive queries, triggers and arrays (SQL:1999), XML features and window functions (SQL:2003), SQL/XML (2006), temporal data (SQL:2011), JSON operations (SQL:2016) and property graph queries (SQL:2023). In practice virtually no implementation adheres fully, and most SQL needs some changes to move between databases; for example, the standard folds unquoted names to upper case but PostgreSQL folds them to lower case. Michael Stonebraker and Andrew Pavlo argue that the standard is how SQL absorbed the best ideas of its rivals.

nodes.title: Database Driver APIs (ODBC, JDBC, DB-API)
nodes.short: Standard interfaces that let a program talk to many databases through drivers: ODBC (1992), JDBC (1997) and Python's DB-API.
nodes.long: A driver API lets one application talk to any database that has a driver. ODBC (Open Database Connectivity), developed by Microsoft and Simba Technologies in the early 1990s, reached version 1.0 in September 1992, and its early drivers were noted for poor performance. Sun released JDBC as part of JDK 1.1 on 19 February 1997. Python's DB-API, specified in PEP 249 in 1999, defines connect, cursor, execute, fetch, commit and rollback calls, plus a paramstyle constant that names the placeholder style. The pattern is the same in every language: open a connection, send a SQL statement with placeholders, bind the values separately, fetch rows, commit or roll back, and close. Opening connections to a server database is expensive, so applications keep a small pool of them, and PgBouncer is a connection pooler for PostgreSQL.
nodes.sleeper: Bigger pools are not faster. According to the HikariCP guide, an Oracle performance demonstration cut a pool from 2,048 to 96 connections and response times fell from about 100 ms to about 2 ms.

code.text:
import sqlite3                              # any DB-API driver follows the same steps
conn = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")          # 1. open a connection
conn.execute("CREATE TABLE creators (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT)")
conn.execute("INSERT INTO creators VALUES (3, 'Niklaus Wirth')")
cur = conn.cursor()
cur.execute("SELECT name FROM creators WHERE id = ?", (3,))   # 2-3. placeholder, value bound separately
print(cur.fetchall())                       # 4. fetch rows: [('Niklaus Wirth',)]
conn.commit()                               # 5. commit (or conn.rollback())
conn.close()                                # 6. close

refs.label: PEP 249: Python Database API Specification v2.0

nodes.title: Isolation Levels
nodes.short: Settings that decide how much concurrent transactions can see of each other's work. A 1995 paper showed the SQL standard's definitions were not enough.
nodes.long: Isolation levels let an application trade throughput for correctness when many transactions run at once. The SQL-92 standard defines four levels, READ UNCOMMITTED, READ COMMITTED, REPEATABLE READ and SERIALIZABLE, in terms of three anomalies called dirty read, non-repeatable read and phantom. The 1995 paper "A Critique of ANSI SQL Isolation Levels", by Berenson, Bernstein, Gray, Melton and the two O'Neils, showed that these phenomena and the ANSI definitions fail to characterize several popular isolation levels, and it defined snapshot isolation. PostgreSQL defaults to Read Committed. You can request all four levels, but internally only three are distinct, because Read Uncommitted behaves like Read Committed. Readers do not block writers, since each transaction sees a snapshot, and Serializable uses serializable snapshot isolation.

code.text:
import sqlite3, os, tempfile
path = os.path.join(tempfile.mkdtemp(), "demo.db")
a, b = sqlite3.connect(path), sqlite3.connect(path)    # two clients of the same database
a.execute("CREATE TABLE t (x)")
a.execute("INSERT INTO t VALUES (1)")                  # a's transaction is still open
print(b.execute("SELECT COUNT(*) FROM t").fetchone())  # (0,): b cannot see uncommitted work
a.commit()
print(b.execute("SELECT COUNT(*) FROM t").fetchone())  # (1,)

refs.label: Berenson et al., A Critique of ANSI SQL Isolation Levels (1995)

nodes.title: YAML
nodes.short: An indentation-based text format popular for configuration, with type-guessing traps such as the bare word NO loading as false.
nodes.long: YAML is a text format that uses indentation instead of brackets and allows comments, which made it popular for configuration files. Its first working draft, "Yet Another Markup Language", is dated 10 December 2001, and the name was later re-expanded as "YAML Ain't Markup Language". The authors include Oren Ben-Kiki, Clark Evans and Ingy döt Net. The specification's history notes that, by sheer coincidence, JSON was almost a complete subset of YAML, and YAML 1.2 was made a strict superset of it. The current revision is 1.2.2, from 1 October 2021. Parsers that still follow the older 1.1 rules guess types aggressively, so an unquoted NO can load as false and 1.10 as the number 1.1.

code.text:
import yaml                       # PyYAML, installed with pip
print(yaml.safe_load("country: NO
answer: yes
version: 1.10
zip: 01234
name: 'NO'"))
# {'country': False, 'answer': True, 'version': 1.1, 'zip': 668, 'name': 'NO'}

nodes.title: Google Bigtable
nodes.short: Google's 2006 paper on a distributed storage system: a sparse sorted map indexed by row, column and timestamp. It inspired HBase and Cassandra.
nodes.long: Bigtable is a distributed storage system for structured data, designed to scale to petabytes across thousands of commodity servers. Its paper, by Chang and colleagues at Google (OSDI 2006), calls a Bigtable a sparse, distributed, persistent multi-dimensional sorted map, indexed by a row key, a column key and a timestamp. Bigtable clusters had been in production since April 2005, and by August 2006 more than sixty Google projects used it, including web indexing, Google Earth and Google Finance. HBase, a Bigtable-style store on Hadoop first released in March 2008, and Cassandra followed its design. Michael Stonebraker and Andrew Pavlo observe that Google itself later built relational systems on top of Bigtable, first Megastore and then Spanner, and rewrote Spanner to remove Bigtable remnants.

refs.label: Chang et al., Bigtable: A Distributed Storage System for Structured Data (2006)

nodes.title: Amazon Dynamo
nodes.short: Amazon's 2007 key-value store that gave up some consistency to stay always available. Its ideas shaped Cassandra and Amazon's DynamoDB service.
nodes.long: Dynamo, described by DeCandia and colleagues at SOSP in 2007, is a highly available key-value storage system that some of Amazon's core services use to provide an always-on experience. To reach that availability, the paper says, Dynamo sacrifices consistency under certain failure scenarios. The motivating example was the shopping cart: customers should be able to view and add items even if disks are failing, network routes are flapping or data centers are being destroyed by tornados. The paper measures latency at the 99.9th percentile rather than the average. Cassandra borrowed its replication techniques. Amazon DynamoDB, released on 18 January 2012, is a different, managed service that Werner Vogels described as the result of 15 years of learning in large-scale non-relational databases and cloud services.

refs.label: DeCandia et al., Dynamo: Amazon's Highly Available Key-value Store (2007)

nodes.title: Neo4j
nodes.short: The best-known graph database: it stores nodes and relationships directly and queries them in Cypher. Its edges are pointers, as in CODASYL.
nodes.long: Neo4j is a graph database founded in 2007 in Sweden as an open-source project by Emil Eifrem, Johan Svensson and Peter Neubauer. It stores nodes and the relationships between them directly and uses the Cypher query language; the company contributed to GQL, the graph query language that became ISO/IEC 39075 in April 2024. Michael Stonebraker and Andrew Pavlo note that Neo4j supports edges using pointers, as CODASYL did, which suits long chains of relationships where a relational system has to use joins. They also point out that a graph can be simulated with node and edge tables, that SQL:2023 added property graph queries (SQL/PGQ), and that they do not expect specialized graph databases to be a large market. Neo4j was first among graph systems and twentieth overall on DB-Engines in September 2026.

nodes.title: Apache Cassandra
nodes.short: A wide-column store from Facebook that combines Amazon Dynamo's replication techniques with Google Bigtable's data model, first built for inbox search.
nodes.long: Cassandra was developed at Facebook by Avinash Lakshman, a co-author of the Dynamo paper, and Prashant Malik, for inbox search. It combines Amazon's Dynamo distributed storage and replication techniques with Google's Bigtable data storage engine model. Facebook released it as open source on Google Code in July 2008, it entered the Apache Incubator in March 2009, and it became a top-level Apache project on 17 February 2010. Michael Stonebraker and Andrew Pavlo are critical of the column-family model: they write that Cassandra and HBase copied Bigtable's limitations, including the lack of joins and secondary indexes. Like most NoSQL systems it later gained a SQL-like language, CQL. It was twelfth overall on DB-Engines in September 2026 and first among wide-column stores.

refs.label: Stonebraker and Pavlo, What Goes Around Comes Around... And Around... (2024)

nodes.title: Protocol Buffers
nodes.short: Google's compact binary format: describe your data once in a schema, generate code for many languages, and exchange small messages that can evolve.
nodes.long: Protocol Buffers, usually called protobuf, is a way to serialize structured data that Google developed for internal use and released publicly on 7 July 2008. You describe your messages once in a .proto file, and a compiler generates code in many languages that writes and reads a compact binary form. Google's overview calls it like JSON except smaller and faster, with native language bindings, and the most commonly used data format at Google. New fields can be added and old ones removed without breaking existing services. The price is readability, because the field names are not in the bytes and both sides need the schema. A message with name John and id 1234 takes 9 bytes in protobuf against 25 bytes as compact JSON.

nodes.title: Managed Cloud Database
nodes.short: A database that a cloud provider runs for you as a service. Amazon RDS (2009) started with managed MySQL, and the cloud has reshaped how databases are built.
nodes.long: A managed cloud database is one that a cloud provider runs for you as a service, so you rent it instead of operating your own server. Amazon RDS, released on 26 October 2009 as managed MySQL, added Oracle in June 2011, SQL Server in May 2012, PostgreSQL in November 2013 and MariaDB in October 2015. Other landmarks include BigQuery (announced May 2010), DynamoDB (January 2012), Redshift (preview November 2012), Aurora (November 2014) and Snowflake. Michael Stonebraker and Andrew Pavlo say the cloud forced databases to be completely re-architected around network-attached object storage, and they warn that except for embedded systems, any product not starting with a cloud offering will likely fail. They also describe the danger that open-source databases are monetized by the big cloud providers, the background to the Redis, Elastic and MongoDB license changes.
nodes.sleeper: Around 1990 a database meant a server you bought, installed and tended. Today a rented one is common: Azure SQL Database, DynamoDB and BigQuery were all in DB-Engines' top 20 in September 2026.

refs.label: Stonebraker and Pavlo, What Goes Around Comes Around... And Around... (2024)

nodes.title: Elasticsearch and Lucene
nodes.short: Full-text search servers: Lucene is the Java search library, and Elasticsearch wraps it in a distributed server with an HTTP and JSON interface.
nodes.long: Lucene is a Java search library originally written by Doug Cutting in 1999 and later an Apache project. Elasticsearch, built on Lucene by Shay Banon and first released on 8 February 2010, is a distributed full-text search engine with an HTTP and JSON interface; Solr is the other well-known engine built on Lucene. Both offer little or no transaction support, and Michael Stonebraker and Andrew Pavlo point out that all the leading relational databases now support full-text search indexes as well. In 2021 Elastic changed its license after problems with AWS, which led to Amazon's OpenSearch fork; in August 2024 Shay Banon announced that Elasticsearch and Kibana can be called open source again, with the AGPL added as a license option. Elasticsearch also tops DB-Engines' small vector-database category.

code.text:
GET /articles/_search
{ "query": { "match": { "body": "binary search bug" } } }

refs.label: Elastic: Elasticsearch is Open Source, Again

nodes.title: Google Spanner and NewSQL
nodes.short: Google's globally distributed database with SQL and real transactions, built after Bigtable proved hard to use. NewSQL is the label for systems with similar aims.
nodes.long: Google's Spanner (OSDI 2012) is a globally distributed, synchronously replicated database that its authors call the first system to distribute data at global scale and support externally consistent distributed transactions. It relies on the TrueTime API, which exposes clock uncertainty using GPS and atomic clocks, generally less than 10 milliseconds. Spanner evolved from a Bigtable-like key-value store because users complained that Bigtable was hard to use for complex, evolving schemas or for strong consistency across wide areas; it gained a SQL-based query language, and its first customer was F1, a rewrite of Google's advertising backend. NewSQL, a term used by Matthew Aslett in 2011, covers relational systems that promise NoSQL-like scale with ACID guarantees, such as CockroachDB, TiDB and YugabyteDB. Adoption has been modest because existing databases were good enough.
nodes.sleeper: Eventual consistency was the fashion in 2007. By 2012 Google had chosen real transactions at global scale, and Amazon now sells Aurora DSQL, a PostgreSQL-compatible distributed SQL database.

refs.label: Corbett et al., Spanner: Google's Globally-Distributed Database (2012)
Pavlo and Aslett, What's Really New with NewSQL? (2016)

nodes.title: Apache Parquet
nodes.short: A column-oriented file format for analytics: the values of each column are stored together, so queries read less and the files compress well.
nodes.long: Apache Parquet is an open source, column-oriented data file format designed for efficient storage and retrieval. A CSV file, a JSON file or a classic database table keeps each record together, whereas a Parquet file keeps all the values of one column together, so an analytic query reads only the columns it needs and similar values compress well. The project began as a joint effort of Twitter and Cloudera, was inspired by Google's Dremel paper, released version 1.0 in July 2013 and became a top-level Apache project in April 2015. In one DuckDB test on a million rows of artificial, repetitive data, the Parquet file took about 5.1 MB against 24.2 MB for the CSV, and an average-by-region query ran about twelve times faster.
nodes.sleeper: Parquet plays the part the data warehouse extract file once did. Instead of loading it into a warehouse first, tools such as DuckDB can query the file where it sits.

nodes.title: Apache Arrow
nodes.short: A shared in-memory column format, so pandas, Polars, DuckDB and Spark can hand tables to one another without copying them.
nodes.long: Apache Arrow defines a column-oriented layout for tables held in memory, described by its project as a high-performance cross-system data layer for columnar in-memory analytics. Parquet is the format for files on disk and Arrow the format for data already loaded, so tools that agree on Arrow can exchange columns without converting or copying them; Polars, for example, says it can consume and produce Arrow data, often with zero-copy operations. The Apache Software Foundation announced Arrow as a top-level project on 17 February 2016. Michael Stonebraker and Andrew Pavlo name Arrow as the in-memory exchange format of the open data-lake stack, alongside Parquet and ORC for files. Its core is written in C++, with Python bindings called PyArrow.

code.text:
import pyarrow as pa                                          # pip install pyarrow
t = pa.table({"region": ["east", "west"], "units": [3, 5]})    # columns stored in Arrow's layout
print(t.column("units").to_pylist(), t.num_rows)               # [3, 5] 2

nodes.title: Data Lakehouse
nodes.short: Warehouse-style SQL and transactions on open files in cheap cloud storage. Databricks coined the term; Delta Lake and Iceberg supply the table features.
nodes.long: A data lake is cheap storage, now usually cloud object storage such as S3, holding raw data in open file formats like Apache Parquet and ORC, with the schema applied when the data is read. That is flexible, but as the Databricks authors admit it punts data quality and governance downstream, so companies often added a separate warehouse such as Redshift or Snowflake on top, a two-tier design. In a 2021 paper at the CIDR conference, Michael Armbrust, Ali Ghodsi, Reynold Xin and Matei Zaharia argued for the lakehouse: open direct-access formats, first-class support for machine learning and warehouse-grade performance on one platform. Table formats such as Delta Lake, Iceberg and Hudi add transactional updates on top of Parquet files. The authors work for Databricks, which coined the term.

refs.label: Armbrust et al., Lakehouse: A New Generation of Open Platforms (CIDR 2021)

nodes.title: Numerics, Matrices & AI
nodes.short: Numbers in bulk: arrays and matrices, the libraries that crunch them, and the machine learning built on top.
nodes.long: From FORTRAN's numeric libraries to Python's NumPy and GPU-trained neural networks, the same operation recurs: multiplying large arrays of numbers quickly.

nodes.title: Matrix
nodes.short: A rectangle of numbers with rules for adding and multiplying. The workhorse of graphics, statistics and AI.
nodes.long: A matrix is a grid of rows and columns. Multiplying matrices combines transformations, solves linear systems and powers neural networks. In code it is a two-dimensional array stored row by row (C) or column by column (Fortran).

nodes.title: GPUs for Computing
nodes.short: Graphics chips with thousands of simple cores that turned out to be matrix-multiplication engines. They are the hardware that made deep learning practical.
nodes.long: A graphics processing unit, or GPU, is a chip with thousands of simple cores built for graphics, where every vertex of a 3D scene is multiplied by a transformation matrix, so matrix arithmetic was already its daily work. Larsen and McAllister published 'Fast matrix multiplies using graphics hardware' at the SC 2001 supercomputing conference, and Ian Buck and colleagues published Brook for GPUs in 2004. NVIDIA's CUDA (2007) then made the hardware programmable as an extension of C. In 2009 Raina, Madhavan and Ng reported training up to 70 times faster than on a dual-core CPU, and in 2012 AlexNet was trained on two GPUs. The year here follows the first published GPU matrix multiplication; 2007, the CUDA release, is the other date in use.
nodes.sleeper: Where you would once have expected the CPU to do all the arithmetic, a modern machine-learning job sends its heavy matrix multiplication to GPUs or TPUs.

refs.label: Larsen and McAllister: Fast matrix multiplies using graphics hardware (SC 2001)
Buck et al.: Brook for GPUs (SIGGRAPH 2004)

nodes.title: The Transformer
nodes.short: Google's 2017 architecture built on attention, not recurrence. It is mostly matrix multiplication, so it scales on GPUs, and today's language models use it.
nodes.long: Vaswani and colleagues at Google introduced the Transformer in June 2017, describing a model 'based solely on attention mechanisms, dispensing with recurrence and convolutions entirely'. It scored 28.4 BLEU (a translation-quality score) on WMT 2014 English-to-German, and 41.8 on English-to-French after 3.5 days of training on eight GPUs. Attention packs all the queries into a matrix Q and is computed with two matrix products, softmax(QK^T / sqrt(d)) V, which the authors say can use highly optimized matrix multiplication code. BERT, GPT-3 and the large language models that followed are built on the design. The paper has been cited about 194,600 times.
nodes.sleeper: Earlier sequence models used recurrence, stepping through a sentence one word at a time. The Transformer dropped recurrence, so it can process every position at once with large matrix products, which suits GPUs.

refs.label: Vaswani et al.: Attention Is All You Need (2017)

nodes.title: Large Language Models
nodes.short: Neural networks with billions of parameters, trained on text to predict what comes next. They run on matrix multiplication, from chatbots to coding assistants.
nodes.long: A large language model, or LLM, is a Transformer network with billions of parameters, trained on very large amounts of text to predict what comes next. GPT-3 in 2020, with 175 billion parameters, was ten times larger than any earlier non-sparse language model, and OpenAI released ChatGPT on 30 November 2022. Training is a loop of forward pass, error, gradient and small weight update repeated enormously often, costing about six floating-point operations per parameter per training token; inference runs only the forward pass, through the same matrix multiplications. The software stack is shared: Python code on PyTorch, Hugging Face Transformers to load models, vLLM to serve them. The Chinchilla study of 2022 found that each doubling of model size should come with a doubling of training tokens.
nodes.sleeper: In the 1980s 'AI' meant rules written by experts. Here nothing is written by hand: behavior comes from billions of numbers learned from text, applied by repeated matrix multiplication.

refs.label: Brown et al.: Language Models are Few-Shot Learners (2020)

nodes.title: Matrix Multiplication
nodes.short: Combining two matrices: each entry is a row of the first multiplied term by term with a column of the second. Graphics and neural networks are built from it.
nodes.long: In the product of two matrices, entry (i, j) is the dot product of row i of the first with column j of the second: multiply matching entries, then add them up. Arthur Cayley's 1858 memoir on matrices gave the first abstract definition of a matrix algebra. Read as transformations, the product means 'apply the right-hand matrix first, then the left-hand one', so order matters and A times B is generally not B times A. The same operation chains 3D graphics transformations, advances a neural-network layer and computes attention in a Transformer. Multiplying two 4096 by 4096 matrices takes about 137 billion floating-point operations, which is why tuned libraries, GPUs and specialized chips exist to speed it up.
nodes.sleeper: Python got a matrix-multiply operator late: PEP 465 (proposed in 2014, shipped in Python 3.5) added @, because * could mean only elementwise or matrix multiplication, and NumPy's arrays and its older matrix class chose differently.

nodes.title: Perceptron
nodes.short: Frank Rosenblatt's 1958 learning machine: weighted inputs, a threshold, and a rule that nudges the weights after each mistake.
nodes.long: The perceptron is a single artificial neuron. It multiplies each input by a weight, adds the results and fires if the total passes a threshold; when its answer is wrong, the learning rule adjusts the weights toward the right one. Frank Rosenblatt of the Cornell Aeronautical Laboratory published it in Psychological Review in 1958, after obtaining funding in 1957 to build the Mark I Perceptron, a custom analog computer. Marvin Minsky and Seymour Papert's 1969 book Perceptrons showed that a single layer cannot learn XOR. The book is often blamed for the first neural-network lull, though that reading is disputed, since both authors already knew that multi-layer networks can produce XOR.
nodes.sleeper: A perceptron's weighted sum is the same dot product that each layer of a modern network computes, for thousands of neurons at once, as one matrix multiplication.

code.text:
import numpy as np
X, y = np.array([[0, 0], [0, 1], [1, 0], [1, 1]]), np.array([0, 0, 0, 1])   # logical AND
w, b = np.zeros(2), 0.0
for _ in range(20):
    for xi, yi in zip(X, y):
        err = yi - int(w @ xi + b > 0)       # 0 if right, +1 or -1 if wrong
        w += err * xi; b += err              # nudge the weights toward the right answer
print(w, b)   # [2. 1.] -2.0

nodes.title: Expert Systems
nodes.short: 1980s programs that encoded a specialist's knowledge as if-then rules. XCON, which configured DEC VAX orders, was the flagship before the AI winter.
nodes.long: An expert system is a program that encodes a specialist's knowledge as if-then rules. The flagship was XCON, or R1, written in the OPS5 rule language by John McDermott of Carnegie Mellon in 1978 to configure orders for DEC's VAX computers. It entered use in 1980 at DEC's plant in Salem, New Hampshire, held about 2,500 rules and had processed 80,000 orders by 1986 at 95 to 98 percent accuracy, according to Wikipedia. Its reported savings differ between sources ($25 million a year versus $40 million over six years), so treat them as unverified. The boom was tied to Lisp machines and Japan's Fifth Generation project; the Lisp-machine market collapsed in 1987, and many expert systems were abandoned in the 1990s.
nodes.sleeper: If you remember 1980s AI, it was this: rules typed in by engineers and domain experts. Today's systems instead learn billions of numeric parameters from data, as in large language models.

nodes.title: BLAS
nodes.short: Basic Linear Algebra Subprograms: a standard set of vector and matrix routines. Vendors tune them once, and every program that calls them runs fast on that machine.
nodes.long: The BLAS are a standard interface for the basic operations of linear algebra. Level 1, published in 1979 by Lawson, Hanson, Kincaid and Krogh, covers scalar and vector operations, Level 2 (1988) covers matrix-vector operations, and Level 3 (1990) covers matrix-matrix operations such as C = alpha*A*B + beta*C. The reference version on netlib is portable but not fast, so vendors and projects supply tuned versions with the same interface: OpenBLAS, Intel MKL, Apple Accelerate and, on GPUs, NVIDIA's cuBLAS. Because the interface stays fixed, libraries such as LAPACK and SciPy are written against it once and inherit the tuning. Jack Dongarra co-authored the Level 2 and 3 specifications.
nodes.sleeper: The names have outlived the Fortran era. GEMM, the Level 3 matrix multiply, is the routine NVIDIA's guides still cite as the building block of neural-network layers.

nodes.title: Backpropagation
nodes.short: The method of computing how much each weight in a multi-layer network contributed to the error, by applying the chain rule backward from the output.
nodes.long: Backpropagation computes how much each weight in a multi-layer network contributed to its error by applying the chain rule backward from the output. Rumelhart, Hinton and Williams published 'Learning representations by back-propagating errors' in Nature in 1986, a paper cited about 32,500 times. Earlier roots exist: Seppo Linnainmaa's 1970 master's thesis introduced reverse-mode automatic differentiation, and Paul Werbos applied backpropagation to multi-layer perceptrons in 1982. Training repeats four steps: run examples forward, measure the error, backpropagate to get gradients, and adjust every weight slightly. In PyTorch the backward step is the call loss.backward().
nodes.sleeper: The 1986 method is the one still in use; what changed is scale. GPT-3 (2020) has 175 billion parameters, and training costs about six floating-point operations per parameter for each training token.

code.text:
import torch
model = torch.nn.Linear(3, 1)                 # weights: a 1x3 matrix plus a bias
x, y = torch.randn(8, 3), torch.randn(8, 1)   # a batch of 8 examples with known answers
loss = ((model(x) - y) ** 2).mean()           # forward pass (a matrix multiply) and the error
loss.backward()                               # backpropagation: gradients of the error
with torch.no_grad():
    model.weight -= 0.1 * model.weight.grad   # gradient descent: a small step downhill

refs.label: Rumelhart, Hinton and Williams: Learning representations by back-propagating errors (Nature, 1986)

nodes.title: LAPACK
nodes.short: The standard library for dense linear algebra (solving equations, least squares, eigenvalues, SVD), first released in 1992 and built on blocked BLAS operations.
nodes.long: LAPACK, the Linear Algebra PACKage, had its first public release on 29 February 1992, provided by the University of Tennessee, UC Berkeley, the University of Colorado Denver and NAG. Its original goal was to make EISPACK and LINPACK run efficiently on shared-memory vector and parallel processors, because the older code ignored the memory hierarchy and spent too much time moving data. LAPACK reorganized the work into blocks that use Level 3 BLAS. It is written in Fortran 90, handles dense and banded matrices but not general sparse ones, and offers LU, Cholesky, QR, SVD and Schur factorizations in real and complex, single and double precision. Version 3.12.1, released in January 2025, was still the latest on netlib in September 2026.

nodes.title: Vectorization
nodes.short: Writing whole-array operations so the looping happens in compiled code, not in the interpreter. In Python it can be hundreds of times faster than an explicit loop.
nodes.long: Vectorized code states an operation on whole arrays, such as 1.0 / x, with no explicit loop; the loop still runs, but inside precompiled C or Fortran, which avoids the interpreter's cost for each element. The idea reached Python with Numeric in 1995 and carried on in NumPy. In one published test, reciprocals of one million integers took 2.91 seconds in a Python loop and 4.6 milliseconds vectorized, about 630 times faster. In an MIT course benchmark, multiplying two 4096 by 4096 matrices took 21,042 seconds in nested Python loops and 0.41 seconds in Intel MKL, about 51,000 times faster; most of that gap came from cache use, parallel threads and vector instructions rather than from C itself. Loop-heavy code is the worst case, so typical programs gain less.
nodes.sleeper: In 1990, speed meant writing the loop in Fortran or C. In scientific Python the advice runs the other way: avoid writing the loop at all, and hand whole arrays to a compiled library.

code.text:
import numpy as np
x = np.arange(1, 1_000_001)
slow = [1.0 / v for v in x]   # interpreted loop, one element at a time
fast = 1.0 / x                # one expression; the loop runs in compiled C

nodes.title: SciPy
nodes.short: Python's library of scientific algorithms on top of NumPy: optimization, linear algebra, sparse matrices, signal processing and statistics. Much of it wraps Fortran.
nodes.long: SciPy grew out of packages that Travis Oliphant wrote on top of Numeric, joined by Pearu Peterson's F2PY tool for binding Python to Fortran. In 2001 Eric Jones and Travis Vaught founded Enthought and started the SciPy project to bring these pieces together, and the 0.1 announcement came on 20 August 2001. It offers optimization, sparse and dense linear algebra, signal processing, statistics and fast Fourier transforms. Much of that rests on established Fortran libraries such as QUADPACK, FITPACK and ODEPACK, and on BLAS and LAPACK. The 2020 SciPy paper counted over 600 contributors and over 100,000 dependent repositories.
nodes.sleeper: In 2020 about a quarter of SciPy's code was Fortran. Its roadmap now aims to remove all of it, because Fortran 77 is hard to maintain and complicates builds on platforms such as macOS arm64 and Windows on Arm.

code.text:
from scipy.optimize import minimize
result = minimize(lambda x: (x[0] - 3) ** 2, x0=[0.0])
print(result.x)   # close to [3.]

nodes.title: Matplotlib
nodes.short: Python's foundational plotting library, begun by John D. Hunter around 2002 to 2003, which turns arrays and tables into line plots, histograms and other charts.
nodes.long: Matplotlib draws charts from Python data. The documentation names John D. Hunter (1968 to 2012) as the original author, its copyright notice runs from 2002, and Wikipedia gives 2003 as the first release. Other plotting libraries build on it, such as Seaborn for statistical charts, and it plots NumPy arrays and pandas tables. Hunter's 2007 paper in Computing in Science and Engineering has been cited about 25,900 times. Matplotlib 3.11.2 appeared on 11 September 2026, and the package had about 162 million downloads that month.

code.text:
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
plt.plot([1, 2, 3], [1, 4, 9])
plt.show()

nodes.title: Deep Learning
nodes.short: Neural networks with many layers, trained on large data sets using GPUs. Hinton's 2006 deep-belief-net paper is the usual marker of the revival.
nodes.long: Deep learning means neural networks with many layers, trained by backpropagation on large amounts of data. Hinton, Osindero and Teh's 2006 paper on deep belief nets is the usual marker of its revival, though that is an interpretation rather than a formal date. Three things made it practical: GPUs, which in 2009 cut one network's training time from several weeks to about a day in work by Raina, Madhavan and Ng; the ImageNet data set (2009); and AlexNet, which won the ImageNet contest in 2012. Open frameworks (Theano, TensorFlow, PyTorch) then let researchers write networks as ordinary code, and the 2017 Transformer made the approach scale to language.
nodes.sleeper: The neural networks you may remember from the 1980s had few layers and ran on ordinary processors. Their descendants have many layers and up to hundreds of billions of parameters (AlexNet 60 million, GPT-3 175 billion), and they run on GPUs.

refs.label: Hinton, Osindero and Teh: A fast learning algorithm for deep belief nets (2006)
Raina, Madhavan and Ng: Large-scale deep unsupervised learning using graphics processors (ICML 2009)

nodes.title: NumPy
nodes.short: Python's fast array library. Nearly every scientific and machine learning package builds on it.
nodes.long: Travis Oliphant unified the Numeric and Numarray projects into NumPy. It stores arrays in compact C memory and calls optimized BLAS and LAPACK routines, so a vectorized operation can beat a Python loop by orders of magnitude.

code.text:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([[1, 2], [3, 4]])
print(a @ a)  # matrix product

nodes.title: CUDA
nodes.short: NVIDIA's platform for general computation on GPUs, programmed as an extension of C. Released in 2007, it sits beneath PyTorch and other frameworks.
nodes.long: CUDA, short for Compute Unified Device Architecture, is NVIDIA's platform for running general computation on its GPUs. It was led by Ian Buck, a Stanford PhD student who had developed Brook and joined NVIDIA in 2004, and by John Nickolls, then director of architecture for GPU computing. The CUDA 1.0 programming guide says its API is an extension to the C programming language for a minimum learning curve. Wikipedia lists the first release as February 2007, while NVIDIA's CUDA 1.0 manuals are dated June 2007, so 2007 is the safe year. CUDA can be programmed from C++, Python and Fortran or through libraries such as PyTorch, and CUDA 13.4 Update 1 was current in September 2026.
nodes.sleeper: GPUs once ran only graphics code. CUDA let C programmers use them for general computation, and libraries such as cuBLAS and cuDNN, and frameworks such as PyTorch, now sit on top of it.

nodes.title: scikit-learn
nodes.short: Python's general-purpose toolkit for classical machine learning: regression, classification, clustering and preprocessing behind one fit and predict interface.
nodes.long: scikit-learn began in 2007 as a Google Summer of Code project by David Cournapeau. Its first public release came on 1 February 2010 from Fabian Pedregosa, Gaël Varoquaux, Alexandre Gramfort and Vincent Michel of INRIA. It provides regression, classification, clustering and data preprocessing, and models such as random forests and support vector machines all share the same fit and predict calls. It builds on NumPy and SciPy and uses the BSD license. The 2011 paper describing it has about 95,000 citations, and the package had about 188 million downloads in September 2026.

code.text:
from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeClassifier
X = [[0, 0], [0, 1], [1, 0], [1, 1]]
y = [0, 0, 0, 1]                        # logical AND
model = DecisionTreeClassifier().fit(X, y)
print(model.predict([[1, 1]]))          # [1]

nodes.title: pandas
nodes.short: Wes McKinney's DataFrame library for Python: tables with named columns that can be read from files, cleaned, joined, grouped and summarized.
nodes.long: Wes McKinney began pandas in 2008 at AQR Capital Management and open-sourced it by the end of 2009. Its central object, the DataFrame, is a table with named columns held in memory, with operations to read files such as CSV, clean and join data, and group and summarize it. It is built on NumPy arrays. McKinney's 2010 SciPy conference paper, 'Data Structures for Statistical Computing in Python', has been cited about 9,600 times. In September 2026 pandas was downloaded about 547 million times from PyPI, ranking 40th overall and second to NumPy among scientific packages, and version 3.0.6 appeared on 17 September 2026.

code.text:
import pandas as pd
df = pd.DataFrame({"region": ["east", "west", "east"], "total": [10, 20, 30]})
print(df.groupby("region")["total"].sum())   # east 40, west 20

refs.label: McKinney: Data Structures for Statistical Computing in Python

nodes.title: AlexNet
nodes.short: The 2012 convolutional network that won the ImageNet contest with a 15.3 percent top-5 error, against 26.2 percent for the runner-up, after training on two GPUs.
nodes.long: Alex Krizhevsky, Ilya Sutskever and Geoffrey Hinton at the University of Toronto entered AlexNet in the 2012 ImageNet contest (ILSVRC-2012) and won with a top-5 test error of 15.3 percent; the second-best entry reached 26.2 percent. It has 60 million parameters and 650,000 neurons, with five convolutional and three fully connected layers, and took five to six days to train on two GTX 580 GPUs with 3 GB of memory each. The authors wrote that their results could be improved simply by waiting for faster GPUs and bigger datasets. Presented at NIPS 2012, the paper has been cited about 131,600 times, counting its later reprint in Communications of the ACM.

refs.label: Krizhevsky, Sutskever and Hinton: ImageNet Classification with Deep Convolutional Neural Networks (NIPS 2012)

nodes.title: Jupyter Notebook
nodes.short: A notebook is a web page mixing code, results and prose. Jupyter, spun out of IPython in 2014, is the usual notebook tool for data science and AI work.
nodes.long: A notebook is a document opened in a web browser that mixes code cells, their output and explanatory text, so an analysis can be read and run as one page. The IPython Notebook appeared in 2011, and in 2014 it was spun off as Project Jupyter by seven founding members including Fernando Pérez, Brian Granger and Min Ragan-Kelley. GitHub counted 2.42 million repositories containing a notebook in 2025, up 75 percent from 1.4 million in 2024. Cells can be run in any order, which causes trouble: of 936 published notebooks that should have been runnable, 73 percent could not be reproduced by straightforward means, and only 879 of 22,578 Python notebooks from biomedical papers gave identical results when re-run.
nodes.sleeper: In 1990 a program was a file run from start to finish. A notebook keeps state between cells and lets you run them in any order, which makes exploration easy and results hard to repeat.

refs.label: Wang et al.: Assessing and Restoring Reproducibility of Jupyter Notebooks (ASE 2020)

nodes.title: Keras
nodes.short: François Chollet's high-level neural-network API, begun in March 2015. Keras 3 runs on top of JAX, TensorFlow or PyTorch.
nodes.long: Keras is a library for assembling neural networks from layers, created by François Chollet; its first commit is dated 28 March 2015. For years it ran on top of other engines: up to version 2.3 it supported TensorFlow, Microsoft's CNTK, Theano and PlaidML as back ends. Keras 3, described as a full rewrite, runs on JAX, TensorFlow or PyTorch, plus OpenVINO for inference only. The package uses the Apache-2.0 license, had about 64,300 stars on GitHub in October 2026 and about 12 million downloads in September 2026.

code.text:
import keras
model = keras.Sequential([keras.Input(shape=(3,)), keras.layers.Dense(1)])
model.summary()   # one Dense layer: a 3-by-1 weight matrix plus one bias

nodes.title: Tensor
nodes.short: In machine learning code, an array with any number of dimensions. Mathematicians use the word more narrowly, for a coordinate-free object such as a stress tensor.
nodes.long: Programmers use a ladder of names for arrays: a scalar is a single number, a vector is a list, a matrix is a grid, and a tensor is the general case with any number of axes, such as a color video indexed by frame, row, column and color channel. In frameworks such as PyTorch a tensor is an array that can also live on a GPU and record the operations applied to it, so that gradients can be computed. The 'n-way array' sense is older than the frameworks, as in Kolda and Bader's 2009 survey of tensor methods, but TensorFlow (2015) put the word in a major framework's name. Mathematics means something narrower: an object describing a multilinear relationship, defined without reference to coordinates, like the stress tensor of a material. NumPy's guide advises avoiding the mathematical names for plain arrays.
nodes.sleeper: In C or Fortran terms, a machine-learning tensor is simply a multidimensional array. The extras are GPU placement and gradient tracking, not new mathematics.

code.text:
import numpy as np
video = np.zeros((10, 480, 640, 3))   # frames, rows, columns, color channels
print(video.ndim, video.shape)        # 4 (10, 480, 640, 3)

refs.label: NumPy docs: The absolute basics for beginners
Kolda and Bader: Tensor Decompositions and Applications

nodes.title: TensorFlow
nodes.short: Google's machine-learning framework, open-sourced in November 2015. It built models as dataflow graphs, and PyTorch overtook it in research papers by 2019.
nodes.long: Google Brain released TensorFlow as open source on 9 November 2015. The 2016 paper describes it as an interface for expressing machine-learning algorithms and an implementation for running them on anything from mobile devices to thousands of GPU cards. TensorFlow 1.x had users define a graph of operations and then run it; TensorFlow 2.0, released on 30 September 2019, made line-by-line eager execution the default. Counts of papers at top conferences show PyTorch overtaking it in research during 2018 and 2019. TensorFlow remains maintained and widely installed, with about 12 million PyPI downloads in September 2026 against 62 million for torch, and its only 2026 minor release so far was 2.21.0 in March.
nodes.sleeper: TensorFlow 1.x made you describe a computation as a graph first and run it afterwards, unlike ordinary code. Version 2 (2019) switched to running line by line, which is how PyTorch had worked from the start. PyTorch 2 (2023) later added compilation, so the two designs have converged.

nodes.title: PyTorch
nodes.short: The dominant deep-learning framework: tensors on GPUs with automatic differentiation.
nodes.long: Released by Facebook's AI group in 2016, PyTorch overtook TensorFlow in research by making models feel like ordinary Python. Training a neural network is mostly matrix multiplication on GPUs.

nodes.title: Hugging Face Transformers
nodes.short: The Python library that downloads and runs pretrained models such as BERT and later large language models. Begun in 2018 by Hugging Face.
nodes.long: Transformers began with a first commit by Thomas Wolf on 29 October 2018. It was first released as pytorch-pretrained-bert, then as pytorch-transformers in 2019, and then simply as transformers. It downloads pretrained models from the Hugging Face Hub and runs them in a few lines of Python, which made the Transformer architecture a pip install away. Hugging Face was founded in 2016 by Clément Delangue, Julien Chaumond and Thomas Wolf. The library uses the Apache-2.0 license and had about 96 million downloads in September 2026, with its companion huggingface-hub package at about 232 million.

code.text:
from transformers import pipeline
classify = pipeline("sentiment-analysis")
print(classify("I love this"))   # a label such as POSITIVE, with a score

nodes.title: GPT-3
nodes.short: OpenAI's May 2020 language model with 175 billion parameters, ten times more than any earlier non-sparse language model.
nodes.long: GPT-3, described by Brown and colleagues at OpenAI in May 2020, is an autoregressive language model, meaning that it predicts the next piece of text from the text so far, with 175 billion parameters. The paper calls this 10 times more than any previous non-sparse language model, and it has been cited about 64,000 times. It followed OpenAI's first GPT of 2018 and Google's BERT. ChatGPT, the OpenAI chat product, was released on 30 November 2022, and Meta's LLaMA paper of February 2023 reported that its 13-billion-parameter model outperformed GPT-3 on most benchmarks.

refs.label: Brown et al.: Language Models are Few-Shot Learners (2020)

nodes.title: Open-Weight Models
nodes.short: Models whose trained parameters can be downloaded and run, such as LLaMA, Mistral 7B and DeepSeek-R1. The code, data and license may differ from open source.
nodes.long: Open weights means that a model's trained parameters are published for download, while the training code, data and license terms may differ. Meta's LLaMA, in February 2023, was trained on publicly available datasets only, and its paper reports that LLaMA-13B outperforms GPT-3 (175B) on most benchmarks. Llama 2 followed in July 2023 under a custom license, Mistral 7B in September 2023 under Apache-2.0, DeepSeek-R1 in January 2025 under MIT, and OpenAI's gpt-oss-120b in August 2025 under Apache-2.0. These models run on a shared Python stack: PyTorch, Hugging Face Transformers and its Hub, and vLLM, with PyTorch and vLLM hosted by the PyTorch Foundation.
nodes.sleeper: Open weights is not open source in the sense you may know. The numbers can be downloaded and run, but the training code, data and license may be closed or restricted: Llama 2, for example, has a custom license.

nodes.title: Determinant, Inverse and Eigenvalues
nodes.short: What a square matrix does to space: the determinant says how much areas scale, the inverse undoes it, and eigenvectors are the directions it only stretches.
nodes.long: The determinant is the factor by which a matrix scales areas; a negative value flips orientation, and zero means space is squashed onto a line or a point, so the matrix cannot be undone. The inverse is the matrix that undoes the transformation, and solving A x = v means applying the inverse to v. An eigenvector is a direction the matrix only stretches or squishes, and its eigenvalue is the stretch factor. For the matrix [[2, 1], [1, 2]] the determinant is 3, and the eigenvalues are 3 (direction [1, 1]) and 1 (direction [1, -1]), which multiply to the determinant. James Sylvester coined the word matrix in 1850, and Arthur Cayley published the first formula for an inverse by 1853 and his abstract treatment in 1858.

code.text:
import numpy as np
M = np.array([[2, 1], [1, 2]])
print(np.linalg.det(M))            # about 3.0
print(np.linalg.eigvalsh(M))       # [1. 3.]
print(np.linalg.solve(M, [3, 3]))  # [1. 1.]

nodes.title: Row-Major and Column-Major Storage
nodes.short: Memory is one long line, so a grid of numbers needs a layout rule. C and NumPy store row by row; Fortran, MATLAB, Julia and R store column by column.
nodes.long: A matrix in memory is a flat run of numbers plus a rule for finding element (i, j). Row-major order, used by C and by NumPy by default, stores each row after the previous one, while column-major order, used by Fortran, MATLAB, Julia and R, stores each column in turn. The 2 by 3 matrix [[1, 2, 3], [4, 5, 6]] lies in memory as 1 2 3 4 5 6 in row-major order and as 1 4 2 5 3 6 in column-major order. Fortran, first released in 1957, uses the column convention, and the numerical libraries written in it kept it, so mixing languages means transposing or reading layouts carefully. NumPy records a layout as strides, the byte distances between neighboring rows and columns, and can hold either order; sparse formats such as SciPy's CSR store only the nonzero entries.
nodes.sleeper: Fortran's 1957 column-major layout has outlived Fortran as a default: MATLAB, Julia and R use it too, and NumPy can store arrays in either order so that Fortran and C libraries can read its data directly.

code.text:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([[1, 2, 3], [4, 5, 6]], dtype=np.int64)
print(a.ravel(order="C"))   # [1 2 3 4 5 6]  row by row
print(a.ravel(order="F"))   # [1 4 2 5 3 6]  column by column
print(a.strides)            # (24, 8): 24 bytes to the next row, 8 to the next column

refs.label: NumPy docs: ndarray internal memory layout

nodes.title: Automatic Differentiation
nodes.short: Computing exact derivatives of a program by applying the chain rule to each operation it performs. The reverse mode, from 1970, is what neural-network training uses.
nodes.long: Automatic differentiation obtains the derivative of a computed result by applying the chain rule to each operation the program performs, rather than by manipulating a formula or by approximating with small differences. Seppo Linnainmaa's 1970 master's thesis introduced the reverse mode, which sweeps backward from the output and underlies backpropagation. Frameworks now offer it as a built-in feature: PyTorch's autograd collects the derivatives of the error with respect to the model's parameters, and JAX provides jax.grad. SymPy differentiates symbolically and produces a formula, whereas automatic differentiation produces numbers.

code.text:
import torch
x = torch.tensor(3.0, requires_grad=True)
y = x ** 2
y.backward()
print(x.grad)   # tensor(6.)

refs.label: PyTorch tutorial: Automatic differentiation with autograd

nodes.title: EISPACK
nodes.short: A 1970s Fortran library for the eigenvalues and eigenvectors of matrices, from Argonne National Laboratory and collaborators. LAPACK largely replaced it.
nodes.long: EISPACK is a collection of Fortran subroutines that compute the eigenvalues and eigenvectors of nine classes of matrices. Its documentation dates from 1974 ('How to Use EISPACK') and 1976, when Springer published the EISPACK guide by Smith, Boyle, Dongarra, Garbow, Ikebe, Klema and Moler. Netlib, the online repository that hosts it, says it has been superseded for the most part by LAPACK. Cleve Moler wrote the first MATLAB so that his students could use EISPACK and LINPACK without writing Fortran programs.

nodes.title: LINPACK
nodes.short: A Fortran library for linear equations and least squares, documented in 1979. LAPACK replaced it, but the name lives on as a benchmark.
nodes.long: LINPACK is a collection of Fortran subroutines that analyze and solve linear equations and linear least-squares problems. Its users' guide was published by SIAM in 1979, written by Dongarra, Bunch, Moler and Stewart. It was designed for the supercomputers of the 1970s and early 1980s and used column-oriented algorithms to keep data close together in memory, matching Fortran's column-major layout. Netlib describes it as largely superseded by LAPACK, which reorganized the same kind of work around blocks of data. Moler built MATLAB as a friendlier front end to LINPACK and EISPACK, and the LINPACK name survives as a benchmark.

nodes.title: Convolutional Neural Networks
nodes.short: Neural networks that apply the same small learned filters across an image. LeCun and colleagues' 1989 and 1998 papers describe early examples.
nodes.long: A convolutional neural network applies the same small set of learned weights, called a filter, at every position of an image, so it can respond to an edge or a shape wherever it appears. LeCun and colleagues trained such networks by backpropagation for handwritten zip-code recognition in a 1989 paper, and a 1998 paper applied the approach to document recognition. AlexNet in 2012, with five convolutional and three fully connected layers, carried the idea to large photographs. Convolutional layers are among the operations built on GEMM, the general matrix multiplication. The Caffe framework, from UC Berkeley, was built to train and deploy convolutional networks.

refs.label: LeCun et al.: Backpropagation Applied to Handwritten Zip Code Recognition (1989)
LeCun et al.: Gradient-based learning applied to document recognition (1998)

nodes.title: SVMs, Random Forests and Boosting
nodes.short: The pre-deep-learning toolkit that still does well on medium-sized tables: support vector machines (1992), random forests (2001) and boosting.
nodes.long: Boser, Guyon and Vapnik introduced support vector machines in 1992, and Cortes and Vapnik's 'Support-vector networks' followed in 1995. Breiman's 2001 'Random Forests' defined a combination of tree predictors in which each tree depends on the values of a random vector sampled independently. Gradient boosting, from Friedman's 2001 paper, was later turned into the fast libraries XGBoost and LightGBM. None of these disappeared when neural networks returned: across 45 tabular datasets, a 2022 study found tree-based models still state of the art on medium-sized data of about 10,000 samples. scikit-learn, XGBoost and LightGBM remain among the most downloaded machine-learning packages.

refs.label: Grinsztajn et al.: tree-based models on tabular data (2022)

nodes.title: PageRank
nodes.short: Google's original ranking method. A page's score is the principal eigenvector of the web's link matrix, found by repeated multiplication.
nodes.long: Sergey Brin and Larry Page described PageRank in a 1998 paper on the Google search engine. Each page passes its score along its outgoing links, and the scores form a probability distribution over pages. The result corresponds to the principal eigenvector of the normalized link matrix of the web, and a simple iterative algorithm computes it; the paper reported 26 million pages processed in a few hours on a medium-size workstation. In miniature, three pages with links A to B, A to C, B to C and C to A settle at scores 0.4, 0.2 and 0.4 when a starting guess is multiplied by the link matrix over and over. The paper's formula adds a damping factor d, which this miniature leaves out.

code.text:
import numpy as np
L = np.array([[0, 0, 1], [0.5, 0, 0], [0.5, 1, 0]])   # column j: where page j sends its score
r = np.ones(3) / 3                                      # start with equal scores
for _ in range(100):
    r = L @ r                                           # pass scores along the links
print(r)   # [0.4 0.2 0.4]

nodes.title: ATLAS, OpenBLAS and Intel MKL
nodes.short: Faster, hardware-specific builds of the BLAS. ATLAS tunes itself at install time, OpenBLAS descends from GotoBLAS, and Intel MKL is the chip maker's own.
nodes.long: The reference BLAS on netlib are portable but slow, so tuned versions exist with the same interface. ATLAS (Whaley, Petitet and Dongarra, described in a 2001 paper) generates its kernels by automated search at install time; its last stable release is 3.10.3 of July 2016. GotoBLAS, by Kazushige Goto, used register and cache blocking, described in a 2008 paper with Robert van de Geijn, and lives on as OpenBLAS, a BSD-licensed fork of GotoBLAS2 maintained by developers including Zhang Xianyi and Martin Kroeker. Intel MKL is Intel's tuned BLAS and LAPACK; in an MIT benchmark it multiplied two 4096 by 4096 matrices in 0.41 seconds, about 40 percent of the machine's peak.
