nodes.sleeper: In Python you rarely choose a BLAS yourself. NumPy and SciPy pick one when they are built, and SciPy's build documentation lists OpenBLAS (the default), MKL, Apple Accelerate, BLIS and ATLAS as options.

nodes.title: OpenCV
nodes.short: An open-source computer-vision library in C++ with Python bindings, first released in June 2000 according to Wikipedia.
nodes.long: OpenCV is a library of computer-vision routines written in C++ with Python bindings, released under the Apache-2.0 license; in Python, cv2.imread reads an image file. Its developers have included Intel, Willow Garage and Itseez, and Wikipedia gives June 2000 as its first release, while a start at Intel in 1999 could not be verified. Because an image is a grid of numbers, many of its operations are matrix operations on pixels. The unofficial opencv-python wheels on PyPI had about 31 million downloads in September 2026 and the headless variant about 38 million, and the repository had about 91,000 GitHub stars.

nodes.title: IPython
nodes.short: Fernando Pérez's enhanced interactive Python shell, started in 2001. It added 'magic' commands and became the kernel inside Jupyter.
nodes.long: IPython is an interactive Python shell that adds conveniences to the plain prompt, such as 'magic' commands: %timeit sum(range(1000)) times an expression. Fernando Pérez started it in 2001. The IPython Notebook, a browser document mixing code, results and prose, first appeared in 2011, and in 2014 that part was spun off as Project Jupyter, with IPython remaining as the kernel that runs the Python code. Pérez and Granger's 2007 paper about it has been cited about 2,900 times, and version 9.17.1 was released on 1 September 2026.

nodes.title: Matrix Factorization and the Netflix Prize
nodes.short: A 2006 contest with a US$1 million prize for better movie recommendations, and the matrix factorization used to predict ratings from a mostly empty matrix.
nodes.long: In 2006 Netflix released more than 100 million ratings from about 500,000 anonymous customers on more than 17,000 movies, and offered US$1 million to the first team to beat its own recommendation algorithm by 10 percent. The data forms a very large users-by-movies matrix that is almost entirely empty, because each customer rates only a small share of the films. Matrix factorization places every user and every movie in a shared space of a few hidden factors, so that a predicted rating is the inner product of a user vector and a movie vector. The two main training methods were stochastic gradient descent and alternating least squares. Koren, Bell and Volinsky summarized the approach in a 2009 IEEE Computer article.

code.text:
import numpy as np
P = np.array([[1, 0], [0, 1], [1, 1]])   # three users, two hidden factors each
Q = np.array([[5, 2], [1, 4], [3, 3]])   # three movies, two hidden factors each
print(P @ Q.T)   # predicted ratings: [[5 1 3] [2 4 3] [7 5 6]]

refs.label: Koren, Bell and Volinsky: Matrix Factorization Techniques for Recommender Systems

nodes.title: SymPy
nodes.short: A pure-Python library for symbolic mathematics: it manipulates formulas, so differentiating x cubed gives 3 times x squared, not a number.
nodes.long: SymPy does algebra with symbols instead of numbers: asked to differentiate x cubed, it returns the exact formula, 3 times x squared, not an approximation. It is written in pure Python by a community known as the SymPy Development Team; Wikipedia dates it to about 2007, and PyPI's first upload is dated 26 April 2008. A 2017 paper in PeerJ Computer Science describes it, with authors including Meurer, Smith, Paprocki and Rocklin. Its latest PyPI release was 1.14.0 in April 2025, although the project's repository was still receiving changes in October 2026, and it had about 130 million downloads in September 2026.

code.text:
from sympy import symbols, diff
x = symbols("x")
print(diff(x**3, x))   # 3*x**2

refs.label: SymPy: computer algebra in Python (PeerJ CS, 2017)

nodes.title: ImageNet
nodes.short: A labeled image data set from 2009 that gave computer vision a shared benchmark. AlexNet won its 2012 contest.
nodes.long: ImageNet, described by Deng and colleagues at CVPR 2009, is a large collection of labeled images. AlexNet's authors describe it as over 15 million labeled high-resolution images in roughly 22,000 categories. The yearly ImageNet Large Scale Visual Recognition Challenge, ILSVRC, gave researchers a shared test on the same data: in 2012 AlexNet won it with a top-5 error rate of 15.3 percent against 26.2 percent for the second-best entry. The CVPR paper has been cited about 76,300 times.

nodes.title: The Two-Language Problem
nodes.short: The split between a friendly high-level language for prototyping and a fast low-level one for production. Julia was designed to remove it; Python works around it.
nodes.long: In numerical computing the common practice was to prototype in a high-level language and then rewrite for speed or deployment. The Julia language, announced on 14 February 2012 by Bezanson, Karpinski, Shah and Edelman and released as version 1.0 on 8 August 2018, was built to remove that split. Their 2017 SIAM Review paper lists it among the 'laws of nature' that Julia questions: that high-level dynamic programs have to be slow, and that one must prototype in one language and then rewrite in another for speed or deployment. Python took the other route, keeping a friendly front end and pushing the loops into compiled libraries such as NumPy and BLAS, or into Cython, Numba and Pythran. The cost shows in SciPy, which in 2020 was about half Python, a quarter Fortran and a fifth C.

refs.label: Bezanson et al.: Julia, a fresh approach to numerical computing (SIAM Review)

nodes.title: Attention Mechanism
nodes.short: A way for a network to weigh which parts of its input matter for each output. Introduced for translation in 2014, it became the core of the Transformer.
nodes.long: In 2014 Bahdanau, Cho and Bengio let a translation network look back at the input words that matter while it produces each output word, learning to align the two at the same time. The Transformer of 2017 kept only this idea. Each query is compared with every key by a dot product, the scores are turned into weights that add up to one by a function called softmax, and the output is the weighted sum of the values. Written with matrices this is softmax(QK^T / sqrt(d)) V, two matrix products, which is why GPUs handle it well. The 2014 paper has been cited about 30,100 times.

code.text:
import numpy as np

def attention(Q, K, V):
    scores = Q @ K.T / np.sqrt(K.shape[1])   # compare every query with every key
    w = np.exp(scores)
    w = w / w.sum(axis=1, keepdims=True)     # softmax: each row sums to 1
    return w @ V                             # weighted sum of the values

I = np.eye(2)
print(attention(I, I, I))   # about [[0.67 0.33] [0.33 0.67]]

refs.label: Bahdanau, Cho and Bengio: Neural Machine Translation by Jointly Learning to Align and Translate (2014)

nodes.title: cuBLAS and cuDNN
nodes.short: NVIDIA's GPU versions of the BLAS (cuBLAS, 2007) and of deep-learning primitives (cuDNN, 2014), the vendor kernel libraries beneath PyTorch and other frameworks.
nodes.long: cuBLAS, first documented in June 2007 as CUBLAS 1.0, implements the BLAS on top of CUDA. To stay compatible with Fortran environments it uses column-major storage and one-based indexing, and its manual even includes Fortran bindings and a Fortran 77 example. cuDNN, described in a 2014 paper, supplies optimized deep-learning primitives; its authors argued that kernels must be reoptimized for each new processor, the same reasoning that created the BLAS. In the usual stack, Python code calls a framework such as PyTorch, which calls cuDNN and cuBLAS, which run on CUDA and the GPU.
nodes.sleeper: NVIDIA's GPU library of 2007 used column-major storage and counted from 1, to stay compatible with Fortran, whose first compiler dates from 1957.

refs.label: Chetlur et al.: cuDNN, efficient primitives for deep learning (2014)

nodes.title: Dask
nodes.short: A Python library that splits NumPy- and pandas-style work across many cores or machines. Matthew Rocklin's first commit is dated December 2014.
nodes.long: Dask lets code written in the style of NumPy arrays and pandas tables run in pieces across the cores of one machine or across a cluster. Matthew Rocklin made the first commit on 21 December 2014, and the first PyPI upload followed on 29 January 2015. A call such as dd.read_csv('sales-*.csv').groupby('region').total.sum().compute() reads many files in pieces and combines the results. Dask uses the BSD-3 license, had about 25.7 million downloads in September 2026 and about 13,900 GitHub stars. PySpark, a comparable tool, had about 48.3 million downloads that month.

code.text:
import dask.array as da
x = da.ones((10000, 10000), chunks=(1000, 1000))   # 100 blocks of 1000 by 1000
print(x.sum().compute())                            # 100000000.0

nodes.title: XGBoost and LightGBM
nodes.short: Libraries for gradient-boosted decision trees: XGBoost (2014) and LightGBM (2016). Boosted trees remain a strong choice for tables of data.
nodes.long: Gradient boosting builds many small decision trees in sequence, each correcting the errors of the earlier ones; Friedman published the method in 2001. XGBoost, whose first commit by Tianqi Chen is dated 6 February 2014, made it fast and easy to use, and its 2016 paper with Guestrin has about 62,800 citations. LightGBM, begun by Guolin Ke at Microsoft in August 2016, is a faster alternative. A 2022 study across 45 tabular datasets found tree-based models still state of the art on medium-sized data of about 10,000 samples. In September 2026 XGBoost had about 30 million PyPI downloads and LightGBM about 19 million.

nodes.title: TPUs
nodes.short: Google's custom chips for neural-network arithmetic, running in its data centers since 2015. At the core is a large matrix-multiply unit.
nodes.long: The Tensor Processing Unit is a custom chip that Google designed to accelerate neural networks, and it had been running in Google's data centers since 2015. Its first generation handled inference, the running of trained networks. In the 2017 paper by Jouppi and colleagues, the heart of that chip was a matrix multiply unit with 65,536 8-bit multiply-accumulators, a peak of 92 trillion operations per second and 28 MiB of software-managed on-chip memory. Cloud TPU v2 and v3 use Google's bfloat16 format in a 128 by 128 grid of arithmetic units called a systolic array. Ironwood, the seventh generation, was announced on 9 April 2025 and is described as the first designed specifically for inference, with pods of up to 9,216 chips.

refs.label: Jouppi et al.: In-Datacenter Performance Analysis of a Tensor Processing Unit (2017)

nodes.title: Google Colab
nodes.short: Google's hosted Jupyter notebook service, released in 2017. It needs no setup and offers free access to GPUs and TPUs.
nodes.long: Google Colab, short for Colaboratory, is a hosted Jupyter notebook service from Google Research. Google describes it as needing no setup and providing free access to computing resources, including GPUs and TPUs, so a browser is enough to run machine-learning code on accelerator hardware. It is proprietary and freemium, it is not distributed on PyPI, and Wikipedia gives 2017 as its release year.

nodes.title: ONNX
nodes.short: Open Neural Network Exchange: a file format that lets a model trained in one framework run in another runtime. Started by Facebook and Microsoft in 2017.
nodes.long: ONNX, started in September 2017 by Facebook and Microsoft and now under the Linux Foundation, is a shared file format for neural networks, so that a model trained in one framework can run in a different runtime. Microsoft's ONNX Runtime executes such files and had about 70 million PyPI downloads in September 2026, against 13 million for the onnx package itself. When Microsoft ended its CNTK framework with release 2.7 in 2019, the README encouraged users to operationalize models through ONNX and ONNX Runtime. The onnx package uses the Apache-2.0 license; the project initially used MIT.

nodes.title: Tensor Cores
nodes.short: Matrix-multiply units inside NVIDIA GPUs, introduced with the Volta V100 in 2017, that multiply small blocks of numbers in a single step.
nodes.long: Tensor Cores first appeared in NVIDIA's Volta generation, the V100 of 2017. Each one is a 4 by 4 by 4 matrix processing array that computes D = A * B + C, taking half-precision inputs and accumulating in 16-bit or 32-bit floating point, and performing 64 fused multiply-add operations per clock. A V100 holds 640 of them, eight per streaming multiprocessor, and NVIDIA quoted up to 125 Tensor TFLOPS. Performance is best when matrix dimensions are multiples of 16 bytes, or 128 bytes on the later A100. Tensor Cores put the central operation of neural networks directly into the silicon.
nodes.sleeper: Numerical computing once defaulted to double precision. Tensor Cores multiply half-precision inputs, and Google's bfloat16 keeps FP32's exponent range with only 7 mantissa bits, because neural networks care more about the exponent.

refs.label: NVIDIA: Programming Tensor Cores in CUDA 9

nodes.title: BERT
nodes.short: Google's October 2018 language model, pretrained on text and then fine-tuned for tasks. The name means Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers.
nodes.long: BERT, from Devlin and colleagues at Google in October 2018, is a Transformer model that is first pretrained on large amounts of text and then fine-tuned for specific tasks. Its paper contrasts the approach with earlier work by Peters and colleagues and with OpenAI's first GPT (Radford and colleagues, 2018). It has been cited about 121,700 times. The library that became Hugging Face Transformers was first released as pytorch-pretrained-bert in November 2018.
nodes.sleeper: Older models still dominate downloads on the Hugging Face Hub: on 1 October 2026 bert-base-uncased had about 40.6 million recent downloads and gpt2 about 15.7 million.

nodes.title: JAX
nodes.short: Google's library for array computation with automatic differentiation and program transformations, aimed at accelerators such as GPUs and TPUs.
nodes.long: JAX, begun at Google in 2018, describes itself as a Python library for accelerator-oriented array computation and program transformation. Its README names eleven authors, including James Bradbury, Roy Frostig, Peter Hawkins, Matthew Johnson, Dougal Maclaurin and Adam Paszke. Code is ordinary array code, and functions such as jax.grad turn a function into one that computes its derivative. JAX uses the Apache-2.0 license. It is small next to PyTorch in downloads, about 8.6 million on PyPI in September 2026 against 12 million a year earlier, and it is one of the back ends of Keras 3.

code.text:
import jax
print(jax.grad(lambda x: x ** 2)(3.0))   # 6.0

nodes.title: Polars
nodes.short: A DataFrame library written from scratch in Rust, started in 2020 by Ritchie Vink. It runs queries in parallel and exchanges data with Arrow.
nodes.long: Polars is a DataFrame library written from scratch in Rust, with a Python interface. Ritchie Vink made the first commit on 10 May 2020. It runs queries in parallel across cores and can consume and produce Apache Arrow data, often without copying. It is a newer alternative to pandas, and part of a pattern of the early 2020s in which a Python front end sits on compiled code written in Rust or C++, as with Ruff, uv and DuckDB. Polars downloads rose from about 0.1 million in September 2022 to 25 million in September 2025 and 52 million in September 2026.

code.text:
import polars as pl
df = pl.DataFrame({"region": ["east", "west", "east"], "total": [10, 20, 30]})
print(df.group_by("region").agg(pl.col("total").sum()))

nodes.title: Scaling Laws
nodes.short: Empirical findings that a language model's loss falls as a smooth power law in model size, data and compute, which made scaling up a predictable recipe.
nodes.long: In January 2020 Kaplan and colleagues reported that the loss of a language model scales as a power law with model size, dataset size and the compute used for training, with some trends spanning more than seven orders of magnitude. Training compute is roughly C = 6NBS, where N is the number of parameters, B the batch size and S the number of steps, which works out to about six floating-point operations per parameter per training token. In March 2022 Hoffmann and colleagues, in the Chinchilla study, concluded that for every doubling of model size the number of training tokens should also be doubled; a 70-billion-parameter model trained on four times more data than the 280-billion-parameter Gopher outperformed it.

refs.label: Kaplan et al.: Scaling Laws for Neural Language Models (2020)
Hoffmann et al.: Training Compute-Optimal Large Language Models (2022)

nodes.title: LangChain
nodes.short: A Python framework for chaining language-model calls, prompts, tools and document retrieval. Harrison Chase made the first commit in October 2022.
nodes.long: LangChain is a framework for building applications around language models by chaining model calls, prompt templates, tools and retrieval of documents. Harrison Chase made the first commit on 24 October 2022, about five weeks before ChatGPT's release on 30 November 2022. The package uses the MIT license. Downloads grew from about 5.2 million in September 2023 to 80 million in September 2025 and 171 million in September 2026, with the langchain-core package at 147 million. LlamaIndex, begun in November 2022 by Jerry Liu, is a similar framework for connecting your own documents to a model, a technique called retrieval-augmented generation.

nodes.title: vLLM
nodes.short: An open-source engine from UC Berkeley for serving language models to many users. PagedAttention manages memory the way an operating system pages virtual memory.
nodes.long: vLLM runs language models for many users at once at high throughput. Woosuk Kwon made the first commit on 9 February 2023 at the Sky Computing Lab of UC Berkeley. Its PagedAttention technique manages the memory cache that attention needs the way an operating system manages virtual memory, and the 2023 SOSP paper reports that it improves the throughput of popular models by 2 to 4 times at the same latency. It uses the Apache-2.0 license and is hosted by the PyTorch Foundation, with about 2.1 million PyPI downloads in September 2026 and about 93,000 GitHub stars.
nodes.sleeper: The operating-system idea of virtual memory reappears here as a way to manage the memory that attention needs.

refs.label: Kwon et al.: Efficient Memory Management for LLM Serving with PagedAttention

nodes.title: Tooling
nodes.short: Everything around the code: version control, builds, editors, debuggers.
nodes.long: Good tools turned programming from solitary typing into collaborative engineering.

nodes.title: Version Control
nodes.short: A recorded history of every change, so teams can merge work and undo mistakes.
nodes.long: SCCS (1972), RCS, CVS and Subversion gave each file a history on a central server. Distributed systems such as Git and Mercurial let everyone hold the full history and branch freely.
nodes.sleeper: If you remember copying folders named final_v2, version control replaced that. Git is the universal standard.

nodes.title: Build Systems
nodes.short: Software that turns source code into something runnable and works out which steps are out of date, so only those are redone. Make began the idea in 1976.
nodes.long: Building means compiling each source file, linking the pieces, copying resources, running tests and packaging the result. A build system knows that recipe and works out which steps are out of date, so changing one file does not redo everything. Google's engineering book says a developer should be able to type one command and get the binary, and that the same inputs should give the same result on any machine. Hand-written scripts stop scaling, with teams spending almost as much time on build scripts as on real code. Stuart Feldman's make (1976) set the model of targets, prerequisites and timestamps; its recursive style, one Makefile per directory, builds an inaccurate dependency graph, as Peter Miller argued. Later tools each fixed one pain: portability (Autotools), Java conventions (Maven, Gradle), speed (Ninja), cached isolated builds (Bazel) and front-end bundling (webpack, Vite).
nodes.sleeper: If you remember a Makefile or a Borland project file, the core idea is unchanged: rebuild only what is out of date. What changed is scale. Very large codebases pushed builds toward generators, sandboxed steps and caches shared across a team.

code.text:
# Change util.h and both objects rebuild; change only main.c and util.o is reused.
app: main.o util.o
	gcc -o app main.o util.o
main.o: main.c util.h
	gcc -c main.c
util.o: util.c util.h
	gcc -c util.c

refs.label: Software Engineering at Google, ch. 18: Build Systems and Build Philosophy
Mokhov, Mitchell and Peyton Jones: Build Systems a la Carte (2018)

nodes.title: Git
nodes.short: Linus Torvalds's distributed version control system, now used by almost every developer.
nodes.long: Torvalds wrote Git in April 2005 after the Linux kernel lost access to BitKeeper. It stores snapshots as a graph of commits identified by hashes. GitHub (2008) built a social platform around it and Microsoft bought GitHub in 2018.

code.text:
git clone https://github.com/torvalds/linux
git switch -c my-fix
git commit -am "Fix off-by-one"
git push origin my-fix

nodes.title: Visual Studio Code
nodes.short: Microsoft's free, extensible code editor, announced in 2015. About three quarters of the developers in Stack Overflow's 2025 survey used it regularly.
nodes.long: Microsoft announced Visual Studio Code on April 29, 2015 at its Build conference and released the open-source project under the MIT licence on GitHub on November 18, 2015. The downloadable product is proprietary but built on that MIT-licensed code, and it runs on Electron, a web-technology shell derived from the Atom editor. It is an editor that gains IDE features from extensions and from language servers, using the protocol its own team announced in 2016. Its share of Stack Overflow respondents rose from about 7 percent in 2016 to 35 percent in 2018 and 75.9 percent in 2025. Forks include VSCodium, Cursor and Windsurf, and its extension marketplace carries AI assistants such as GitHub Copilot and Claude Code. Its repository had about 193,000 GitHub stars in September 2026.
nodes.sleeper: Turbo Pascal cost $49.95 by mail order in 1983. The most-used editor in 2025 is free to download and is built on Electron, which packages web technologies as a desktop program.

nodes.title: Language Server Protocol
nodes.short: A standard way for an editor to ask a separate language server for completion, go to definition and error checks. Microsoft announced it in June 2016.
nodes.long: The Language Server Protocol, or LSP, defines how an editor talks to a language server, a separate program that provides features such as autocomplete, go to definition and find all references. Before it, the work of adding those features for a language had to be repeated for each development tool; with LSP one server can serve many editors, which turns an editors-times-languages problem into editors plus languages. The VS Code team announced it on June 27, 2016 at the DevNation conference, together with Red Hat and Codenvy, and Red Hat committed to publish a standalone Java language server. It is an open protocol built on JSON-RPC, and the latest specification version is 3.18. A companion Debug Adapter Protocol does the same job for debuggers. Linters and type checkers now ship as language servers, and Neovim added a built-in client in 2021.
nodes.sleeper: Each editor once needed its own support for each language. Now a language ships one server, and Vim, Neovim, Emacs, Zed and VS Code can all offer IDE-grade features from it.

refs.label: VS Code blog: Language Server Protocol (27 June 2016)

nodes.title: Emacs
nodes.short: An extensible editor that began at MIT in 1976 as macros for TECO. Richard Stallman's GNU Emacs, first public in 1985, is extended in its own Lisp dialect.
nodes.long: The original EMACS, short for Editor MACroS, was developed in 1976 at the MIT AI Lab as macros for the TECO editor. Guy Steele began unifying the divergent TECO macro packages, and Richard Stallman largely completed and extended the result. James Gosling wrote Gosling Emacs in 1981, the first Emacs-like editor on Unix, and Stallman began GNU Emacs in 1984; its first public release, version 13, came on March 20, 1985. Emacs Lisp, the language users extend it with, replaced Gosling's Mocklisp. Lucid Emacs, a fork from 1991, later became XEmacs. GNU Emacs 31.1 was released on August 24, 2026.

nodes.title: Make
nodes.short: Rebuild only what changed. Stuart Feldman's build tool from Bell Labs, still used in countless projects.
nodes.long: A Makefile lists targets, their dependencies and the commands that build them. Newer systems (CMake, Gradle, Bazel) scale the idea.

nodes.title: vi and Vim
nodes.short: vi is the Unix screen editor Bill Joy wrote at Berkeley in the 1970s. Vim, begun by Bram Moolenaar in 1988, is its improved clone, and Neovim is a 2014 fork.
nodes.long: Bill Joy created vi at UC Berkeley, dated 1976 in most accounts. It grew from the line editor ed through em, en and ex, and vi was the visual mode added to ex in 1977. Its terminal shaped it: the Lear Siegler ADM-3A had the Escape key within easy reach and arrows printed on the h, j, k and l keys, which is why vi moves with those letters, and 300-baud modems favored terse commands. Ex 1.1 shipped with the first BSD Unix in March 1978, and POSIX standardizes a portable subset of vi's behavior. Bram Moolenaar began Vim in 1988, based on the Stevie editor, and finished its first public release, version 1.14, on November 2, 1991; the name first meant Vi IMitation and later Vi IMproved. Vim 9.2 came out on February 14, 2026. Neovim, a fork begun in 2014, added a built-in LSP client in 2021. In Stack Overflow's 2025 survey 24.3 percent of respondents used Vim and 14 percent Neovim.
nodes.sleeper: You may remember vi on Unix, shipped since the first BSD release. What changed is that Vim and Neovim now do IDE-style work, such as completion and jump to definition, by talking to language servers.

nodes.title: Integrated Development Environment
nodes.short: One program that holds the editor, compiler and debugger together, so you can write, run and fix code without leaving it. Turbo Pascal made it mainstream in 1983.
nodes.long: An integrated development environment, or IDE, puts an editor, a compiler or build step, and a debugger in one program. An earlier Pascal system from UC San Diego wrapped a text editor, a file system and a debugger around a portable compiler and distributed it for $50. Turbo Pascal made the idea mass-market in 1983 by keeping editor and compiler in memory, so compiling was nearly instant. Visual Studio 97 bundled Microsoft's separate language products, IntelliJ IDEA (2001) added advanced code navigation and refactoring for Java, Eclipse (also 2001) became the most popular Java IDE until 2016, and Xcode arrived in 2003. Visual Studio Code, announced in 2015, is a lighter editor that gains IDE features from extensions and language servers. In Stack Overflow's 2025 survey 75.9 percent of respondents used it regularly, against 29 percent for Visual Studio and 27.1 percent for IntelliJ IDEA.
nodes.sleeper: The IDE you may remember compiled your code and showed errors. Today's tools analyze the whole program as you type, offering completion, jump to definition and refactoring, and since 2016 a shared protocol lets even small editors borrow the same intelligence.

nodes.title: Turbo Pascal
nodes.short: Borland's $49.95 Pascal compiler with a built-in editor, launched in November 1983. Compiling was nearly instant, and it set the pattern for the IDE.
nodes.long: Philippe Kahn's company Borland released Turbo Pascal on November 20, 1983, licensing Anders Hejlsberg's compiler core, PolyPascal, from his Danish company Poly Data. It was sold by direct mail order for US$49.95, about one-tenth the price of comparable products, and it combined editor, compiler and linker in memory, so compiling was nearly instant. One reviewer wrote that under IBM Pascal the average program took two weeks to write and with Turbo Pascal two days. It sold about 250,000 copies in two years and later over 400,000, in a market once estimated at only 30,000 potential buyers. Version 3.0 appeared in September 1986, 5.0 in August 1988 and 7.0 in October 1992. Delphi replaced it in 1995.
nodes.sleeper: Press a key, see the error, jump to the line: this is the program that made that loop feel instant. Today's IDEs still work that way, though they also analyze the whole program as you type.

nodes.title: CVS
nodes.short: Concurrent Versions System: several people edit the same files at once and merge afterwards. Open-source projects widely adopted it in the 1990s.
nodes.long: Dick Grune created CVS so that he could cooperate with his students Erik Baalbergen and Maarten Waage on the Amsterdam Compiler Kit, since their work schedules did not match. He posted the improved scripts to the comp.sources.unix newsgroup on June 23, 1986, and about two years later Brian Berliner turned them into C code, which he described at the 1990 Winter USENIX Conference. CVS let several people edit the same files at once and combine the results later, a style called copy-modify-merge, instead of taking turns with locks. Its flaws were real: an interrupted commit, the step that saves your changes to the repository, could leave it inconsistent, directories were not versioned, renames were not tracked, and branches, parallel lines of development, were expensive. Subversion was started to fix them.
nodes.sleeper: If you remember CVS, the central server is what Git dropped. Every Git clone now carries the full history, so most commands work offline and you can keep committing while a server is down.

refs.label: Dick Grune: the origin of CVS

nodes.title: GDB and LLDB
nodes.short: Command-line debuggers: GDB, begun by Richard Stallman in 1986, and LLDB from the LLVM project. They stop a running program so you can inspect and step through it.
nodes.long: A debugger runs a program under control so that you can stop it, look inside and step through it. Richard Stallman began GDB, the GNU debugger, in 1986, modeled on Berkeley's dbx. It supports C, C++, Fortran, Ada, Go, Rust and many other languages, can debug embedded systems remotely, has offered reverse debugging, which steps backwards, and Python scripting since version 7.0, and is the usual back end behind IDE debuggers such as those in Eclipse and Qt Creator. LLDB, created by Chris Lattner as part of LLVM, is built from reusable components including the Clang expression parser and has been Xcode's default debugger since Xcode 5. The rr tool records a failing run once and lets you replay it deterministically under GDB, including backwards. GDB 18.1 was released on September 25, 2026, and LLDB 23.1.2 on September 22, 2026.

nodes.title: Visual Studio
nodes.short: Microsoft's full IDE, first shipped as Visual Studio 97. It later brought in the .NET environment and C#. It is a different product from Visual Studio Code.
nodes.long: Visual Studio 97, released on March 19, 1997, bundled products that Microsoft had sold separately, including Visual Basic, Visual C++, Visual FoxPro and Visual SourceSafe, along with Visual J++ 1.1 and Visual InterDev. Visual Studio .NET 2002, released on February 13, 2002, introduced the managed .NET environment and C#. Microsoft announced a free Community edition on November 12, 2014. The Microsoft C++ compiler, MSVC, is part of it. Visual Studio 2026 is the current release, in its 18.10 series by September 2026, and 29 percent of respondents to Stack Overflow's 2025 survey used Visual Studio regularly. It is a different product from Visual Studio Code, which is a lighter editor.

nodes.title: CMake
nodes.short: A generator for C and C++ builds: describe the project once and CMake writes Makefiles, Ninja files or Visual Studio projects. Kitware began it in 1999.
nodes.long: In 1999 the US National Library of Medicine engaged a small company, Kitware, to develop a better way to configure, build and deploy complex software across many platforms, starting with the Insight Segmentation and Registration Toolkit (ITK). Before CMake a project usually kept a configure script and Makefiles for Unix plus Visual Studio project files for Windows, so adding a source file was painful. CMake depends only on a C++ compiler and is a generator: it writes native build files, such as Makefiles, Visual Studio projects or Ninja files, instead of compiling anything itself. Development began in 1999 and the first release came in 2000, so sources differ on the year. Version 4.4.3 was released on August 25, 2026.
nodes.sleeper: In the Make era you wrote a Makefile per platform, or a configure script. For C and C++ the usual approach is now two steps: a generator such as CMake describes the project, and a fast executor, Ninja, runs the build.

refs.label: The Architecture of Open Source Applications: CMake

nodes.title: Subversion
nodes.short: Version control started by CollabNet in 2000 to fix CVS without changing its working model. Centralized; version 1.0 came in 2004 and releases continue in 2026.
nodes.long: CollabNet started Subversion in early 2000, with Karl Fogel and Jim Blandy. In the project's own words, the aim was not to break new ground in version control but to match CVS's features and keep its development model without CVS's most obvious flaws. It hosted its own source from August 31, 2001 and reached 1.0 in February 2004. Merging was its sore spot: before version 1.5 in June 2008 added merge tracking, people had to record by hand which changes had already moved between branches, and the project's own book calls those manual methods painful. Subversion joined the Apache Incubator in November 2009 and became a top-level Apache project on February 17, 2010. It stays centralized, and a 1.15.0 release candidate was dated September 11, 2026.

nodes.title: IntelliJ IDEA
nodes.short: JetBrains' Java IDE from 2001, one of the first with built-in code navigation and refactoring. Android Studio is built on its open-source edition.
nodes.long: JetBrains first released IntelliJ IDEA in January 2001. It was one of the first Java IDEs with advanced code navigation and refactoring, meaning safe automatic restructuring of code, built in. JetBrains released the source under the Apache License 2.0 in 2009 as a Community Edition, while the Ultimate edition stays paid. Android Studio is based on the open-source Community Edition. IntelliJ IDEA overtook Eclipse as the most popular Java IDE in 2016, and in Stack Overflow's 2025 survey 27.1 percent of respondents used it, with PyCharm and Android Studio at 15 percent each. JetBrains added support for AI coding agents, including Anthropic's Claude, in September 2025, and version 2026.2 was released on July 16, 2026.

nodes.title: Maven
nodes.short: A Java build tool built on convention over configuration: a standard project layout and a declarative list of dependencies. Started 2001, Maven 1 in 2004.
nodes.long: Maven's own history, written in October 2005 by one of its creators, says it began in the Jakarta Alexandria project, with the first import of prototype sources in August 2001. It then grew in the Turbine project, where the author was tired of maintaining several nearly identical builds. Maven 1 followed in 2004, which is why sources give different years. Builds made with Apache Ant, the XML-based Java tool of 2000, each looked different, and the creator recalls that it was rare for an Ant build to work out of the box. Maven's answer was convention over configuration: a standard directory layout, a project model, and a declarative list of dependencies that the tool can analyze. Stack Overflow's 2025 survey found 16.4 percent of respondents using Maven, and version 3.9.16 came out on May 17, 2026.

nodes.title: Git Branches and Merges
nodes.short: In Git a branch is a 41-byte pointer to a commit, so branching and merging cost almost nothing. A short session shows commit, branch, merge and log.
nodes.long: In Git a branch is a lightweight movable pointer to one commit, and creating one is as quick as writing 41 bytes to a file. Each commit names its parent, or two parents after a merge, so history forms a graph that only points backwards in time. The session below commits, branches, commits on both lines, merges and prints the result, where the merge commit has two parents. Rebase, Git's other way to combine work, replays one branch's commits on top of another for a straight line at the price of new commit hashes, the fingerprints that identify commits; the rule in Pro Git is never to rebase anything you have pushed. Vincent Driessen's Git Flow (2010) used long-lived branches, and in 2020 he advised teams that deliver continuously to use a simpler workflow. Pro Git also warns that submodules, which pin another repository at an exact commit, are not without hiccups.
nodes.sleeper: Branching used to mean copying the whole tree, and merging back, as with Subversion before 1.5 in 2008, meant tracking by hand what was already merged. Git made both routine.

code.text:
git init -b main hello && cd hello
git config user.name "Ada Example" && git config user.email ada@example.com
echo "Hello" > hello.txt && git add hello.txt       # stage the file
git commit -m "Add hello.txt"                        # first snapshot
git switch -c feature/farewell                       # new branch: a 41-byte label
echo "Goodbye" > bye.txt && git add bye.txt
git commit -m "Add bye.txt"                          # only on the feature branch
git switch main
echo "Hello, world" > hello.txt
git commit -am "Make the greeting friendlier"        # history has now diverged
git merge --no-edit feature/farewell                 # merge commit with two parents
git log --oneline --graph                            # the two lines joining again

refs.label: Pro Git: Branches in a Nutshell

nodes.title: Infrastructure as Code
nodes.short: Managing servers and networks from definition files kept in version control, not by hand. Examples are Puppet, Chef, Ansible, CloudFormation and Terraform.
nodes.long: Infrastructure as code means managing and provisioning data-center resources through machine-readable definition files rather than through physical hardware configuration or interactive tools. Mark Burgess's CFEngine (1993) described system configuration in a declarative language, which is why some date the idea to 1993; this map uses 2005, the year of Puppet. Chef followed in 2009, AWS CloudFormation in 2011, Ansible in 2012 and Terraform in 2014. A declarative tool states what the final configuration should be, while an imperative one states the steps to change it. Because the definitions are files, they can be kept in version control, reviewed and rerun, which brought software practices to operations and made the approach a core part of DevOps.
nodes.sleeper: Setting up a server used to be a person at a console. Now a file in version control describes it, a tool applies it, and changes are reviewed like code.

nodes.title: Bazel
nodes.short: Google's build system, begun in 2006 as Blaze and open-sourced in 2015. It runs each step in isolation so results can be cached and shared across a team.
nodes.long: Google began an internal build tool called Blaze in 2006 to get both speed and correctness in a very large monorepo, a single repository holding most of a company's code. Bazel was released as open source in March 2015 and reached 1.0 in October 2019. Google's engineering book explains the design: in task-based tools such as Ant and Maven, tasks can do anything, so there is no general way to check whether one already ran. Bazel instead takes a declarative description of what to build, runs every action in a filesystem sandbox, and first asks a remote cache whether the result already exists. It also requires every dependency version to be stated by hand. Rules are written in Starlark, a Python-like language that avoids side effects. Users include SpaceX, Stripe, Spotify, Uber and BMW.

refs.label: Software Engineering at Google, ch. 18: Build Systems and Build Philosophy

nodes.title: Gradle
nodes.short: A build tool for Java, Kotlin and Android by Hans Dockter, configured in Groovy or Kotlin code instead of XML. Android Studio adopted it in 2013.
nodes.long: Hans Dockter created Gradle and released it in 2008, with version 1.0 following in June 2012. It builds on ideas from Ant and Maven but uses Groovy or Kotlin as its configuration language instead of XML, models its work as a directed graph of tasks, and supports parallel execution, incremental builds, a build cache and a wrapper that pins the tool's own version. Because every task declares its inputs and outputs, Gradle can compute a cache key for its results, and teams can share a remote cache filled by their continuous integration builds. Google's May 2013 announcement of Android Studio said it used a new build system based on Gradle. Stack Overflow's 2025 survey found 14.4 percent of respondents using it, and Gradle 9.8.0 was released on September 24, 2026.

refs.label: Android Developers Blog: Android Studio (15 May 2013)

nodes.title: Pull Requests
nodes.short: A web page where a proposed change is discussed, reviewed and merged. GitHub, launched in 2008, made it the standard way to contribute to a project.
nodes.long: A pull request is not a Git command. GitHub defines it as a proposal to merge code changes into a project, with a conversation tab for discussion, a view of the changed files, and a merge status that shows blockers and missing approvals. Git itself ships git request-pull, which writes an email-style request asking an upstream project to pull your changes, the form long used on the Linux kernel's mailing list. GitHub launched on April 10, 2008 and made the pull request its unit of collaboration; forks, personal copies of a repository, let anyone propose a change without the upstream project's permission. GitHub's 2025 Octoverse report counts 43.2 million pull requests merged per month. A Microsoft study of 570 review comments found only 14 percent concerned defects; the benefits were mainly knowledge transfer, team awareness and maintainability.
nodes.sleeper: Since 2025 AI coding agents open pull requests too. GitHub's Octoverse report counted more than 1 million of them between May and September 2025.

nodes.title: webpack
nodes.short: A JavaScript module bundler by Tobias Koppers that joins files and their imports into browser-ready bundles. Widely used, but often named as hard to configure.
nodes.long: Browsers originally had no module system, so one script tag per feature caused network bottlenecks, and wrapping files in immediately invoked function expressions avoided name clashes but meant rebuilding everything after any change. Bundlers such as Browserify, RequireJS and SystemJS appeared to bring Node-style modules to browsers. Tobias Koppers' webpack (listed as 2014) infers the dependency graph from what each file imports and exports and offers loaders, code splitting and a hot-reloading development server. That displaced task runners such as Grunt and Gulp, which made developers declare every dependency up front. State of JS 2025 respondents named configuration and setup the biggest pain of build tools, and webpack drew the lowest admiration in Stack Overflow's 2025 chart, 25.7 percent, yet it had about 65 million npm downloads in one week of September 2026.

nodes.title: Vite
nodes.short: Evan You's front-end build tool, released in April 2020. It serves source files to the browser as native modules for fast startup and bundles for production.
nodes.long: Evan You released Vite on April 20, 2020, and it is now backed by VoidZero Inc. Its stated reason for existing is that developers on large projects had painfully slow dev server startups, sluggish hot updates and long production builds with bundler-first tools. Vite serves source files to the browser as native ES modules on demand and pre-bundles dependencies with fast native tooling, though production builds still bundle because unbundled modules cause too many network round trips. Vite 8, announced on March 12, 2026, uses Rolldown, a Rust bundler, as its single bundler and claims builds 10 to 30 times faster. Stack Overflow's 2025 survey found 25.4 percent of respondents using Vite and 18.4 percent webpack. npm counted about 219 million Vite downloads in the week of September 23 to 29, 2026, including installs by other tools.
nodes.sleeper: Front-end builds used to mean bundling everything before the browser could show anything. Vite relies on browsers now understanding modules natively, so it serves source files on demand and bundles only for production.

nodes.title: SCCS
nodes.short: The Source Code Control System, written at Bell Labs in 1972. It kept every revision of a file inside one file and let one person edit at a time.
nodes.long: Marc Rochkind wrote SCCS at Bell Labs. The first version, from 1972, was written in SNOBOL4 for an IBM System/370 under OS/360 MVT, and in 1973 it was rewritten in C for Unix on a PDP-11. Its storage trick, called interleaved deltas or the weave, keeps every revision of a file inside one file, with each line tagged by the change that added or removed it. A programmer checks a file out, edits it and checks it back in, and the history stays behind as stored changes called deltas. That cycle became the model that RCS, CVS and Visual SourceSafe inherited. Rochkind published the design in IEEE Transactions on Software Engineering in December 1975. SCCS is legacy today, though maintained forks exist.
nodes.sleeper: SCCS and RCS made one person lock a file while editing it. That lock-then-edit habit gave way to everyone editing freely and merging afterwards, which Git now makes the everyday routine.

nodes.title: RCS
nodes.short: Revision Control System, by Walter Tichy at Purdue (1982). It stores the newest revision in full, keeps older ones as reverse edits, and locks files while you edit.
nodes.long: Walter F. Tichy of Purdue University released RCS in 1982 and described it in the journal Software: Practice and Experience in July 1985. Its main change from SCCS was the reverse delta: the newest revision is stored in full and older ones are rebuilt by applying edit instructions backwards, which Tichy argued is faster because recent revisions are the ones people ask for most. RCS works on one file at a time and uses locking, so only one user can edit a file at once. The GNU project maintains it, and Pro Git notes that it is still distributed with many computers. It is regarded as an early design that distributed systems such as Git have superseded.

nodes.title: Autotools
nodes.short: GNU Autoconf, Automake and Libtool: a generated ./configure script probes the machine, then make builds. Common in older C and Unix software.
nodes.long: David MacKenzie created Autoconf in the summer of 1991 while working for the Free Software Foundation. It generates a shell script called configure that tests what the machine and compiler actually offer, such as whether a function exists, instead of checking operating-system names, and then writes headers and a Makefile from templates. Developers write configure.ac in the m4 macro language, and users type ./configure && make && make install, needing only a Bourne-compatible shell. The suite also includes Automake and Libtool. Opinions are divided: Meson's author called the syntax of common free build systems obtuse, Poul-Henning Kamp argued that the configure approach lets code look portable without being so, and John Calcote defended Autotools' transparency.
nodes.sleeper: If you ever built free Unix software, you probably typed ./configure && make && make install. That ritual still works for many older projects, while many newer C and C++ projects use CMake or Meson instead.

nodes.title: Perforce
nodes.short: A commercial centralized version control system from 1995, strong with very large repositories and with big binary files such as game assets.
nodes.long: Christopher Seiwald founded Perforce in 1995 in Alameda, California. It is centralized, and it submits several files together as one unit called a changelist, so a commit is atomic: it lands whole or not at all. Its strength is large binary files alongside code, and it is used in game development and other binary-heavy shops. Microsoft's internal Source Depot was a Perforce variant, and Facebook engineers wrote in 2014 that Perforce cheats on scale by forcing users to say in advance which files they will edit. Ownership has changed several times: Summit Partners bought the company in 2016, Clearlake Capital in 2018, and Francisco Partners took a 50 percent stake in 2019. Perforce acquired Puppet in 2022. The product is now also called Helix Core.

refs.label: Facebook Engineering: Scaling Mercurial at Facebook (2014)

nodes.title: BitKeeper
nodes.short: A proprietary distributed version control system the Linux kernel used from 2002 to 2005. Losing its free licence led directly to Git and Mercurial.
nodes.long: BitKeeper was a proprietary distributed version control system from Larry McVoy's company BitMover, first released publicly on May 4, 2000. The Linux kernel adopted it in 2002, a choice that Richard Stallman and other open-source purists objected to. In April 2005 BitMover withdrew free access, citing Andrew Tridgell's work on a client that would expose the repository's metadata. Pro Git describes the relationship as breaking down and the tool's free-of-charge status being revoked. Within weeks that produced Git and Mercurial. Linus Torvalds wrote at the time that it was a gray and bleak world while he worked out the alternatives. BitKeeper moved to an open-source licence on May 9, 2016, later Apache 2.0, and is no longer maintained.
nodes.sleeper: From 1991 to 2002 the kernel's changes were passed around as patches and archived files. A commercial tool ended that in 2002, and its withdrawal in 2005 is the reason Git exists.

refs.label: LWN: the kernel SCM saga (6 April 2005)
Pro Git: A Short History of Git

nodes.title: Eclipse
nodes.short: An open-source Java IDE that grew from IBM's VisualAge code. It was the most popular Java IDE until 2016, when IntelliJ IDEA passed it.
nodes.long: Eclipse's codebase came from IBM's VisualAge. A consortium was formed in November 2001 with a board of stewards, after IBM had already invested nearly $40 million, and the Eclipse Foundation was created in January 2004. Since Eclipse 3.0 in 2004, plug-ins are bundles built on Equinox, an implementation of the OSGi module system. Eclipse was the most popular IDE for Java development until 2016, when IntelliJ IDEA surpassed it. It uses the Eclipse Public License, which is incompatible with the GPL. Version 4.41.0 appeared on September 9, 2026, on a quarterly schedule, yet only 7.1 percent of respondents to Stack Overflow's 2025 survey used it, against 27.1 percent for IntelliJ IDEA. Why it declined is not established; the explanation of plugin sprawl has no study behind it.

nodes.title: Profilers and Tracers
nodes.short: Tools that show where a running program spends its time or what it is doing: Linux perf, flame graphs, DTrace and eBPF.
nodes.long: A profiler samples a running program to show where its time goes, and a tracer records what it does. DTrace, designed by Bryan Cantrill, Mike Shapiro and Adam Leventhal at Sun Microsystems, was available in November 2003 and released with Solaris 10 in January 2005; users write programs in the D language that attach to probes in a running system. Linux gained perf in kernel 2.6.31 in 2009, and eBPF lets sandboxed programs run safely inside the kernel for observability, networking and security. Brendan Gregg invented flame graphs, charts of sampled stack traces in which wider frames appear in more samples, while working on a MySQL performance issue at Joyent, and released them in December 2011. Apple added DTrace to Mac OS X 10.5, and Microsoft released a Windows version in 2019.
nodes.sleeper: Debugging once meant print statements and a symbolic debugger. Now sampling profilers draw flame graphs, and tracers such as DTrace and eBPF examine live production systems.

nodes.title: Mercurial
nodes.short: A distributed version control system announced by Matt Mackall on April 19, 2005, days after BitKeeper's withdrawal. Written in Python, now a minority tool.
nodes.long: Matt Mackall, now Olivia Mackall, announced Mercurial on April 19, 2005, days after BitKeeper's free licence ended. It is distributed, so every clone holds the full history, and it is written in Python with C for the speed-critical parts and, increasingly, Rust. Facebook adopted it in 2013 and explained in 2014 that its Python code was clean and extensible; Mozilla used it from 2007 until moving to Git in 2023, and OpenJDK used it until Java 16. Bitbucket dropped Mercurial in 2020, citing a Stack Overflow figure of almost 90 percent of developers using Git against about 3 percent for Mercurial, and saying that supporting two systems split its focus. Version 7.2 was released on January 29, 2026.

refs.label: Atlassian: Sunsetting Mercurial support in Bitbucket

nodes.title: Fossil
nodes.short: A distributed version control system by SQLite's author, D. Richard Hipp. One program also holds a wiki, bug tracker, forum and web interface.
nodes.long: D. Richard Hipp, the architect of SQLite, began Fossil in 2007. The project's own history says that around 2005 Git and Mercurial were considered, but none supported sync over ordinary HTTP, none could be run from an inexpensive shell account on a leased server, and none had anything like the wiki and ticket features of CVSTrac. Fossil is a single executable that holds version control, a wiki, tickets, a forum and a web interface. The first project it hosted was Fossil itself, then the SQLite documentation, and finally SQLite's source code.

nodes.title: Gerrit
nodes.short: A code review platform for Git, built at Google by Shawn Pearce. Each revision of a change is reviewed as a patch set; Android, Chromium and Qt use it.
nodes.long: Gerrit describes itself as an open source, patchset-based code review platform for Git-based development: each revised version of a proposed change is a patch set that reviewers examine before the change is merged. Shawn Pearce created it at Google as a fork of Rietveld, a review tool by Guido van Rossum that was open-sourced in 2008, and the independent Gerrit 2 was released on November 2, 2009. The project says its model more closely resembles the mailing-list workflow used by Git itself and the Linux kernel, where patches were emailed for discussion. Android, Chromium, the OpenInfra Foundation, JGit and Qt use it.

nodes.title: Ninja
nodes.short: A small, very fast build executor by Evan Martin of Google's Chrome team. It is meant to be generated by tools such as CMake and Meson, not written by hand.
nodes.long: Evan Martin, on Google's Chrome team, started Ninja as an experiment to see whether Chrome's build could be made faster; the work dates from 2011 to 2012. A build generated by GYP for the SCons build tool could take 30 seconds to start while SCons worked out which files had changed. Ninja's input is only a list of which exact paths produce which exact outputs, and its authors say that where other build systems are high-level languages, Ninja aims to be an assembler, meant to be written by another tool. Martin's yardstick was how long a build with nothing to do takes, just under a second for Chrome. CMake, Meson and other tools can generate Ninja files, and projects such as LLVM and ReactOS build that way. Stack Overflow's 2025 survey found 5.2 percent of respondents using Ninja.

refs.label: The Architecture of Open Source Applications: Ninja

nodes.title: Electron
nodes.short: A framework that packages web technologies as desktop programs. It came out of GitHub's Atom editor and underlies Visual Studio Code, Slack and GitHub Desktop.
nodes.long: Electron is a framework that wraps web technologies in a desktop program. It came out of GitHub's Atom editor, which GitHub's own blog calls foundational to Electron, and Visual Studio Code, Slack and GitHub Desktop all run on it. GitHub shut Atom down on December 15, 2022, saying that Atom had not had significant feature development for several years, that community involvement had declined, and that it preferred to focus on cloud development with GitHub Codespaces. Electron outlived the editor. Atom's other by-products were Tree-sitter, an incremental parsing system for programming tools, and the Zed editor from the same creators.

nodes.title: pre-commit Hooks
nodes.short: Checks that run automatically before each Git commit, such as formatters and linters. The pre-commit framework shares them across a team through a config file.
nodes.long: Git can run a script called a hook before it records a commit. The pre-commit hook runs before the commit message is requested and can be skipped with the --no-verify option. Hooks live in the repository's hooks directory rather than in version-controlled files, which is why a framework is needed to share them. The pre-commit framework, whose repository dates from March 2014, reads a .pre-commit-config.yaml file that lists hook repositories, runs only on staged files by stashing unstaged changes, and can check the whole repository with pre-commit run --all-files. Husky does a similar job for JavaScript projects. Because hooks can be skipped, the authoritative run happens in continuous integration, a server that builds and tests every change and can require checks to pass before a branch is merged.
nodes.sleeper: A modern repository runs the same checks at four points: in the editor, in a commit hook, in continuous integration and as automated review comments. Style arguments that once cost review time are now settled by tools.

code.text:
# .pre-commit-config.yaml
repos:
-   repo: https://github.com/pre-commit/pre-commit-hooks
    rev: v2.3.0
    hooks:
    -   id: check-yaml
    -   id: end-of-file-fixer
    -   id: trailing-whitespace
-   repo: https://github.com/psf/black
    rev: 22.10.0
    hooks:
    -   id: black

nodes.title: Terraform and OpenTofu
nodes.short: HashiCorp's infrastructure-as-code tool from 2014, and OpenTofu, the community fork made in 2023 after HashiCorp changed Terraform's licence.
nodes.long: HashiCorp was founded in 2012 by Mitchell Hashimoto and Armon Dadgar, and Terraform followed in 2014 as a declarative tool for describing infrastructure in files. On August 10, 2023 HashiCorp moved Terraform and its other products from the Mozilla Public License to the Business Source License 1.1, which stops vendors from offering competing services built on future releases. A fork called OpenTF appeared that month and was renamed OpenTofu in September over trademark concerns. It is managed by the Linux Foundation under the MPL-2.0 licence. IBM agreed in April 2024 to buy HashiCorp for $6.4 billion and completed the deal on February 27, 2025. OpenTofu 1.12.6 was released on August 19, 2026.

nodes.title: Hermetic Builds and Remote Caching
nodes.short: A build is hermetic when it is isolated from the host machine, so the same inputs always give the same output. That makes results safe to cache and share.
nodes.long: Bazel's documentation defines a hermetic build system as one that, given the same source code and product configuration, always returns the same output by isolating the build from changes to the host system. The listed benefits are speed, because actions can be cached, parallel execution, side-by-side builds, and easier troubleshooting. Bazel enforces this by sandboxing each action and identifying sources by hash. Remote caching builds on this: Bazel keeps a map from each action's hash to its result, so outputs from one machine can safely be reused on another. The Reproducible Builds project frames the goal as verification: given the same source code, build environment and build instructions, any party can recreate bit-by-bit identical copies of the artifacts, so a distributed binary can be checked against its source. That check is one reason supply-chain security work cares about it.

nodes.title: Jujutsu
nodes.short: A Git-compatible version control tool begun by Martin von Zweigbergk in late 2019. The working copy is itself a commit, and there is no staging area.
nodes.long: Martin von Zweigbergk started Jujutsu, abbreviated jj, in late 2019. He works at Google and several Googlers help, but it is not a supported Google product. It uses Git repositories as its storage layer, so its commits look like ordinary Git commits to other people and tools. Its own ideas: the working copy is itself a commit, amended automatically as you edit; when you change a commit, later commits are replayed on top of it automatically; an operation log records every action; conflicts are first-class objects; and there is no staging area, the step in Git where you mark changes for the next commit. It borrows from Git (speed), Mercurial and Sapling (the revset query language and anonymous branches) and Darcs (conflict handling). Its repository showed about 31,800 GitHub stars in September 2026.

nodes.title: OpenTelemetry
nodes.short: A vendor-neutral standard and toolkit for producing traces, metrics and logs from running software, formed from a merger of OpenTracing and OpenCensus.
nodes.long: OpenTelemetry describes itself as an observability framework, a toolkit for generating, exporting and collecting telemetry data (traces, metrics and logs) about what running software is doing. It is vendor and tool agnostic and is not itself an observability backend. It came from a merger of two earlier projects, OpenTracing and OpenCensus, and the Cloud Native Computing Foundation (CNCF) accepted it on May 7, 2019. It reached the Incubating level on August 26, 2021 and the Graduated level on May 11, 2026. Google's 2010 technical report on Dapper, its production tracing system, is an intellectual ancestor of open-source tracers; its goals were low overhead, application-level transparency and ubiquitous deployment, using sampling. The CNCF counts 25,547 contributors from 4,731 organizations.

nodes.title: Sapling
nodes.short: Meta's source control system, open-sourced in November 2022. It began as a Mercurial extension, scales to huge repositories and can work with Git repositories.
nodes.long: Meta open-sourced Sapling on November 15, 2022, describing it as a source control system that emphasizes usability and scalability. It started as an extension to Mercurial, which Facebook had chosen because Git slowed as the number of files grew, and it rapidly became a system of its own. With its server and virtual file system it can serve Meta's internal repository, which has tens of millions of files, commits and branches. The client can clone and work with Git repositories. Features include smartlog, stacks of commits, and undo, redo, uncommit and unamend commands. Giant single repositories need such tooling: Google built the centralized Piper, and Microsoft built GVFS and later Scalar to make Git cope with the Windows repository.

refs.label: Facebook Engineering: Scaling Mercurial at Facebook (2014)

nodes.title: Package Manager
nodes.short: A tool that downloads, installs and updates libraries and their dependencies for you.
nodes.long: Linux's dpkg and apt (1990s) came first, then language ecosystems: CPAN for Perl (1995), pip for Python, npm for JavaScript (2010), Maven, NuGet and Cargo. Lockfiles pin exact versions for repeatable builds.
nodes.sleeper: You no longer download libraries by hand. One command pulls hundreds of dependencies, which is both the magic and the danger.

nodes.title: Packages & Ecosystems
nodes.short: Reusable libraries and the tools that fetch them. Modern programs are mostly other people's code.
nodes.long: Package managers resolve versions of dependencies automatically. The convenience brought huge productivity and a new class of supply-chain risk.

nodes.title: Dependency Management
nodes.short: Declaring which libraries a program needs and letting tools fetch, version and update them, including the libraries those libraries need.
nodes.long: A package is a bundle of code with a manifest that gives its name, its version and what it needs. A dependency is a package your code needs, and a transitive dependency is one that a dependency needs in turn. Dependency management is the practice and tooling for declaring them, fetching them from a registry, choosing versions and updating them. Without it, shared libraries caused trouble. On early Windows, programs shared one folder of DLLs, and installing a newer copy for one program could silently break another, which a 2006 thesis called DLL hell. Linux had a counterpart before apt and yum: chasing down RPM files by hand. Remedies are to isolate each application's libraries, to make versions a machine-readable promise, or to make installs immutable. Google calls two libraries needing different versions of a third "the central problem in dependency management".
nodes.sleeper: A library in 1990 was a file you copied next to your source. A manifest now names your direct dependencies, a tool finds the hundreds of indirect ones, and a lockfile records exactly which versions were chosen.

refs.label: Dolstra: The Purely Functional Software Deployment Model (2006)
Software Engineering at Google, ch. 21: Dependency Management

nodes.title: Software Supply-Chain Security
nodes.short: The risk that the code, build tools and accounts behind the software you use can be compromised, or simply fail, without your noticing.
nodes.long: Every dependency is code written by strangers that runs with your privileges. Ken Thompson's 1984 Turing Award lecture made the point about compilers: you cannot trust code you did not totally create yourself. A 2019 study of npm found that installing an average package placed implicit trust in 79 third-party packages and 39 maintainers. The first systematic dataset, Backstabber's Knife Collection, counted 174 malicious packages used in real attacks between November 2015 and November 2019. Incidents since include left-pad (2016), event-stream (2018), SolarWinds (2020), Log4Shell (2021), xz (2024) and, in 2025, the phishing of the chalk and debug maintainer and the Shai-Hulud worm. Responses include SBOMs, SLSA, Sigstore, trusted publishing, pinning and update delays, and none is a complete answer.
nodes.sleeper: A 1990 program was mostly code you or your vendor wrote. A modern one is mostly other people's code, so attackers aim at maintainers' accounts, build systems and release pipelines rather than at your own code.

refs.label: Russ Cox: Our Software Dependency Problem
Zimmermann et al.: Small World with High Risks (USENIX Security 2019)

nodes.title: Python Standard Library
nodes.short: Python's "batteries included" standard library: JSON, CSV, SQLite, asyncio, venv and much more ship with the language itself.
nodes.long: Python's documentation says the language has a "batteries included" philosophy and that its standard library is extensive. PEP 206, by A. M. Kuchling in July 2000 and now withdrawn, states that the source distribution has long maintained that philosophy, offering a rich library without making users download separate packages. Modules include json, csv, unittest, sqlite3 (added in Python 2.5), multiprocessing (2.6), venv (3.3) and asyncio (3.4). Alongside it, PyPI served about 127.6 billion downloads across roughly 932,000 projects in September 2026, and the most downloaded packages are mostly plumbing such as boto3, packaging, typing-extensions, urllib3 and certifi.
nodes.sleeper: Programs now routinely pull in hundreds of third-party packages, so the standard library is the starting kit rather than the whole toolkit.

code.text:
import json, sqlite3

db = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
db.execute("select 1")
print(json.dumps({"ok": True}))

nodes.title: RPM, yum and DNF
nodes.short: The package format and tools of Red Hat, Fedora and SUSE Linux; DNF resolves dependencies with a SAT-based solver.
nodes.long: RPM is the package format and command-line tool used by Red Hat Enterprise Linux, Fedora, SUSE Linux Enterprise, openSUSE and others. Its first version control commit dates to 1995, and the format was standardised in the Linux Standard Base. A 2006 thesis noted that RPM installs and verifies packages but has no way to resolve problems by itself, which left users chasing down files, the original Linux dependency hell. Higher-level tools filled the gap: yum, then DNF, which replaced yum as the Fedora default in Fedora 22 (2015) and became the default in RHEL 8 (2019). DNF uses libsolv, a SAT-based resolver from openSUSE. DNF5, rewritten in C++, became the Fedora default in Fedora 41 (2024).

nodes.title: APT
nodes.short: Debian's package installer, which resolves and downloads dependencies from online repositories.
nodes.long: APT, the Advanced Package Tool, was introduced in 1998 as part of the Deity project commissioned by Debian release manager Brian White, and at first it was called dpkg-get. It adds dependency resolution and downloading on top of dpkg, Debian's low-level installer for .deb files, working out an order of installs and removals and then calling dpkg in that sequence. It reads the repositories listed in /etc/apt/sources.list. The first Debian release to include it was Debian 2.1, on 9 March 1999, and by 2021 Debian's repository held over 50,000 packages. dpkg's own date is uncertain: Wikipedia says 1994, while Debian itself began in 1993. In the Stack Overflow 2025 survey 18.4 percent of respondents used APT.
nodes.sleeper: Before tools like this, installing Linux software meant chasing down package files and their prerequisites by hand. One command now fetches a program and everything it needs from the distribution's repositories.

code.text:
sudo apt update
sudo apt install git
apt show git

nodes.title: Version Resolution
nodes.short: Choosing one version of every package so that all stated requirements hold at once, which turns out to be a hard computing problem.
nodes.long: Each package states which versions of its dependencies it accepts, and a resolver must find one set of versions that satisfies everybody. APT added dependency resolution on top of Debian's dpkg in 1998. In December 2016 Russ Cox showed that the general problem is NP-complete, by reduction from 3-SAT, so tools either call SAT solvers (DNF uses libsolv, Composer a solver derived from openSUSE's) or restrict the problem. Dart's pub uses PubGrub, which can explain a conflict in readable terms, and Astral's uv uses a fork of it. Go avoids the hard case with minimal version selection. pip's resolver learned to backtrack, to abandon a bad choice and try another, only in version 20.3.
nodes.sleeper: Conflicts were once settled by a person choosing which library file to keep. Resolvers now search for a consistent set of versions automatically, and a good one such as PubGrub can say why no such set exists.

code.text:
your app  needs  liba and libb
liba 1.0  needs  libbase 1.x
libb 1.0  needs  libbase 2.x
result    no version of libbase satisfies both

nodes.title: RubyGems
nodes.short: Ruby's package system and the rubygems.org registry, begun in 2003, public in March 2004 and part of the standard Ruby distribution since Ruby 1.9.
nodes.long: RubyGems was created by Chad Fowler, Jim Weirich, David Alan Black, Paul Brannan and Richard Kilmer. Development began in November 2003 and it was released to the public on 14 March 2004, Pi Day, and it joined the standard Ruby distribution with Ruby 1.9. Libraries are packaged as gems and served from rubygems.org, which had served about 269 billion downloads by 30 September 2026. RubyGems and Bundler were released together as version 4.0.0 on 3 December 2025, and Trusted Publishing was announced on 14 December 2023. In 2025 former maintainers, in a dispute with Ruby Central, started gem.coop as a separate gem server.

nodes.title: Spring Framework
nodes.short: A Java application framework that appeared in 2003 as a response to J2EE's complexity; 14.7 percent of Stack Overflow 2025 respondents used Spring Boot.
nodes.long: Spring came into being in 2003, in the words of its reference documentation, as a response to the complexity of the early J2EE specifications. The complaint, later made of EJB 2 and SOAP as well, was that the standard approach was complex, XML-heavy and full of ceremony, and each was displaced by something simpler. In September 2000 Martin Fowler, Rebecca Parsons and Josh MacKenzie had coined "POJO", plain old Java object, because simple objects lacked a fancy name, and Spring built its approach on such objects. Spring Boot 4.1.1 was released on 20 August 2026, on Spring Framework 7.0.x. Its API still contains a class named AbstractSingletonProxyFactoryBean, a standing joke about enterprise Java naming.
nodes.sleeper: Enterprise Java around 2000 meant heavyweight server components. Spring's answer was ordinary Java objects with the framework supplying their dependencies, an approach called dependency injection.

nodes.title: Ruby on Rails
nodes.short: David Heinemeier Hansson's Ruby web framework, extracted from Basecamp in 2004, which popularised convention over configuration.
nodes.long: Ruby on Rails was extracted by David Heinemeier Hansson from 37signals's Basecamp application and first released publicly in July 2004, with version 1.0 following in December 2005. It popularised convention over configuration, in which sensible defaults replace pages of settings; database migrations, which version a database's structure alongside the code; and generated scaffolding. It follows the model-view-controller pattern, which separates data, pages and request handling. Django in Python did similar things from 2005, and Rails inspired Laravel, Spring Boot and Phoenix. Hotwire, from the Rails world, follows the same server-rendered idea as htmx.

code.text:
rails new blog
cd blog
bin/rails generate scaffold Post title:string body:text
bin/rails db:migrate

nodes.title: Django
nodes.short: A batteries-included Python web framework from a newspaper's web team, open-sourced in 2005, with an ORM, admin site and templates.
nodes.long: Django was written at World Online, the web department of the Lawrence Journal-World newspaper, by Adrian Holovaty and Simon Willison, and was open-sourced in July 2005; version 1.0 followed in 2008. It is called batteries included because it ships an object-relational mapper for database access, an automatic admin site and a template language. Like Rails a year earlier, it belongs to the generation of model-view-controller frameworks that followed CGI scripts and PHP, ASP and JSP pages. In the Stack Overflow 2025 survey 12.6 percent of respondents used Django. Its PyPI downloads were 42.3 million in September 2026, up from 7.4 million in September 2021, and version 6.1.1 requires Python 3.12 or newer.

code.text:
django-admin startproject mysite
cd mysite
python manage.py runserver

nodes.title: pip and PyPI
nodes.short: Python's installer and package index. Newer tools such as uv make it dramatically faster.
nodes.long: pip installs packages from PyPI. Virtual environments isolate projects. Poetry and Astral's uv (2024) improve resolution speed and reproducibility.

nodes.title: Lockfile
nodes.short: A file recording the exact version of every dependency a build used, so that every machine installs the same code.
nodes.long: A manifest such as a Gemfile or Cargo.toml states what a project will accept, for example any 1.x release of a library. A lockfile records what was actually chosen after resolution, including every indirect dependency, so collaborators and servers install identical code. Ruby's Bundler popularised the Gemfile plus Gemfile.lock pattern; its first release on RubyGems was on 4 August 2009 and 1.0.0 followed on 29 August 2010. Cargo's lockfile came with its 2014 design, Yarn's followed in October 2016, and Python agreed a standard format only in 2025, as pylock.toml in PEP 751. A lockfile has a cost: a patched dependency is not installed until the lockfile is regenerated, a delay researchers call technical lag.
nodes.sleeper: A lockfile is the modern form of keeping the exact library copies you tested next to your source, but as a small text file that tools can check, compare and update.

refs.label: Rust Blog: Cargo, Rust's Community Crate Host (2014)
PEP 751: a file format to record Python dependencies

nodes.title: npm
nodes.short: JavaScript's package registry: millions of packages, including the famous one-line left-pad.
nodes.long: Isaac Schlueter created npm. GitHub acquired it in 2020. Its tiny-package culture produced the 2016 left-pad incident, when a deleted 11-line package broke builds across the web.

nodes.title: Semantic Versioning
nodes.short: A version-numbering convention, MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH, in which the numbers tell users whether an upgrade can break their code.
nodes.long: Semantic Versioning was written by Tom Preston-Werner, a co-founder of GitHub. A version reads MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH: raise MAJOR for incompatible API changes, MINOR for backward compatible new features and PATCH for backward compatible fixes, and treat 0.y.z as initial development where anything may change. The semver.org repository was created in December 2009, version 1.0.0 was tagged in September 2011 and 2.0.0 in June 2013. Cargo assumes packages follow it, and Go builds the major version into import paths from v2 onward. It is a promise made by humans: Google calls it a lossy estimate of how risky a change is, yet a study of 119,879 Maven Central upgrades found that 83.4 percent complied.
nodes.sleeper: Version numbers used to mean whatever a vendor chose. With this convention a tool can accept "any compatible 1.x release" without asking, which large dependency trees rely on.

code.text:
1.4.2 -> 1.4.3   patch: bug fix, nothing breaks
1.4.2 -> 1.5.0   minor: new feature, nothing breaks
1.4.2 -> 2.0.0   major: something may break

refs.label: Software Engineering at Google, ch. 21: Dependency Management

nodes.title: conda and Anaconda
nodes.short: A language-agnostic package and environment manager from Anaconda that installs Python together with non-Python software such as compilers and CUDA.
nodes.long: conda began in 2012 (its first commit is dated 15 October 2012, by Ilan Schnell) and is developed by Anaconda, Inc. It is a cross-platform, language-agnostic package and environment manager, so it can install Python together with compiled non-Python software such as C libraries, compilers and CUDA. Its default channel lists over 7,500 packages, and since conda 23.10.0 in November 2023 the faster libmamba solver has been the default. Anaconda changed its licensing in 2024, and its Terms of Service, effective 15 July 2025, require a paid Business Plan for for-profit organisations with more than 200 employees or contractors. Miniforge, mamba, pixi and uv are alternatives that sidestep that question.

code.text:
conda create -n sci python=3.12 numpy
conda activate sci

nodes.title: React
