nodes.short: Facebook's JavaScript library for building interfaces from components, open-sourced in 2013 and used by 44.7 percent of Stack Overflow 2025 respondents.
nodes.long: Facebook open-sourced React in May 2013. It introduced component-based user interfaces with a virtual DOM, and Pete Hunt's June 2013 post described it as a library for building composable user interfaces. React 16 appeared on 26 September 2017, 18 on 29 March 2022 and 19.0 on 5 December 2024, which made React Server Components stable. On 7 October 2025 the React team announced plans to move React and React Native from Meta to a new React Foundation with independent technical governance. In the Stack Overflow 2025 survey 44.7 percent of respondents used React, and npm counted about 721 million React downloads a month, yet the top pain points in State of JavaScript 2025 were React itself and excessive complexity.
nodes.sleeper: A web page used to be a document that a server assembled for each request. With React, the browser downloads an application once and redraws parts of the page itself, calling servers only for data.

refs.label: React blog: Why did we build React? (2013)
React blog: Introducing the React Foundation

nodes.title: Cargo and crates.io
nodes.short: Rust's build tool and package manager, with crates.io as its registry: one tool for building, testing and fetching dependencies.
nodes.long: Cargo was designed by Carl Lerche and Yehuda Katz and announced by Alex Crichton on the Rust blog on 20 November 2014, then came with Rust 1.0 on 15 May 2015. It follows "the tradition of successes like Bundler and NPM": releases follow semantic versioning, Cargo.lock records exact versions for reproducible builds, and the crates.io registry keeps releases permanently so projects can build with the same versions years later. A year after 1.0, crates.io held at least 5,000 third-party libraries; on 1 October 2026 it listed 343,176 crates and about 466 billion downloads. In the Stack Overflow 2025 survey 14.4 percent of respondents used Cargo, and it scored 70.8 percent in the "most admired" ranking, close behind uv's 74.2 percent.

code.text:
cargo new hello
cd hello
cargo add rand
cargo run

refs.label: Rust Blog: Cargo, Rust's Community Crate Host (2014)

nodes.title: Dependabot
nodes.short: GitHub's automation that alerts you to vulnerable dependencies and opens pull requests to update them.
nodes.long: Dependabot has three features: alerts that tell you about vulnerabilities in the dependencies a repository uses, security updates that raise pull requests for dependencies with known vulnerabilities, and version updates that raise pull requests to keep dependencies current. Its core repository, written in Ruby, was created on 2 June 2017, and it is a GitHub feature. Renovate, from Mend and licensed under AGPL-3.0, is an alternative. Bots that update lockfiles risk pulling in a freshly published malicious release, so as of 2026 Dependabot offers a cooldown option and applies a default 3-day cooldown to version updates, though not to security updates, to give the community time to vet new versions.
nodes.sleeper: Updating a library used to be a manual chore that was easy to postpone. Bots now propose each update as a ready-made change, and the new debate is how long to wait before accepting one.

code.text:
version: 2
updates:
  - package-ecosystem: "npm"
    directory: "/"
    schedule:
      interval: "weekly"
    cooldown:
      default-days: 3

nodes.title: FastAPI
nodes.short: Sebastián Ramírez's Python framework that builds web APIs from type hints, on Starlette and Pydantic; it passed Flask in downloads in 2025 to 2026.
nodes.long: FastAPI's first commit is dated 5 December 2018 and its author is Sebastián Ramírez. You write ordinary functions with type hints, and the framework builds the web API from them. It sits on Starlette, an ASGI toolkit (ASGI is the asynchronous successor to the older WSGI interface), and on Pydantic; Ramírez wrote that after testing several alternatives he decided to use Pydantic. In September 2026 FastAPI had 377 million PyPI downloads, up 2.6 times in a year and well past Flask's 137 million. In the Stack Overflow 2025 survey 14.8 percent of respondents used it, up about 5 points, and the PSF and JetBrains Python survey put it at 38 percent, up from 29.

nodes.title: Go Modules
nodes.short: Go's built-in versioning: go.mod lists requirements, go.sum holds checksums, and a public proxy and checksum database serve and verify the code.
nodes.long: Before modules, go get fetched code with no concept of versioning, and community tools such as godep, gb and glide only vendored copies of dependencies. Russ Cox's post of 20 February 2018, "Go & Versioning", proposed go.mod files, minimal version selection and the end of GOPATH ("Now you just git clone, cd, and start writing. Anywhere."), and modules arrived in Go 1.11 in 2018. From v2 a module's major version is part of its import path, so v1 and v2 can coexist. On 29 August 2019 the Go team launched a module mirror and a checksum database, a Merkle-tree transparency log, so that a proxy or origin server cannot start serving different code without getting caught.
nodes.sleeper: In Go a new major version gets a new import path, so v1 and v2 of a library can be used together as if they were different libraries. Cargo, in Cox's phrase, allows partial upgrades by giving up import uniqueness.

code.text:
go mod init example.com/hello
go get github.com/google/uuid
go list -m all

refs.label: Go Blog: Module Mirror and Checksum Database Launched

nodes.title: SBOMs and Executive Order 14028
nodes.short: A software bill of materials: a machine-readable list of the components in a program, promoted by US Executive Order 14028 in 2021.
nodes.long: An SBOM lists the ingredients of a piece of software so that buyers and defenders can check them against vulnerability reports. The two main formats are SPDX, which began in 2010 inside a Linux Foundation work group and is now the international standard ISO/IEC 5962:2021, and CycloneDX, OWASP's format, standardised as ECMA-424. US Executive Order 14028, signed on 12 May 2021, charged agencies including NIST with software supply chain security, and the NTIA defined minimum SBOM elements. The limits showed quickly: the Cyber Safety Review Board found that none of the organisations that reported to it had used SBOMs to identify vulnerable Log4j deployments, and described SBOMs as limited by inconsistent field descriptions and missing version information.
nodes.sleeper: Software was once judged by what it did. Regulators and buyers now ask what it contains, much as a food label lists ingredients.

refs.label: CSRB: Review of the December 2021 Log4j Event

nodes.title: uv
nodes.short: Astral's very fast Python package and project manager, written in Rust and announced in February 2024 as a drop-in replacement for pip.
nodes.long: Charlie Marsh's company Astral announced uv on 15 February 2024 as an extremely fast Python package resolver and installer written in Rust, a drop-in replacement for pip and pip-tools. Astral reported it as 8 to 10 times faster than pip without caching and 80 to 115 times faster with a warm cache; those are the vendor's own figures. Its documentation now describes one tool that replaces pip, pip-tools, pipx, poetry, pyenv, twine, virtualenv and more, with a universal lockfile, Python version management and a tool runner, uvx. In September 2026 PyPI counted about 129 million uv downloads against pip's 414 million, a count that understates uv because it is mostly installed by other routes. On 19 March 2026 Astral announced an agreement to join OpenAI as part of the Codex team and promised to keep building in the open.
nodes.sleeper: Python packaging was a set of overlapping tools that each did part of the job. uv shows the 2020s habit of rewriting developer tools in Rust behind a familiar interface, and it topped the Stack Overflow 2025 "most admired" list at 74.2 percent.

code.text:
uv init demo
cd demo
uv add requests
uv run python -c "import requests; print(requests.__version__)"

refs.label: Astral: uv, Python packaging in Rust

nodes.title: Package Manager Popularity, 2025 to 2026
nodes.short: In the 2025 Stack Overflow survey npm leads package managers at 56.8 percent, followed by pip, Homebrew, Yarn, NuGet, APT, Maven, Gradle and Cargo.
nodes.long:
In the Stack Overflow 2025 survey the share of all respondents using each tool was: npm 56.8 percent, pip 40.9, Homebrew 25.7, Yarn 21.1, NuGet 18.9, APT 18.4, Maven 16.4, Gradle 14.4, Cargo 14.4, pnpm 13.4, Composer 11, Poetry 9 and Bun 5.5. State of JavaScript 2025 found pnpm the clear leader among monorepo users. In September 2026 pip had about 414 million PyPI downloads and uv 129 million, though uv is mostly installed by other routes.

Registries differ in size: about 4.4 million package records on npm, over 900,000 projects on PyPI, 492,566 hits on NuGet, 469,642 packages on Packagist, 343,176 crates and 25,284 packages on CRAN. Go has built-in modules, Swift has Swift Package Manager, Elixir has Hex, and C and C++ have no single winner. Counts measure installs and uploads, not users.

nodes.title: Software Components (McIlroy)
nodes.short: Doug McIlroy's 1968 call for an industry of catalogued, interchangeable software parts, an early statement of the idea behind libraries and packages.
nodes.long: At the 1968 NATO software engineering conference, Doug McIlroy gave an invited address titled "Mass Produced Software Components". He argued that the software industry was weakly founded because it had no components subindustry, and he said programmers were the crofters to the hardware makers' industrialists. His proposal was catalogues of routines offered in varying degrees of precision, robustness, speed and generality, so that builders could choose parts instead of writing everything again. He tied the idea to interchangeable parts in manufacturing, which he said corresponded roughly to modularity. The talk is an early seed of the library, package and reuse culture that came later.
nodes.sleeper: McIlroy asked for catalogues of parts in 1968. Registries such as npm, PyPI and Maven Central are close to what he described, with the catch that every part brings dependencies of its own.

nodes.title: CPAN
nodes.short: Perl's central archive of modules and its install client, online since 1995, a model that later language registries copied.
nodes.long: The Comprehensive Perl Archive Network was conceived in 1993 and has been online since October 1995. It is based on CTAN, the archive for the TeX typesetting system, and consists of a central repository, mirrors around the world and a client that fetches and installs modules. Its maintainers have included Jarkko Hietaniemi as master librarian. Wikipedia cites, without dating the figures, more than 220,000 modules in 45,500 distributions from 14,500 contributors, on 250 or more mirrors in over 60 countries. The creator of npm has said that npm was inspired by PEAR and CPAN, and the pattern of a central archive, an automatic client and a culture of testing can be seen as the template that RubyGems, PyPI, npm and Cargo later copied.
nodes.sleeper: Languages used to ship with whatever libraries their vendor chose. CPAN showed that a language's library could grow through a shared archive that anyone could contribute to, an idea that is now standard.

nodes.title: CRAN
nodes.short: R's package archive, home to 25,284 packages of statistics and data analysis when checked on 1 October 2026.
nodes.long: The Comprehensive R Archive Network is the main package repository for R, the statistics language that Ross Ihaka and Robert Gentleman announced in 1993. R can be considered a different implementation of S, the language of John Chambers and colleagues at Bell Laboratories, and Ihaka has described it as starting as an experiment in using the methods of Lisp implementors to build a small testbed for a statistical environment, with an S-like syntax. R's source was released under the GNU GPL in June 1995. CRAN's own page listed 25,284 available packages when checked on 1 October 2026.

nodes.title: Nix
nodes.short: A package manager that stores each build under a path named by a hash of its inputs, allowing side-by-side versions and safe rollbacks.
nodes.long: Eelco Dolstra created Nix in 2003 and described it in his 2006 doctoral thesis, The Purely Functional Software Deployment Model. The central idea is to store every software component in isolation in one store, under a path name that contains a cryptographic hash of all the inputs used to build it, for example /nix/store/rwmfbhb2znwp...-firefox-1.0.4. That prevents undeclared dependencies and lets several versions or variants of a component sit side by side. Nix offers atomic upgrades and rollbacks, and NixOS applies the same approach to a whole operating system configured declaratively. Its package collection, nixpkgs, held more than 122,000 packages in January 2025. It is niche but influential.
nodes.sleeper: The old DLL-hell problem came from many programs sharing one folder of libraries. Nix answers it by making installs immutable and addressed by content, so upgrading one program cannot change another's libraries.

code.text:
# fetch the "hello" package and run it without installing it system-wide
nix-shell -p hello --run hello

refs.label: Dolstra: The Purely Functional Software Deployment Model (2006)

nodes.title: Beautiful Soup
nodes.short: Leonard Richardson's Python library for pulling data out of messy HTML, first released in 2004.
nodes.long: Beautiful Soup was created in 2004 by Leonard Richardson. It parses messy HTML and lets a program search the result: BeautifulSoup(html, "html.parser").find_all("a") returns every link. Version 4 is MIT licensed, and version 3 used the PSF licence. Version 4.15.0 appeared on 7 June 2026, and the package had 297 million downloads in September 2026, ranking 99th on PyPI. For crawling many pages there is a separate framework, Scrapy, and for pages that need JavaScript to run there are browser drivers such as Selenium and Playwright.

code.text:
from bs4 import BeautifulSoup html = "

See one and two

" soup = BeautifulSoup(html, "html.parser") print([a["href"] for a in soup.find_all("a")]) # ['/a', '/b']

nodes.title: SQLAlchemy
nodes.short: Michael Bayer's SQL toolkit and object-relational mapper for Python, released in February 2006.
nodes.long: SQLAlchemy was released on 14 February 2006 by Michael Bayer. It is a SQL toolkit and an object-relational mapper, a layer that lets a program treat database rows as Python objects instead of writing every SQL string by hand. In September 2026 it had 332 million downloads, ranking 87th on PyPI, and version 2.1.1 appeared on 25 September 2026. It connects to databases through drivers, such as psycopg for PostgreSQL, whose version 3 had 131 million downloads that month, and it can use the sqlite3 module from the standard library, as in create_engine("sqlite:///x.db").

code.text:
from sqlalchemy import create_engine, text

engine = create_engine("sqlite:///x.db")
with engine.connect() as conn:
    print(conn.execute(text("select 1")).scalar())

nodes.title: Virtual Environments (venv, virtualenv)
nodes.short: A private folder of Python packages for one project, so that projects with conflicting needs do not interfere with each other.
nodes.long: A virtual environment is a folder that holds the installed packages for a single project, together with a Python interpreter set up to use them, so two projects can use different versions of the same library without colliding. Ian Bicking's virtualenv popularised the idea, and PEP 405 added the standard-library venv module in Python 3.3, noting that virtualenv had to duplicate much of Python's site module and manually link an ever-changing set of standard-library modules. PEP 668, first written in 2021, lets operating systems mark their own Python as externally managed, because pip can unintentionally delete packages installed by the OS package manager and corrupt the system. A 2018 xkcd strip about Python environments became the popular shorthand for the mess.
nodes.sleeper: Per-project environments are Python's answer to the shared-folder problem of early Windows: instead of one global place for libraries, every project gets a private one.

code.text:
python -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate    # on Windows: .venv\Scripts\activate
pip install requests

refs.label: PEP 668: Marking Python base environments as externally managed

nodes.title: Bundler
nodes.short: Ruby's dependency tool, which popularised the Gemfile plus Gemfile.lock pattern that Composer and Cargo later followed.
nodes.long: Bundler reads a Gemfile that lists a project's gems and writes a Gemfile.lock recording the exact versions chosen, so every developer and server installs the same set. The Bundler gem metadata lists Carl Lerche and Yehuda Katz among its authors; its first release on RubyGems was 0.3.0 on 4 August 2009 and 1.0.0 followed on 29 August 2010. Lerche and Katz later designed Cargo for Rust. Composer's documentation says Composer is strongly inspired by npm and Bundler, and the Rust team said Cargo follows the tradition of successes like Bundler and npm. Since version 4.0 in December 2025, Bundler is released together with RubyGems.

code.text:
source "https://rubygems.org"
gem "rails", "~> 7.1"
gem "puma"
# bundle install  resolves these and writes Gemfile.lock

refs.label: Rust Blog: Cargo, Rust's Community Crate Host (2014)

nodes.title: Homebrew
nodes.short: A package manager for macOS and Linux, started by Max Howell in 2009, that installs command-line tools and apps from community recipes.
nodes.long: Max Howell created Homebrew in 2009 as a package manager for macOS. Its recipes are called formulae and are Ruby scripts, its "bottles" are pre-built binaries, and "taps" are third-party repositories. It installs into its own directory, /opt/homebrew on Apple silicon and /usr/local on Intel Macs. Linux and Windows Subsystem for Linux have been officially supported since 2019, after a merger with Linuxbrew. The project is run by volunteers with no paid staff. Version 7.0.7 appeared on 28 September 2026, and in the Stack Overflow 2025 survey 25.7 percent of respondents used Homebrew, ahead of APT at 18.4 percent, Chocolatey at 11 percent and Pacman at 8.7 percent.
nodes.sleeper: Homebrew's own installation instruction is one line of shell that downloads and runs a script from the web. Homebrew, uv, rustup and Bun all give such a line, a habit that draws debate about trust.

code.text:
brew install wget
brew upgrade wget
brew list

nodes.title: Flask
nodes.short: Armin Ronacher's "micro" Python web framework from 2010: a small core that you extend yourself, in contrast to Django.
nodes.long: Flask is a "micro" web framework for Python, created by Armin Ronacher of the Pallets project; its first GitHub commit is dated 6 April 2010. Micro here means a small core that leaves other choices, such as database access, to add-on libraries. A minimal application is a function attached to a URL route. Flask was used by 14.4 percent of Stack Overflow 2025 respondents. Its PyPI downloads of 137 million in September 2026 were roughly flat against 149 million a year earlier, while FastAPI's grew from 145 million to 377 million. Version 3.1.3 dates from 19 February 2026.

nodes.title: NuGet
nodes.short: The package manager for .NET: ZIP files with a .nupkg extension holding compiled code and a manifest, hosted at nuget.org.
nodes.long: NuGet is the Microsoft-supported mechanism for sharing code on .NET. A package is a single ZIP file with the .nupkg extension that holds compiled code (DLLs), related files and a manifest describing it, including its version number. When a package depends on others, NuGet fetches those down-level dependencies too, and when three packages need different versions of one library it works out which version satisfies all of them. Projects list their top-level dependencies with PackageReference; the older packages.config is no longer under active development. The nuget.org search API reported 492,566 total hits on 30 September 2026, although Microsoft's documentation still says over 100,000. In the Stack Overflow 2025 survey 18.9 percent of respondents used NuGet.

code.text:
dotnet add package Serilog
# adds a PackageReference to the project file and restores the package

nodes.title: Pillow
nodes.short: The maintained fork of the Python Imaging Library, used to open, resize and save images; the original PIL dates to 1995.
nodes.long: The Python Imaging Library, by Fredrik Lundh and contributors, was first released in 1995 according to Wikipedia. Pillow is a fork of it, first uploaded to PyPI on 31 July 2010. It opens, resizes and saves images in many formats, as in Image.open("a.png").resize((64, 64)). Pillow is licensed under the MIT-CMU (HPND) licence. Version 12.3.0 appeared on 1 July 2026, and the package had 426 million downloads in September 2026, ranking 59th on PyPI.

code.text:
from PIL import Image

Image.open("a.png").resize((64, 64)).save("small.png")

nodes.title: requests
nodes.short: Kenneth Reitz's simple HTTP client library for Python, the seventh most downloaded package on PyPI in September 2026.
nodes.long: requests was released in February 2011 by Kenneth Reitz as a simple way to make HTTP calls from Python: requests.get(url) returns a response with a status code and body. It sits on urllib3, the connection-pooling layer, which is itself the fifth most downloaded PyPI package. In September 2026 requests had about 1.2 billion downloads and ranked seventh on PyPI, with version 2.34.2 dated 14 May 2026 and 54.4 thousand GitHub stars. Much of that traffic comes not from people choosing it but from tools and other packages that depend on it. Newer clients include aiohttp (first commit 2013) and httpx (2019), which offer asynchronous calls.

code.text:
import requests

print(requests.get("https://example.com").status_code)   # 200

nodes.title: Composer
nodes.short: PHP's per-project dependency manager and its Packagist registry, launched in 2012 and modelled on npm and Bundler.
nodes.long: Nils Adermann and Jordi Boggiano launched Composer in 2012. Its documentation describes it as a tool for dependency management in PHP: you declare the libraries a project depends on and Composer installs and updates them, per project, into a vendor directory, and by default it installs nothing globally, unlike Yum or Apt. It is strongly inspired by npm and Bundler and uses a solver based on openSUSE's libzypp SAT solver. Libraries come from Packagist, which listed 469,642 packages and had served about 202 billion downloads when queried on 30 September 2026. Composer 2.10.3 appeared on 27 August 2026, and 11 percent of Stack Overflow 2025 respondents used it.

code.text:
composer require monolog/monolog
# writes composer.json and composer.lock, installs into vendor/

nodes.title: Next.js
nodes.short: Vercel's React framework that renders pages on the server; 20.8 percent of Stack Overflow 2025 respondents used it.
nodes.long: Next.js is a framework from Vercel, dating to 2016, that builds on React. It renders pages on the server so that the browser receives finished HTML, adding JavaScript only where it is needed. Nuxt, SvelteKit, Remix and Astro are similar server-rendering frameworks, and together they brought rendering back to the server after the single-page-app years. React Server Components, stable in React 19 in December 2024, put a related idea inside React itself, although their complexity is contested. Next.js 16, released on 21 October 2025, made Turbopack the default bundler. About 240 million npm downloads a month were counted in September 2026, and 20.8 percent of Stack Overflow 2025 respondents used Next.js.

nodes.title: pnpm
nodes.short: A JavaScript package manager that saves disk space with a shared content-addressable store and stops code from using undeclared dependencies.
nodes.long: pnpm gives its motivation as disk space, speed and strictness. Files are kept once in a content-addressable store and linked into projects with hard links, so if you depend on different versions of a dependency only the files that differ are added to the store. It uses symlinks to place only a project's direct dependencies at the root of node_modules, so code cannot quietly use "phantom" dependencies that it never declared. State of JavaScript 2025 found pnpm the clear leader for monorepo tooling, with 3,940 respondents ahead of npm workspaces (2,129), Yarn workspaces (1,341) and bun install (1,123), and 13.4 percent of Stack Overflow 2025 respondents used it. pnpm 12, released on 26 August 2026, made unrecognised settings an error after a misspelt minimumReleaseAge had silently dropped a delay policy.

nodes.title: pyproject.toml and Packaging PEPs
nodes.short: The standard file where a Python project declares build requirements, metadata and dependencies, defined by a series of PEPs from 2016 on.
nodes.long: The older route, a setup.py script run with python setup.py install, is deprecated according to the Python Packaging User Guide. The declarative alternative is pyproject.toml. PEP 518, created on 10 May 2016, introduced it for build requirements, PEP 621 (22 June 2020) moved project metadata such as name, version and dependencies into it, and PEP 723 (4 August 2023) added inline metadata for single-file scripts. PEP 751, accepted on 31 March 2025, adds a standard lock file, pylock.toml, with mandatory hash verification. These standards are why Poetry, PDM, Hatch and uv can all read the same project file. PEP 772, accepted on 16 April 2026, creates an elected five-member Packaging Council.

code.text:
[build-system]
requires = ["hatchling"]
build-backend = "hatchling.build"

[project]
name = "demo"
version = "0.1.0"
dependencies = ["requests>=2.31"]

nodes.title: Yarn
nodes.short: A JavaScript package manager announced by Facebook with Exponent, Google and Tilde in October 2016, built around a lockfile and checksums.
nodes.long: Facebook announced Yarn on 11 October 2016, together with Exponent, Google and Tilde. It named three problems with the npm client of the time: consistency when installing dependencies across different machines and users, install time, and security, in particular the way the client automatically ran code from some dependencies. Yarn's features were a lockfile that locks installed dependencies to specific versions so every install produces the same file structure in node_modules, an offline cache, and package checksums stored in the lockfile. Yarn Classic's last release was 1.22.22 on 9 March 2024, while the newer Berry line was at 4.18.1 on 24 September 2026. In the Stack Overflow 2025 survey 21.1 percent of respondents used Yarn, behind npm at 56.8 percent.

refs.label: Facebook Engineering: Yarn, a new package manager for JavaScript (2016)

nodes.title: Pydantic
nodes.short: A Python library that validates data against type hints; its Rust core and its use inside FastAPI put it among PyPI's most downloaded packages.
nodes.long: Samuel Colvin made the first commit to Pydantic on 3 May 2017. You declare a class whose fields carry type hints, such as id: int, and Pydantic checks and converts incoming data to match: User(id="3") gives id=3. FastAPI is built on it, and its author wrote that after testing several alternatives he decided to use Pydantic. The validation core, pydantic-core, is written in Rust. In September 2026 pydantic had 843 million downloads, 18th on PyPI, up from 10.7 million in September 2021, and pydantic-core had 809 million.

code.text:
from pydantic import BaseModel

class User(BaseModel):
    id: int

print(User(id="3"))   # id=3

nodes.title: Jakarta EE
nodes.short: The Eclipse Foundation's continuation of Java EE, renamed Jakarta EE in 2018; its 2020 release moved package names from javax to jakarta.
nodes.long: J2EE, the Java 2 Platform, Enterprise Edition, dates from 1999 (version 1.2) and was renamed Java EE in 2005 or 2006. On 12 September 2017 Oracle announced that it would move Java EE to the Eclipse Foundation, which could not use the Java or javax names, so the platform was renamed Jakarta EE in 2018. Jakarta EE 8 followed in September 2019 and Jakarta EE 9 in December 2020, which changed the package namespace from javax to jakarta. Versions 10 and 11 arrived in September 2022 and June 2025. EJB 3.0, in 2006, had already replaced much of the XML of EJB 2 with annotations.

nodes.title: Poetry
nodes.short: A Python tool by Sébastien Eustace that manages dependencies, a lock file and publishing from pyproject.toml.
nodes.long: Poetry began in February 2018 under Sébastien Eustace and put dependency declaration, a lock file and publishing in one Python tool: poetry add requests adds a dependency to pyproject.toml and locks the result. It was one of several tools, with PDM, Hatch and later uv, built on the pyproject.toml standards. PEP 751, accepted on 31 March 2025, notes that Python had no standard lock file format, with proprietary solutions in PDM, pip-tools, Poetry and uv, and standardises pylock.toml. Poetry 2.5.1 appeared on 20 September 2026. Its September 2026 PyPI downloads were about 41.6 million, down from 69.3 million a year earlier while uv's rose, and 9 percent of Stack Overflow 2025 respondents used it.

code.text:
poetry new demo
cd demo
poetry add requests

refs.label: PEP 751: a file format to record Python dependencies

nodes.title: PubGrub
nodes.short: A version-resolution algorithm from Dart's pub that learns from conflicts and can explain in plain terms why no set of versions works.
nodes.long: PubGrub is the version-solving algorithm behind pub, the package manager of the Dart language. It is based on conflict-driven clause learning, an algorithm for solving the NP-hard Boolean satisfiability problem. Its distinctive feature is error reporting: because of the clause learning, it can explain the root causes of a conflict in readable terms, built from a derivation graph, instead of only reporting that no solution exists. Astral's uv, a Python tool written in Rust, depends on a fork of PubGrub, so an algorithm designed for Dart's packages now resolves Python's as well.

nodes.title: Minimal Version Selection
nodes.short: Go's resolution rule: use the highest of the minimum versions that any module asks for, which needs no lockfile and no general solver.
nodes.long: Minimal Version Selection was described by Russ Cox in 2018 as part of the Go modules design. Each module declares the minimum version of each dependency it needs, and a build uses the maximum of all those minimums, so it never selects a release that nobody in the graph asked for. Cox calls such builds high-fidelity, because they differ from the author's own build only when another requirement forces it, and the approach removes the need for a separate lock file. It stays computationally tractable, unlike general constraint solving. The price is that upgrades do not happen until a developer asks for them. Google's engineering book endorses it for builds that stay as close as possible to what the author tested.
nodes.sleeper: Most tools take the newest compatible release by default. MVS never picks a version nobody asked for, which also keeps a freshly published malicious release out. That is a side effect rather than a stated goal.

nodes.title: htmx
nodes.short: A small JavaScript library by Carson Gross that lets HTML attributes fetch server-rendered fragments, as an alternative to single-page apps.
nodes.long: htmx, by Carson Gross, extends plain HTML with attributes so that a server can return fragments of HTML for partial page updates, without a single-page app. It argues that most applications do not need a SPA. State of JavaScript 2025 ranks it last on its front-end framework usage list: real, but niche. It is the best-known example of a hypermedia counter-movement to the single-page app, and Rails' Hotwire and Phoenix LiveView follow a similar server-driven idea.

nodes.title: Sigstore
nodes.short: An open-source project for signing and verifying software artifacts without long-lived keys, using short-lived certificates and a public log.
nodes.long: Sigstore lets developers sign software and users verify it. It has three parts: Cosign, the client that signs and verifies; Fulcio, a code-signing certificate authority that issues short-lived credentials; and Rekor, a transparency log, an immutable append-only ledger of signing events. In keyless signing the signer creates an ephemeral key pair, proves identity with an OpenID Connect token, receives a short-lived certificate and then discards the private key, so no long-lived secret remains to be stolen. Sigstore is maintained under the OpenSSF with support from Google, Red Hat, Chainguard, GitHub and Purdue. Cosign v3.1.3 was released on 6 August 2026.

nodes.title: SLSA
nodes.short: Supply-chain Levels for Software Artifacts, an OpenSSF framework of controls and levels for preventing tampering with how software is built.
nodes.long: SLSA, pronounced "salsa", is a security framework: a checklist of standards and controls meant to prevent tampering, improve integrity and secure packages and infrastructure. It is part of the Open Source Security Foundation (OpenSSF), with Google, the Linux Foundation and CNCF among its founders. Its specification defines Build and Source tracks, and its site lists versions v1.2 and v1.1. A central idea is provenance, a signed record of where and how an artifact was built. Provenance has limits: it shows where and how something was built, not that the pipeline was uncompromised. In May 2026 malicious TanStack packages published through a legitimate CI pipeline reportedly carried valid SLSA provenance attestations issued by npm's signing infrastructure.

refs.label: SLSA: Supply-chain Levels for Software Artifacts

nodes.title: Trusted Publishing
nodes.short: Publishing packages with short-lived credentials issued to a CI workflow, instead of long-lived tokens that can be stolen.
nodes.long: A long-lived publishing token is a secret that lets whoever steals it release new versions of a package. Trusted publishing replaces it with short-lived credentials issued through OpenID Connect: the registry is told to trust one specific CI workflow, and that workflow receives a credential that, at PyPI, is valid for only 15 minutes. RubyGems announced it on 14 December 2023, and crates.io on 11 July 2025, inspired by PyPI. npm supports it for GitHub Actions, GitLab CI/CD and CircleCI, and generates provenance attestations from GitHub Actions or GitLab. The Python Packaging User Guide now recommends it. After the 2025 attacks npm also revoked all classic tokens on 9 December 2025, and npm login now issues a two-hour session token.
nodes.sleeper: Maintainers once published from a laptop with a saved token. Registries now prefer releases from a named CI workflow, which removes a stealable token but not the risk of a compromised workflow.

nodes.title: Quality: Lint, Test, CI
nodes.short: Automated checks that catch mistakes before users do.
nodes.long: Linters, type checkers, tests and continuous integration run on every change. They are the reason modern teams can ship many times a day.

nodes.title: Linting & Static Analysis
nodes.short: Tools that read code without running it and flag likely bugs and style problems. Named after lint on cloth.
nodes.long: Stephen Johnson wrote the original lint for C at Bell Labs in 1978. Today there are style linters, formatters, type checkers, bug finders and security scanners, often run automatically on every commit.
nodes.sleeper: Where you once argued about brace style, a formatter now ends the debate automatically.

nodes.title: Software Security
nodes.short: Keeping code safe when someone hostile uses it: hostile input, memory errors, risky dependencies and leaked secrets. The 1988 Morris worm was an early lesson.
nodes.long: Security became a software concern in November 1988, when the Morris worm spread across the early Internet partly through a buffer overflow in the finger service. The same causes keep returning: memory bugs, input treated as code, over-powerful features in widely shared components and unpatched services. Microsoft reported in 2019 that about 70 percent of the security issues it assigned a CVE to were memory-safety bugs, and Chromium found about the same share among its high-severity bugs. Android's share of memory-safety flaws fell below 20 percent in 2025, and Google credits Rust for new code. Scanners and fuzzers find flaws, dependency tools track known ones, and habits such as parameterized queries, short-lived credentials and zero trust limit the damage.
nodes.sleeper: The new habits are that all input is hostile and all dependencies are code you answer for.

refs.label: Microsoft MSRC: Why Rust for safe systems programming

nodes.title: Ten Kinds of Code Checker
nodes.short: Ten kinds of tool check code, from formatters and linters to fuzzers and proof assistants. Each knows more about the program than the last, and costs more.
nodes.long: Lint has split into about ten kinds of checker. Style linters such as ESLint and Ruff flag suspicious code, one file at a time. Formatters such as gofmt and Black rewrite layout and judge nothing. Type checkers such as mypy test how values are used. Bug finders such as Infer and Coverity follow data flow between functions. Security scanners such as CodeQL look for exploitable patterns. Dependency and secrets scanners such as Dependabot and Gitleaks match libraries against known flaws and hunt for leaked keys. Complexity and architecture checks such as radon and ArchUnit measure structure. Domain linters such as ShellCheck cover one file format each. Sanitizers and fuzzers such as AddressSanitizer and libFuzzer watch a running program, and formal verifiers such as TLA+ and seL4 prove properties. Rice's theorem says none can be perfect.
nodes.sleeper: Checks now run at four points: in the editor, in a pre-commit hook, as a required gate in CI, and as bot comments in code review. Hooks can be skipped, so CI is the enforced one.

refs.label: Sadowski et al., Lessons from Building Static Analysis Tools at Google (CACM 2018)

nodes.title: Automated Testing
nodes.short: Code that checks your code. Unit, integration and end-to-end tests run on every change.
nodes.long: Kent Beck's SUnit led to JUnit and the xUnit family. Test-driven development writes the test first. Evidence for its benefits is mixed, but automated tests plus CI are now the norm.

nodes.title: Continuous Integration
nodes.short: Build and test every change automatically. CruiseControl, Jenkins, then GitHub Actions.
nodes.long: CI servers run the test suite on each commit so broken changes are caught within minutes. Continuous delivery extends the idea to deploying safely many times a day.

nodes.title: Test-Driven Development
nodes.short: Write a failing test, make it pass, then clean up, in short cycles. Kent Beck's practice has mixed evidence: the small steps seem to matter more than test-first.
nodes.long: Test-driven development means writing an automated unit test that fails, writing just enough code to make it pass, then refactoring both, and repeating. Kent Beck is credited with developing or rediscovering it, and says he remembered an old book describing the idea after writing the first xUnit framework in Smalltalk. Extreme Programming Explained appeared in 1999 and Test-Driven Development: By Example in 2002. Early industrial case studies at Microsoft and IBM found 40 to 90 percent lower pre-release defect density and 15 to 35 percent more initial development time, though against similar projects, not in a randomized trial. A 2017 study of 39 professionals found that the order of writing tests and code had no important influence; short, steady cycles mattered. In 2014 David Heinemeier Hansson wrote "TDD is dead", and he, Beck and Martin Fowler held recorded debates about it.
nodes.sleeper: If you remember writing tests after the code, or leaving them to a separate QA group, TDD flipped the order. Later research suggests the small, steady steps matter more than which comes first.

code.text:
# 1. red: write the test first; it fails because price() does not exist yet
def test_ten_percent_coupon():
    assert price(100, coupon="TEN") == 90

# 2. green: write just enough code to make it pass
def price(amount, coupon=None):
    return amount * 0.9 if coupon == "TEN" else amount
# 3. refactor, run the tests again, repeat

refs.label: Fucci et al., Does It Really Matter to Test-First or to Test-Last?
Fowler, Beck and Hansson: Is TDD Dead?

nodes.title: Continuous Delivery
nodes.short: Keep every change in a state that could ship, and release it in small, automated steps. Humble and Farley's 2010 book turned the idea into a method.
nodes.long: Humble and Farley's 2010 book Continuous Delivery defines the practice as the ability to get all kinds of changes into production, or into users' hands, safely, quickly and sustainably. The mechanism is a deployment pipeline that every change passes through, with automated checks at each stage. Their slogan is that if it hurts, you should do it more often and bring the pain forward. Continuous delivery means every passing change is ready to release at the push of a button; continuous deployment releases it automatically with no human step. IMVU reported in 2009 that it deployed about fifty times a day, and Google Search ships a new binary every other day, guarding changes with flags and rolling them out in stages.
nodes.sleeper: If you remember a nightly build and a release every year or two, the pace has inverted: IMVU deployed about fifty times a day in 2009, and Google Search ships a new binary every other day.

nodes.title: DORA and Accelerate
nodes.short: A research program that measures software delivery with a few outcome metrics, and the 2018 book Accelerate. It finds that speed and stability go together.
nodes.long: DORA, now run by Google Cloud, publishes annual State of DevOps research; its first reports appeared around 2012 or 2013, depending on the source. The 2018 book Accelerate, by Nicole Forsgren, Jez Humble and Gene Kim, drew on 23,000 data points and named 24 capabilities and four key metrics. DORA now uses five: deployment frequency, change lead time, failed-deployment recovery time, change failure rate and deployment rework rate. Its headline finding is that speed and stability are not tradeoffs: top performers do well on all of them. The data are surveys and show correlation, and DORA itself warns against setting the metrics as goals or comparing teams, because that invites gaming. Its 2025 report found that AI amplifies what a team already does, with a negative link to delivery stability.
nodes.sleeper: Where older management measured effort, such as lines of code, DORA measures outcomes: how often you deploy, how long a change takes to reach users, how often changes fail and how quickly you recover.

nodes.title: Ruff
nodes.short: A very fast Python linter and formatter written in Rust. It has replaced Flake8, Black and isort in many projects since 2022.
nodes.long: Ruff, written in Rust by Charlie Marsh and Astral, started in August 2022 as a Python linter and grew a formatter that claims drop-in parity with Black. It ships more than 900 built-in rules and also replaces isort, pydocstyle, pyupgrade and autoflake. Its makers claim it is 10 to 100 times faster than the tools it replaces, a speed that makes running it on every save practical. Projects that use it include Apache Airflow, FastAPI, Hugging Face, pandas and SciPy. By default it applies only fixes that cannot change behavior; riskier ones need an explicit flag. In March 2026 Astral announced it was joining OpenAI's Codex team, and OpenAI said it would keep supporting Ruff, uv and ty as open source.
nodes.sleeper: A 1990s lint was a slow, occasional chore. Ruff's makers claim 10 to 100 times the speed of older Python linters, fast enough to check a whole repository on every save and every commit.

nodes.title: Formal Verification
nodes.short: Proving a property of a program or design with mathematics instead of testing examples. Dijkstra, 1972: tests show that bugs are present, never that they are absent.
nodes.long: In his 1972 Turing lecture Edsger Dijkstra said that program testing can be very effective for showing the presence of bugs but is hopelessly inadequate for showing their absence. Formal verification aims at absence. Model checking explores every state of a finite model of a design. Proof assistants such as Rocq and Lean check mathematical proofs, and tools such as SPARK and Frama-C prove properties of programs written in restricted or annotated languages. Rust's borrow checker is a lightweight form that every Rust programmer meets. Rice's theorem is why these methods restrict the language, require annotations or specifications, or look only at a finite abstraction. Memory safety is the usual target: roughly 70 percent of the security issues Microsoft assigns a CVE to are memory-safety bugs.
nodes.sleeper: You may remember formal methods as a niche for avionics. Since 2011 Amazon engineers have model-checked cloud designs, and the Rust compiler's ownership rules act as a built-in proof of memory safety for everyday programmers.

nodes.title: Code Review
nodes.short: Another person reads a change before it merges. Studies at Microsoft and Google find its main payoff is shared knowledge and readable code, not bug-finding.
nodes.long: Fagan formalized structured, line-by-line inspections at IBM in 1976. Modern code review is informal, regular and tool-based, usually a comment thread on a proposed change. Bacchelli and Bird's 2013 study at Microsoft classified 570 review comments: code improvements were the most common at 29 percent, while comments about defects came fourth at 14 percent; the real benefits were knowledge transfer, team awareness and better solutions. Google's 2018 study of 9 million reviewed changes found a median change of 24 lines, a median of one reviewer and a median review time under four hours, and named code understandability and maintainability as the foremost reason for review. Tools now post analyzer findings, formatting fixes and dependency updates straight into the review.
nodes.sleeper: Fagan's 1976 inspections were structured, line-by-line sessions. Modern review is informal and tool-based: at Google the median change is 24 lines, has one reviewer and clears review in under four hours.

refs.label: Bacchelli and Bird, Expectations, Outcomes, and Challenges of Modern Code Review
Sadowski et al., Modern Code Review: A Case Study at Google

nodes.title: lint (the C Program Checker)
nodes.short: Stephen Johnson's 1978 Bell Labs program that checked C code more strictly than the compiler would. Every later linter descends from it.
nodes.long: Stephen C. Johnson wrote lint at Bell Labs because the C compilers were fast partly by skipping deep type checks, especially between separately compiled files. Lint took what its manual called a more global, leisurely view. It flagged unused variables, values used before being set, unreachable statements, functions that return a value on only some paths, mismatched argument types and constructs that break when moved to another machine. The manual already warned that a message of the form "might be a bug" loses credibility if too few turn out to be real bugs, tied dead-code detection to the halting problem, and offered comments such as NOTREACHED to silence a message. Lint reached the wider world with Unix Version 7 (1979). The name is commonly explained by analogy to a clothes-dryer lint trap, an account that rests on a secondary source.
nodes.sleeper: Lint was a separate command you ran by hand, and many programmers skipped it. The same checks now run in the editor on every keystroke, in the compiler, in pre-commit hooks, in CI and as bot comments on code review.

refs.label: Johnson, Lint, a C Program Checker (Unix V7 manual copy)

nodes.title: Fuzzing
nodes.short: Throwing random or mutated input at a program until it crashes. It began as a 1988 class project; Google's OSS-Fuzz now runs it on about 1,000 projects.
nodes.long: The word comes from a 1988 graduate class project of Barton Miller at the University of Wisconsin, and his 1990 study found that fuzzing could crash 25 to 33 percent of the utilities tested. Modern fuzzers are guided by coverage: libFuzzer, part of LLVM, runs your function on mutated inputs inside the process, and you compile it with sanitizers so memory errors are caught the moment they occur. Google's OSS-Fuzz, started in 2016 in response to the Heartbleed flaw in OpenSSL, had helped identify and fix over 10,000 vulnerabilities and 36,000 bugs across about 1,000 projects by August 2023. Fuzzing finds only what the generated inputs reach.
nodes.sleeper: Random input once looked like a crude trick. By August 2023 Google's OSS-Fuzz had helped identify and fix over 10,000 vulnerabilities and 36,000 other bugs in open-source software.

nodes.title: Code Coverage
nodes.short: A measure of which lines or branches tests executed. Useful for spotting untested code, poor as a target because a coverage number is easy to inflate.
nodes.long: Coverage tools report which lines or branches ran during the tests. In the late 1990s Brian Marick wrote "How to Misuse Code Coverage", warning that managers who set a coverage number as a shipping gate distort behavior, like hiring on grade-point average alone. A 2014 study by Inozemtseva and Holmes built 31,000 test suites for five Java systems and found only a low to moderate link between coverage and a suite's ability to catch artificial faults, concluding that coverage should not be a quality target. Google offers 60, 75 and 90 percent as acceptable, commendable and exemplary but rejects company-wide mandates, and prefers to measure coverage on each change. A test that calls code and checks nothing still raises the number, which is where mutation testing helps.
nodes.sleeper: A 1990s manager might set an 85 percent coverage gate for shipping. The research since says a coverage percentage is a good pointer to untested code and a poor target; Google rejects a company-wide threshold.

refs.label: Inozemtseva and Holmes, Coverage Is Not Strongly Correlated with Test Suite Effectiveness
Google Testing Blog: Code Coverage Best Practices

nodes.title: Kinds of Tests
nodes.short: Unit, integration, end-to-end, acceptance, regression, smoke, snapshot, contract and load tests: what each one checks and how fast it runs.
nodes.long: A unit test runs one small piece of code in isolation, in milliseconds, with no network or disk; Google's "small" tests run in a single process and may not sleep or make blocking calls. An integration test runs several real pieces together, such as code and a real database. An end-to-end test drives the whole product as a user would, often through a browser, and is slow and fragile but closest to reality. An acceptance test checks that the software does what the customer asked, ideally in the customer's words. A regression test guards old behavior against new changes, a smoke test is a quick check that the basics work, a snapshot test fails when stored output changes, a contract test checks that two services agree on their messages, and a load test simulates many users with tools such as Locust, Gatling or k6.
nodes.sleeper: You may remember testing as a manual phase near the end of a project. Today nearly every kind listed here is code that a server runs on each commit, and the main new problem is tests that fail at random.

code.text:
# unit: one function, no I/O, runs in milliseconds
def test_discount():
    assert price(100, coupon="TEN") == 90
# integration: real code with a real database
def test_order_is_saved(db):
    save_order(db, total=90)
    assert db.count("orders") == 1
# end-to-end: a real browser drives the finished product
def test_checkout(page):
    page.goto("/checkout"); page.click("text=Pay")
    assert page.is_visible("text=Thank you")

refs.label: Software Engineering at Google, ch. 11: Testing Overview

nodes.title: xUnit and JUnit
nodes.short: The family of test frameworks that began with Kent Beck's SUnit and the 1997 JUnit: write a test as code, run it by machine, see a green or red bar.
nodes.long: Kent Beck wrote the first xUnit framework, SUnit, for Smalltalk. JUnit, for Java, was born on a flight from Zurich to the 1997 OOPSLA conference in Atlanta, where Beck and Erich Gamma wrote it pair-programming, test first. It introduced the red and green bar, took off quickly, and nearly every language now has a JUnit port: CppUnit, NUnit for .NET and many others. They share one shape: test cases made of assertions, grouped into suites, set up with fixtures and run by a runner that can report in XML for CI servers. A 2013 study of 10,000 GitHub Java projects found JUnit, tied with slf4j-api, the most commonly included external library. JUnit 5 appeared in 2017.

nodes.title: SQL Injection
nodes.short: Attacker-supplied text becomes part of a database query. Described publicly in 1998, still fifth on OWASP's 2025 list, and prevented by parameterized queries.
nodes.long: SQL injection happens when a program builds a query by pasting in user input, so that the input can become part of the SQL. Jeff Forristal, writing as rain.forest.puppy, described the technique for Microsoft SQL Server in Phrack issue 54 on 25 December 1998. OWASP put injection in its top ten in 2007 and 2010 and first in 2013, and in the 2025 list it is still fifth. The fix is the parameterized query, which sends the values separately so they can never be read as SQL. Placeholders protect values only; table and column names must come from a fixed list. Albert Gonzalez's ring, which used SQL injection to plant backdoors, stole more than 170 million card and ATM numbers from 2005 to 2007, and the 2023 MOVEit Transfer breach began with an SQL injection flaw.
nodes.sleeper: Nothing about the bug is new, and every database library now has a safe placeholder API. It persists because it comes from how programs build strings, which makes it a matter of habit and legacy code, not a missing fix.

code.text:
import sqlite3
db = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
db.execute("CREATE TABLE users (name TEXT)")
db.executemany("INSERT INTO users VALUES (?)", [("ann",), ("bob",)])
evil = "x' OR '1'='1"
print(db.execute(f"SELECT name FROM users WHERE name = '{evil}'").fetchall())    # both rows: injected
print(db.execute("SELECT name FROM users WHERE name = ?", (evil,)).fetchall())   # []: plain text

nodes.title: AddressSanitizer and Valgrind
nodes.short: Tools that watch a running program for memory errors. Valgrind (2002) is thorough but over 20 times slower; AddressSanitizer (2012) costs roughly 2 times.
nodes.long: Valgrind, whose Memcheck tool tracks memory accesses and uninitialized values, was first released in 2002 and is used by thousands of C and C++ programmers, at the cost of a mean 22 times slowdown in a 2007 benchmark. Serebryany, Bruening, Potapenko and Vyukov, all at Google, published AddressSanitizer in 2012. It poisons "redzones" around objects and keeps a shadow map of memory, finding out-of-bounds accesses and use-after-free bugs with an average slowdown of 73 percent, and it found over 300 previously unknown bugs in Chromium. Sibling sanitizers cover data races (ThreadSanitizer) and undefined behavior (UBSan). Because the bug really happened, these tools almost never give false alarms, but they only see code that the tests actually run.
nodes.sleeper: Heavyweight memory checkers of the early 2000s slowed programs 20 times or more. AddressSanitizer finds the same class of bugs at roughly 2 times, cheap enough to run in routine tests.

nodes.title: Coverity
nodes.short: A commercial bug finder built in 2002 from a Stanford research checker. Its engineers' 2010 account of false positives shaped the whole field.
nodes.long: Coverity began in November 2002 as a company built around a Stanford research bug finder, with Dawson Engler as technical adviser. It found bugs by following data and control flow through whole programs, ran overnight, and was unsound by design: its authors tried to find as many bugs as possible rather than prove none remained. By December 2009 about 700 customers had licensed it, covering somewhat more than a billion lines of code. A free Coverity Scan service, run under a 2006 US Department of Homeland Security contract, examined more than 150 open-source applications, and about 6,000 of the bugs it found were fixed across 53 projects. Synopsys bought the company in 2014 for $375 million in cash. The 2010 paper by its engineers is the standard source on why false positives sink static analysis.
nodes.sleeper: A Coverity co-founder recalled in 2010 that pitching a static bug finder had drawn "Huh?" or "Lint? Yuck." Companies now run such analyzers on every code change.

nodes.title: SAST
nodes.short: Static application security testing: tools that read source code for exploitable patterns such as SQL injection. Their best-known weakness is noise.
nodes.long: SAST tools analyze source or compiled code for security flaws. OWASP says they scale to large codebases, repeat scans cheaply, find well-known problems such as buffer overflows and SQL injection, and point to the file and line. Its list of weaknesses is just as clear: high numbers of false positives, no view of configuration problems, little ability to find broken authentication or access control, and trouble with code that cannot be built. The first commercial products appeared in the early 2000s, including Coverity in 2002 and Checkmarx in 2006. Open-source examples are Bandit for Python, Brakeman for Rails, Semgrep and SpotBugs; commercial ones include Fortify, Veracode and Snyk Code. Semgrep matches patterns that look like source code, while CodeQL lets analysts write queries.

code.text:
import sqlite3
db = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
db.execute("CREATE TABLE users (name TEXT)")
name = "x' OR '1'='1"
# before: Bandit B608 flags SQL built by string formatting
rows = db.execute("SELECT * FROM users WHERE name = '%s'" % name).fetchall()
# after: the driver passes the value separately
rows = db.execute("SELECT * FROM users WHERE name = ?", (name,)).fetchall()

nodes.title: pytest
nodes.short: Python's dominant test framework. Tests are plain functions with ordinary assert statements, and fixtures supply what each test needs.
nodes.long: pytest grew out of test tools that Holger Krekel and others wrote from about 2003, as part of the PyPy project, and was released as a separate package with pytest 2.0 in November 2010. Its defining features are plain assert statements, which it rewrites to show both sides of a failed comparison, and fixtures, functions that set up what a test needs. A plugin layer lets other tools hook in, and the coverage tool is commonly run as "coverage run -m pytest". In the September 2026 PyPI download ranking pytest was 24th with about 780 million downloads, three times a year earlier, probably because of continuous-integration traffic rather than new users, which is an inference and not a measurement. Version 9.1.1 was released in June 2026.

nodes.title: Selenium
nodes.short: The tool that let programs drive a web browser for testing. Begun at ThoughtWorks in 2004, it merged with WebDriver in 2007.
nodes.long: Selenium began in 2004 at ThoughtWorks in Chicago, when Jason Huggins built a JavaScript test runner for an internal time and expenses application. Selenium Remote Control came from Bea engineers Dan Fabulich and Nelson Sproul, and Shinya Kasatani wrote Selenium IDE in 2006. In 2007 Simon Stewart created WebDriver, which uses browser-specific drivers instead of injected JavaScript; Huggins joined Google and the two projects merged. IMVU's 2009 pipeline, which deployed fifty times a day, ran over an hour of Internet Explorer tests through Selenium. Google measured Java WebDriver tests as 10.45 percent flaky and Python ones as 18.72 percent, against 1.65 percent for all tests. Selenium remains active, while Playwright and Cypress became the defaults for many new web projects.

code.text:
from selenium import webdriver

driver = webdriver.Chrome()
driver.get("https://example.com")
print(driver.title)          # Example Domain
driver.quit()

nodes.title: CodeQL
nodes.short: GitHub's code-query engine. Analysts describe a bug pattern as a query in QL, a Datalog-style language. It began as the Oxford spin-out Semmle.
nodes.long: CodeQL grew out of Semmle, founded in December 2006 in Oxford by Oege de Moor of the University of Oxford. Its query language, QL, is described as an object-oriented version of Datalog: instead of coding a checker, an analyst writes a query that describes a pattern, such as untrusted input reaching a database call, and the engine reports the code that matches. GitHub, owned by Microsoft, acquired Semmle on 18 September 2019, and in November 2019 made CodeQL free for research and open-source projects. It is one of the best-known tools in the SAST class.

nodes.title: The Test Pyramid
nodes.short: Many fast unit tests, fewer integration tests and very few slow end-to-end tests. Mike Cohn's picture, and Google's 70/20/10 rule of thumb.
nodes.long: Mike Cohn described the test pyramid in his 2009 book Succeeding with Agile; he and Lisa Crispin had drawn it around 2003 to 2004. Martin Fowler's 2012 account puts unit tests at the base, a service layer in the middle and UI tests at the top, and says you should do much more testing through unit tests than through the GUI. Google's testing blog suggested in 2015 a first guess of 70 percent unit tests, 20 percent integration tests and 10 percent end-to-end tests, and its 2020 book says about 80, 15 and 5. The usual anti-pattern is the "ice cream cone", with most testing at the slow, flaky top. Google's Mike Wacker called a tenth of a second slow for a unit test.

refs.label: Wacker: Just Say No to More End-to-End Tests

nodes.title: Jenkins
nodes.short: The long-running open-source automation server for building and testing code. It began as Hudson and was renamed in 2011 after a dispute with Oracle.
nodes.long: Jenkins began as Hudson, a Java continuous integration server that around 2007 became known as a better alternative to CruiseControl, the first open-source CI tool (2001). Hudson won a Duke's Choice Award at JavaOne in May 2008. After Oracle acquired Sun it claimed trademark rights to the Hudson name in December 2010; the community voted to rename the project Jenkins in January 2011, and Oracle said it would continue Hudson and treat Jenkins as a fork. Jenkins won the community: by June 2019 it had 667 GitHub members to Hudson's 28. Its Pipeline plugin 2.0, released in April 2016, let a build be defined in a file in the repository called a Jenkinsfile. Hosted services such as Travis CI, CircleCI and finally GitHub Actions later became the default for many projects.

nodes.title: TLA+ at AWS
nodes.short: Since 2011 Amazon engineers have used the TLA+ specification language and its model checker to find subtle design bugs in S3, DynamoDB and other systems.
nodes.long: In a 2014 paper, Newcombe and colleagues at Amazon Web Services described using formal specification and model checking since 2011 to find design bugs in critical systems. They had applied TLA+, the specification language created by Leslie Lamport, to 10 large systems, including S3, DynamoDB and an internal lock manager. In every case it either found subtle bugs they were sure testing would have missed or gave them enough confidence to make aggressive performance optimizations. One DynamoDB replication bug that could lose data needed a 35-step sequence of failures and recoveries to appear. Engineers from entry level to principal learned TLA+ in two to three weeks. The authors state the limit themselves: nothing proves that the executable code matches the verified design.

refs.label: Newcombe et al., Use of Formal Methods at Amazon Web Services (2014)

nodes.title: mypy
nodes.short: Python's best-known static type checker. It reads optional type hints and reports mismatches before the program runs, without making Python statically typed.
nodes.long: Jukka Lehtosalo started mypy in 2012 as optional static typing for Python. Its approach became the model for PEP 484, which Guido van Rossum, Lehtosalo and Łukasz Langa wrote in 2014 and which arrived in Python 3.5 as standard type hints. The PEP says it was strongly inspired by mypy, that Python will remain dynamically typed, and that the authors never want type hints to be mandatory. A study that added types by hand to real, already-fixed JavaScript bugs found that Flow and TypeScript each caught 15 percent of them, bugs that had survived testing and review. Microsoft's Pyright and Astral's ty, a Rust checker still in beta whose makers claim it is 10 to 100 times faster, compete with mypy.
nodes.sleeper: A language you may remember as purely dynamic now has an optional type layer: PEP 484 added type hints in Python 3.5, and checkers such as mypy read them without making them mandatory.

refs.label: To Type or Not to Type (Gao, Bird and Barr)

nodes.title: ESLint
nodes.short: The standard JavaScript linter. Plugins check style, bugs and framework rules.
nodes.long: Nicholas Zakas created ESLint in 2013. Faster Rust-based tools such as Biome and oxlint now compete with it.

nodes.title: Style Wars and Auto-Formatting
nodes.short: Arguments over braces, tabs and line width ended not with a winner but with tools that rewrite code into one layout, so reviewers stopped debating it.
nodes.long: Programmers have always argued about layout: where the brace goes, tabs or spaces, how long a line may be. Written style guides settled these questions only as long as someone enforced them by hand. Formatters changed that by removing the choice. A 2013 Go blog post promised an end to debates about spacing, and Prettier and Black later made the same offer. Google says too much review time had been spent arguing over formatting, and that its automated formatters beat humans by a significant margin. Formatters make no claim about whether code is correct, so they cannot raise false alarms, which is why teams can enforce them fully automatically. The evidence is practitioner testimony from tool documentation and Google's experience, not a controlled study.
nodes.sleeper: Where teams once enforced a written style guide by hand in review, a formatter now rewrites the file, and Google says formatting "becomes a non-issue during code review."

refs.label: Go blog: go fmt your code
Software Engineering at Google, ch. 8: Style Guides and Rules

nodes.title: Tricorder (Google)
nodes.short: Google's code-review analysis platform. It posts static-analysis findings on changed lines, and kept false alarms low enough that engineers acted on them.
nodes.long: Tricorder, described in a 2015 paper by Sadowski and colleagues, is Google's platform for running program analyzers on every code review. Results appear as robot comments on the lines the author changed, with one-click fixes where possible. Analyzers that more than 10 percent of readers mark not useful are put on probation or switched off, and per-user settings and severity ratings were removed. By January 2018 it handled about 50,000 reviews a day with 146 analyzers; reviewers clicked "Please fix" more than 5,000 times a day and authors applied automated fixes about 3,000 times a day. Google's later account recounts three failed FindBugs efforts: a 2006 dashboard few opened, a 2009 "Fixit" week that fixed 640 of 1,746 filed bugs, and a code-review integration dropped in 2011.

refs.label: Sadowski et al., Lessons from Building Static Analysis Tools at Google (CACM 2018)

nodes.title: GitHub Actions
nodes.short: GitHub's built-in automation, generally available in November 2019. Workflows stored in the repository run tests and deployments on hosted machines.
nodes.long: GitHub announced Actions in October 2018 and made it generally available on 13 November 2019. A workflow is a YAML file in the repository that says what to run on which events, on hosted Linux, Windows or macOS machines, with a marketplace of reusable actions. Because it sits beside the code and the pull request, it took over from separate CI services: Travis CI ended free builds for open-source projects in December 2020, and many of them moved to Actions. Required status checks from workflows can block a merge into a protected branch. The convenience has a cost: workflows that handle untrusted pull-request input with elevated rights were the root cause of the August 2025 Nx compromise and, together with cache poisoning, of the May 2026 TanStack one.
nodes.sleeper: CI used to mean running a server such as CruiseControl or Jenkins yourself. Now the pipeline is a YAML file in the repository and the machines are hosted for you.

code.text:
# .github/workflows/tests.yml
name: tests
on: [push, pull_request]
jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - run: pip install pytest && pytest

nodes.title: Playwright
nodes.short: Microsoft's browser-testing library, released in 2020. One API drives Chromium, Firefox and WebKit, and it waits automatically for pages to be ready.
nodes.long: Playwright, from Microsoft, was first released on 31 January 2020. One programming interface drives three browser engines: Chromium, Firefox and WebKit. It was built by engineers who had previously worked on Puppeteer at Google. Its automatic waiting for elements to become ready targets the biggest single cause of flaky browser tests, which a 2014 study found was not waiting properly for asynchronous work. The GitHub repository has about 97,000 stars, ahead of Cypress (about 51,000) and Selenium (about 34,500), and Playwright and Cypress have become the defaults for many new web projects.

code.text:
from playwright.sync_api import sync_playwright

with sync_playwright() as p:
    browser = p.chromium.launch()
    page = browser.new_page()
    page.goto("https://example.com")
    print(page.title())          # Example Domain
    browser.close()

nodes.title: Hoare Logic
nodes.short: Tony Hoare's 1969 notation for proving a program correct: if a precondition holds before the code runs, a stated postcondition holds after.
nodes.long: In "An Axiomatic Basis for Computer Programming", published in the Communications of the ACM in October 1969, C. A. R. Hoare of Queen's University Belfast wrote that programming is an exact science in that all the properties of a program can in principle be found out from its text by deductive reasoning. His notation, now called a Hoare triple, says that if assertion P holds before program Q starts, then assertion R holds when it finishes. The paper gives rules for assignment and loops and works through a division program. Hoare credited Robert Floyd, whose treatment applied to flowcharts rather than program text, and admitted that proofs would be hard even for skilled programmers and suited only to simple designs. Wirth later observed that the idea passed virtually unnoticed in industry, because the examples were small and industry's systems were huge.
nodes.sleeper: Hoare's proofs were done by hand on small programs. Tools now generate and check such conditions: Frama-C's site claims it proves up to 98 percent of them automatically, and SPARK proves the absence of runtime errors.

code.text:
def divide(x, y):
    assert x >= 0 and y > 0                 # precondition P
    r, q = x, 0
    while y <= r:
        r, q = r - y, q + 1                 # keeps x == r + y*q true
    assert x == r + y * q and r < y         # postcondition R
    return q, r
print(divide(17, 5))                        # (3, 2)

refs.label: Hoare, An Axiomatic Basis for Computer Programming (1969)
Wirth, 2008 essay on the history of programming

nodes.title: Cyclomatic Complexity
nodes.short: Thomas McCabe's 1976 count of the independent paths through a function. A simple gauge of how tangled code is, with no proof that lowering it removes bugs.
nodes.long: In 1976 Thomas J. McCabe proposed counting the linearly independent paths through a program's control flow; for a simple function that is one plus its number of decisions such as if, while and logical and/or. He recommended splitting modules that scored above 10. Tools such as radon for Python now report it. Critics note that the score tracks program size and that reducing it has not been shown to reduce the number of errors. The same family of checkers measures duplication (jscpd), dead code (Vulture) and module dependencies (madge), and ArchUnit turns an architecture rule, such as "UI code may not call the database", into an ordinary unit test.

code.text:
def grade(score):          # complexity 4: one base path, plus one per decision
    if score >= 90:        # decision 1
        return "A"
    elif score >= 80:      # decision 2
        return "B"
    elif score >= 70:      # decision 3
        return "C"
    return "F"

nodes.title: Mutation Testing
nodes.short: A test of your tests: a tool plants small deliberate bugs and checks whether any test fails. A mutant that survives points to a weak test.
nodes.long: Mutation testing makes tiny changes to code, such as flipping a less-than to less-or-equal or deleting a line, and reruns the tests. A failing run kills the mutant; a passing run means the tests did not notice. The mutation score is the share of mutants killed. Richard Lipton proposed the idea as a student in 1971, DeMillo, Lipton and Sayward described it in "Hints on test data selection" in April 1978, the same year as lint, and Timothy Budd built the first tool in 1980. PIT for the JVM and Stryker for JavaScript are current tools. Running every mutant proved too costly at scale, so Google generates at most one mutant per line, skips "arid" lines such as logging, and shows results in code review; about 6,000 engineers used it by 2018.

refs.label: Petrovic and Ivankovic, State of Mutation Testing at Google (2018)

nodes.title: seL4, SPARK, Rocq and Lean
nodes.short: Tools for proving software correct: SPARK for Ada (1987), the seL4 kernel, and the Rocq and Lean proof assistants, which check proofs by machine.
nodes.long: SPARK began at the University of Southampton in 1987 as a provable subset of Ada, sponsored by the UK Ministry of Defence. Its prover can show that a program has no runtime errors, and it has been used in Rolls-Royce Trent engines, the Eurofighter Typhoon, UK air traffic management and rail signaling. Rocq, formerly Coq, is a proof assistant that has hosted CompCert, a verified C compiler, and a proof of the Four-Color theorem. Lean, begun by Leonardo de Moura at Microsoft Research in 2013, has a library, Mathlib, with over 210,000 theorems. The seL4 kernel has machine-checked proofs of functional correctness and integrity, and confidentiality proofs were completed on AArch64 in August 2026. RustBelt, a 2018 project, used Coq to prove that a core of Rust's ownership rules is sound.

code.text:
theorem add_zero' (n : Nat) : n + 0 = n := rfl         -- true by the definition of +
theorem zero_add' (n : Nat) : 0 + n = n := by omega    -- needs a little arithmetic
#check @zero_add'

nodes.title: Test Doubles and Mocking
nodes.short: Stand-in objects that replace a real database, network or service in a test. Fowler's vocabulary: dummy, fake, stub, spy and mock.
nodes.long: A test double replaces a real collaborator so that a test can run quickly and predictably. Martin Fowler's "Mocks Aren't Stubs", using Gerard Meszaros's terms, separates five kinds: a dummy is passed around but never used; a fake is a working shortcut implementation, unsuitable for production; a stub returns canned answers; a spy is a stub that records how it was called; and a mock is pre-programmed with expectations about the calls it should receive. Mock objects came out of the Extreme Programming community, with the original paper presented at XP2000. Two styles result: classical tests check the final state, while mockist tests check the interactions. Over-mocking has a cost, and critics such as David Heinemeier Hansson say it produces an overly complex web of indirection.

code.text:
from unittest.mock import Mock

gateway = Mock()                       # a mock: records calls and returns canned answers
gateway.charge.return_value = "ok"

def checkout(total, gateway):
    return gateway.charge(total)

assert checkout(90, gateway) == "ok"
gateway.charge.assert_called_once_with(90)   # mockist style: verify the behavior

nodes.title: Property-Based Testing
nodes.short: Instead of hand-picked examples, state a rule that should always hold and let the tool try hundreds of random inputs, shrinking any failure to a small one.
nodes.long: A property-based test states a general rule, for example that reversing a list twice gives back the original list, and a library generates many random inputs to look for a counterexample. When one fails, the tool shrinks it to a minimal case that is easier to debug. QuickCheck, by Koen Claessen and John Hughes at Chalmers University, introduced the approach for Haskell at ICFP in 2000: properties are written as Haskell functions and tested on random input, with custom generators when needed. Hypothesis brings the idea to Python. It resembles fuzzing in using random inputs, but the checks are explicit statements about behavior.

code.text:
import Test.QuickCheck

prop_reverseTwice :: [Int] -> Bool
prop_reverseTwice xs = reverse (reverse xs) == xs

main :: IO ()
main = quickCheck prop_reverseTwice   -- +++ OK, passed 100 tests.

nodes.title: OWASP Top 10
nodes.short: A community-maintained list of the most critical web application risks. In the 2025 edition Broken Access Control is first, supply chain third and Injection fifth.
nodes.long: OWASP, a community project on application security, publishes the OWASP Top 10, a ranked list of the most critical web application risks. The 2025 edition runs: A01 Broken Access Control, A02 Security Misconfiguration, A03 Software Supply Chain Failures, A04 Cryptographic Failures, A05 Injection (which includes cross-site scripting), A06 Insecure Design, A07 Authentication Failures, A08 Software or Data Integrity Failures, A09 Security Logging and Alerting Failures, and A10 Mishandling of Exceptional Conditions. Injection ranked first in 2013 and is now fifth. OWASP also publishes the standard definition of static application security testing, lists of scanning tools, and cheat sheets such as the one on parameterized queries.

nodes.title: Behavior-Driven Development
nodes.short: Dan North's 2006 refinement of TDD: name tests as sentences about behavior, in language the customer understands. RSpec and Cucumber grew from it.
nodes.long: Dan North introduced behaviour-driven development in a September 2006 article. Programmers kept asking where to start, what to test, how much to test at once, what to call tests and why a test failed. His answer grew out of two ideas: agiledox, a utility by his colleague Chris Stevenson that turned JUnit test method names into plain sentences, and a naming habit of writing "the class should do something". BDD then widened into agile analysis and automated acceptance tests written in the customer's language. RSpec, a Ruby tool begun in 2005, reads like a specification with describe, it and expect, and Cucumber for Ruby carries the idea into acceptance tests.
