RSpec's latest release in the sources is 3.13.0, from February 2024.

code.text:
def price(amount, coupon: nil) = coupon == "TEN" ? amount * 0.9 : amount

RSpec.describe "price" do
  it "takes ten percent off with the TEN coupon" do
    expect(price(100, coupon: "TEN")).to eq(90)
  end
end

nodes.title: SonarQube
nodes.short: A commercial code-quality platform from Sonar of Geneva. Independent research found that most of its Java rules are weak predictors of real faults.
nodes.long: SonarQube applies large rule sets to source code, with 202 rules for Java alone, and reports findings with ratings and a quality gate that new code must pass. The product was first released around 2007. Sonar, the company behind it, was founded in 2008 in Geneva by Olivier Gaudin, Freddy Mallet and Simon Brandhof, raised $412 million in 2022 at a $4.7 billion valuation, and reports more than 28,000 enterprise customers, including 75 percent of the Fortune 100. A study of 21 open-source projects by Lenarduzzi and colleagues found that only 25 of those 202 Java rules had relatively low fault-proneness and that violations SonarQube labels bugs were generally not fault-prone, which suggests a gate built on those rules measures something other than defects.

refs.label: Lenarduzzi et al., Are SonarQube Rules Inducing Bugs?

nodes.title: gofmt
nodes.short: Go's standard formatter. One layout for every Go program, so style arguments never start; about 70 percent of public Go packages followed it by 2013.
nodes.long: gofmt rewrites Go source into a single canonical layout and offers almost no style options. A January 2013 post on the Go blog by Andrew Gerrand promised that you would "never have a debate about spacing or brace position ever again", and claimed that formatted code is easier to write, read and maintain and that the result is uncontroversial. A survey cited there found about 70 percent of Go packages in the wild already followed gofmt. Rob Pike summed up the trade in 2015 with the Go Proverb "Gofmt's style is no one's favorite, yet gofmt is everyone's favorite." Google uses gofmt for Go, alongside clang-format for C++ and other formatters elsewhere. Prettier and Black later offered the same bargain to other languages.

refs.label: Go blog: go fmt your code

nodes.title: Baselining Legacy Code
nodes.short: Adopting a strict rule on old code by recording today's violations and failing only on new ones, instead of demanding they all be fixed first.
nodes.long: Turning on a new check in a large old codebase can produce thousands of warnings, and old code that has not changed in years is risky to touch. Coverity's authors reported in 2010 that many customers independently invented the answer: record the current bugs, leave them alone, and fix only new ones. ESLint now supports this with bulk suppressions that can only shrink, since it warns when a suppression no longer occurs. Ruff can add a marker comment to each existing violation so a rule can be enforced from today. Google took a different route: it fixed every existing instance with automated large-scale changes, then turned the check into a compiler error, and shows findings in review only on changed lines. SonarQube's "Clean as You Code" applies the same idea by judging only new code.

code.text:
def legacy(): raise RuntimeError
# before: ruff check reports E722 here
try:
    legacy()
except:
    pass
# after: ruff check --add-noqa records the old violation, and only new ones fail
try:
    legacy()
except:  # noqa: E722
    pass

nodes.title: Feature Flags and Canary Releases
nodes.short: Switches that turn code on or off without redeploying, and staged releases that show a change to a few users first. They make small, frequent releases safe.
nodes.long: A feature flag, or toggle, lets a team change system behavior without changing code. Pete Hodgson's 2017 survey on Martin Fowler's site names four kinds: release toggles, short-lived and used to ship unfinished code switched off; experiment toggles for A/B tests; ops toggles that act as kill switches; and permission toggles that can last for years. He warns that toggles are inventory with a carrying cost. Two staged-release patterns go with them. Blue-green deployment, described on Fowler's site in March 2010, keeps two identical production environments and switches traffic to the new one. A canary release, written up there in 2014, exposes a change to a small subset of users before everyone. Google guards all changes with flags and rolls out in stages.

nodes.title: Domain Linters (IaC, Docker, CI)
nodes.short: Linters for one file format each: shell scripts, Dockerfiles, CSS, YAML, Terraform, SQL and CI workflow files, where a small mistake can cause an outage.
nodes.long: Generic linters read programming languages. A growing family reads the configuration and glue around them. ShellCheck, written in Haskell with a repository dating from 2012, catches shell mistakes such as unquoted variables; hadolint checks Dockerfiles, stylelint checks CSS, yamllint and markdownlint check their formats, tflint checks Terraform, SQLFluff checks and formats SQL, and actionlint checks GitHub Actions workflow files. Checkov, from Bridgecrew, scans infrastructure-as-code for cloud misconfigurations during the build. These tools are mostly rule-based and precise, and they matter because configuration errors cause outages. CI configuration became code in its own right: CircleCI's config file was reported as the fastest-growing YAML file on GitHub in 2018.

code.text:
# before: ShellCheck SC2086 (unquoted variable); with BUILD_DIR empty this becomes rm -rf /*
echo rm -rf $BUILD_DIR/*
# after: quoted, and it aborts if BUILD_DIR is unset or empty
echo rm -rf "${BUILD_DIR:?}"/*

refs.label: Sadowski et al., Lessons from Building Static Analysis Tools at Google (CACM 2018)

nodes.title: Hypothesis
nodes.short: Python's property-based testing library, by David MacIver. It generates inputs, finds a failing case and shrinks it.
nodes.long: Hypothesis is a Python library for property-based testing. A test states a property and a strategy for generating inputs, such as lists of integers; Hypothesis tries many of them and shrinks any failing input to a smaller one. The first commit is dated March 2013 and the author is David R. MacIver. It is released under the Mozilla Public License 2.0, has about 9,000 GitHub stars, and ranked 407th in PyPI downloads in September 2026 with about 52 million. It follows the idea that QuickCheck introduced for Haskell in 2000.

nodes.title: Jepsen
nodes.short: Kyle Kingsbury's tests of distributed databases under network failures. His 2013 test showed MongoDB losing 42 percent of acknowledged writes in a partition.
nodes.long: Jepsen is the project of Kyle Kingsbury, who goes by aphyr, for testing whether distributed databases keep their promises when machines and networks fail. In May 2013 his test of MongoDB 2.4 with a five-node replica set during a network partition sent 6,000 writes; 5,700 were acknowledged to the client but only 3,319 survived, because the old primary's writes were rolled back after a new primary was elected. MongoDB's own documentation admitted a primary may revert operations. A 2020 Jepsen report on MongoDB 4.2.6 found that even at the strongest read and write concern levels it failed to preserve snapshot isolation. The lesson the reports support is that defaults decide durability for most users, and claims of strong guarantees need independent testing.

nodes.title: Flaky Tests
nodes.short: Tests that sometimes pass and sometimes fail on the same code. Google measured about 1.5 percent of test runs flaky in 2016, and large browser tests the worst.
nodes.long: Google defines a flaky test as one that shows both a passing and a failing result with the same code. In 2016 it reported about 1.5 percent of all test runs flaky, almost 16 percent of tests with some flakiness, and about 84 percent of pass-to-fail transitions involving a flaky test. A 2017 analysis found 0.5 percent of small tests flaky, 1.6 percent of medium tests and 14 percent of large ones, so size predicted flakiness better than the tool did; Java and Python WebDriver tests were 10 to 19 percent flaky. A 2014 study of 201 fixes in 51 open-source projects found the top causes were not waiting properly for asynchronous work (45 percent), concurrency (20 percent) and tests that depend on running order (12 percent). Flaky tests teach people to ignore failures, which is how real bugs slip through.
nodes.sleeper: With thousands of automated tests running on every change, tests that fail at random became a daily cost. Google reported in 2016 that about 84 percent of its pass-to-fail transitions involved a flaky test.

code.text:
import threading, time

def run_job(out):
    time.sleep(0.05)
    out.append("done")

out = []; t = threading.Thread(target=run_job, args=(out,)); t.start()
time.sleep(0.05)               # flaky: guesses how long the job takes
print(out)                     # usually ['done'], sometimes []
t.join()                       # fix: wait for the job itself, then check
print(out)                     # always ['done']

refs.label: Micco: Flaky Tests at Google and How We Mitigate Them
Luo et al., An Empirical Analysis of Flaky Tests (FSE 2014)

nodes.title: Flow, Sorbet and Hack
nodes.short: Type checkers that big companies built for dynamic languages: Facebook's Flow for JavaScript, Facebook's Hack for PHP and Stripe's Sorbet for Ruby.
nodes.long: Companies with huge codebases in dynamic languages built type checkers for them rather than rewrite. Facebook's Flow, whose repository dates from October 2014, checks JavaScript. Hack, which Facebook opened in March 2014 for its HHVM runtime, is typed PHP; it checks files incrementally as you edit and typically finishes in under 200 milliseconds. Stripe's Sorbet does the same job for Ruby, and its repository dates from 2018. Flow was one of the two checkers in the study that found each of Flow and TypeScript catching 15 percent of real JavaScript bugs. Microsoft's TypeScript took a different route, a new language that compiles to JavaScript, while Flow remains active with a smaller footprint.

refs.label: To Type or Not to Type (Gao, Bird and Barr)

nodes.title: Warning Fatigue and False Positives
nodes.short: A static-analysis warning is worth reading only if it is usually right. Johnson saw this in 1978, and Coverity, Google and Facebook later measured it.
nodes.long: Johnson's 1978 lint manual said that "might be a bug" messages are acceptable only in proportion to the share of real bugs they find. Coverity's engineers put the line at about 30 percent false positives: past that, people ignore the tool, real bugs get lost, and low trust becomes a vicious cycle. Google defines an "effective false positive" as any report a developer chooses not to act on, and holds compiler-time checks to none and code-review checks to under 10 percent. Where the warning appears matters too. Google found 74 percent of problems flagged at compile time were judged real, against 21 percent of those found in checked-in code, and Facebook's fix rate rose from near zero to over 70 percent when the same analysis moved into code review. Rice's theorem explains why no analyzer can avoid both false alarms and missed bugs.

refs.label: Sadowski et al., Lessons from Building Static Analysis Tools at Google (CACM 2018)

nodes.title: Facebook Infer
nodes.short: Facebook's open-source bug finder. Switching it from a batch report to comments during code review lifted its fix rate from near zero to over 70 percent.
nodes.long: Infer is a static analyzer written in OCaml whose public repository dates from 2015. It checks Java, C, C++, Objective-C and Erlang code for null dereferences, data races and many other problems, and it runs in continuous integration on every change across Facebook, Messenger, Instagram and WhatsApp. Its most-quoted lesson is about timing, not technique. Run as a nightly batch job, it produced lists of issues that engineers almost never fixed. Run at "diff time", as a bot commenting during code review, the same analysis with the same false-positive rate had a fix rate of over 70 percent. By 2019 developers had fixed over 100,000 reported issues before the code reached production. A sibling tool, Zoncolan, looks for security bugs in Facebook's Hack code.

refs.label: Distefano et al., Scaling Static Analyses at Facebook (CACM 2019)

nodes.title: Prettier
nodes.short: An opinionated code formatter popular in the JavaScript world. Its stated goal is to stop style debates, and it only reprints code without changing behavior.
nodes.long: Prettier reprints source code in its own consistent style, and its documentation names the main reason to adopt it: to stop all the ongoing debates over style. It calls itself the only "style guide" that is fully automatic. Its first requirement is to output valid code with exactly the same behavior as before formatting, because it only prints code and does not transform it. The GitHub repository dates from November 2016 and has more than 52,000 stars. Because it covers layout only, it is a formatter and not a linter; Biome's makers claim their Rust formatter is about 35 times faster with 97 percent compatibility with Prettier's output.

nodes.title: The Testing Trophy
nodes.short: Kent C. Dodds's alternative to the pyramid: a base of static analysis, a few unit tests, mostly integration tests and a few end-to-end tests.
nodes.long: The testing trophy descends from a December 2016 tweet by Guillermo Rauch: "Write tests. Not too many. Mostly integration." Kent C. Dodds turned it into a picture with static analysis at the base, then unit tests, a wide band of integration tests, and a few end-to-end tests at the top. His central principle is that the more your tests resemble the way your software is used, the more confidence they can give you. He counts linters and type checkers as the static layer of testing. The idea also echoes David Heinemeier Hansson's 2014 call to shift emphasis from isolated unit tests toward tests that exercise more of the system.

refs.label: Dodds: The Testing Trophy and Testing Classifications

nodes.title: Dependency and Secrets Scanners
nodes.short: Tools that compare your libraries against lists of known vulnerabilities and licenses, and search code and git history for leaked passwords and keys.
nodes.long: Modern programs are mostly other people's code, so a class of checker reads each project's manifest and lockfile and compares every library version with databases of known vulnerabilities and licenses. Dependabot, from GitHub, raises alerts and opens pull requests that update vulnerable or outdated dependencies; Renovate, from Mend, does similar work across platforms; npm audit and pip-audit check one ecosystem each. Trivy, from Aqua Security, scans containers and repositories, and Gitleaks searches code and git history for secrets. These tools only know about published problems, and they can flag a vulnerable function your code never calls. In 2026 Dependabot began applying a three-day delay to non-security updates by default, a defense against freshly poisoned releases.
nodes.sleeper: You used to pick libraries yourself and rarely heard about their flaws. Now a bot compares every dependency with databases of known vulnerabilities and opens a pull request to update it.

code.text:
# .github/dependabot.yml
version: 2
updates:
  - package-ecosystem: "npm"
    directory: "/"
    schedule: { interval: "weekly" }

nodes.title: Black
nodes.short: Python's "uncompromising" code formatter. You give up control of layout and get deterministic output and smaller diffs in code review.
nodes.long: Black formats Python code one way and allows almost no configuration. Its documentation says that by using it you agree to cede control over the minutiae of hand-formatting, and in return get speed, determinism and freedom from style nagging. Because the output is predictable, it also produces the smallest possible diffs, which makes code review faster, and Black-formatted code looks the same in every project. The repository was created in March 2018 and has more than 40,000 stars. Ruff now ships a formatter that claims drop-in parity with Black.

nodes.title: Zero Trust and Secrets Management
nodes.short: Do not trust a request because it comes from inside the network, and keep passwords and keys out of source code. NIST formalized zero trust in August 2020.
nodes.long: Zero trust drops the old "castle and moat" model, in which anything inside the corporate network was trusted. Every request is authenticated and authorized wherever it comes from. NIST formalized the approach in Special Publication 800-207 in August 2020, after Google's BeyondCorp. Its companion habit is secrets management: passwords, API keys and certificates must not sit in source code or container images, but in a secrets manager such as HashiCorp Vault or a cloud secret store, rotated regularly, with repositories scanned for leaks by tools such as Gitleaks. Credentials are trending shorter-lived: PyPI's trusted publishing mints a token valid for only 15 minutes, and in December 2025 GitHub permanently revoked all existing npm classic tokens.
nodes.sleeper: The firewall used to be the wall around trusted systems. Zero trust assumes the network is already hostile and checks every request, wherever it comes from.

code.text:
import os
# before: a key typed into source stays in the git history (Gitleaks flags it)
API_KEY = "sk_live_EXAMPLE_ONLY"
# after: read it from the environment; a secrets manager supplies the real value
API_KEY = os.environ.get("API_KEY")
if API_KEY is None:
    raise SystemExit("API_KEY is not set")

nodes.title: Biome
nodes.short: A Rust formatter and linter for JavaScript and TypeScript, forked from Rome Tools. It aims to replace Prettier and much of ESLint with one fast tool.
nodes.long: Biome is a code formatter and linter for JavaScript and TypeScript written in Rust, forked in 2023 from the Rome Tools project. Its maintainers claim about 35 times Prettier's speed on one benchmark machine and 97 percent compatibility with Prettier's output, and it ships several hundred lint rules. Version 2, released in June 2025, added type-aware lint rules that do not depend on the TypeScript compiler; an early benchmark found its floating-promise rule catching about 75 percent of the cases that typescript-eslint caught, at much lower cost. Biome and Oxlint are the two main Rust challengers to ESLint. The speed figures come from the projects themselves, not from independent benchmarks.

nodes.title: Oxc and Oxlint
nodes.short: A Rust toolkit for JavaScript and its linter, Oxlint, which claims 50 to 100 times ESLint's speed. Oxlint reached version 1.0 in June 2025.
nodes.long: Oxc is a collection of JavaScript and TypeScript tools written in Rust by VoidZero, and Oxlint is its linter. Oxlint 1.0 appeared in June 2025 with a claim of 50 to 100 times ESLint's speed: 615 milliseconds against 33.5 seconds on the makers' own benchmark. Airbnb reported linting more than 126,000 files in about 7 seconds on CI, Mercedes-Benz reported a 71 percent drop in lint time, and Shopify, Bun and Preact also use it. By 2026 it had more than 865 rules, and its type-aware mode calls tsgo, the native TypeScript 7 compiler, instead of reimplementing type checking. VoidZero has announced it is joining Cloudflare. As with Biome, the speed figures are the vendor's.

nodes.title: Methods & Evidence
nodes.short: How teams organize the work, and what research really shows about what helps.
nodes.long: From waterfall to Agile to DevOps, each fashion promised more predictable delivery. Studies support some practices (small batches, code review, continuous delivery) and cast doubt on others.

nodes.title: The Software Crisis
nodes.short: The late-1960s complaint that big software projects ran late, over budget and unreliable. It gave the 1968 NATO conference its agenda.
nodes.long: By the mid-1960s computers had become far more powerful, yet large systems such as IBM's OS/360 were chronically late, over budget and unreliable. At the 1968 NATO conference in Garmisch, Germany, participants openly debated what some called a "software crisis", and the word was disputed: one attendee said crises affected only large systems, while another compared the situation to a heart attack that matters whatever the state of the other organs. Edsger Dijkstra's 1972 Turing lecture blamed the machines themselves: once computers became a thousand times more powerful, society's ambitions grew in proportion, and programming became an equally large problem. The phrase survives as shorthand, and in 1986 Fred Brooks argued that no single cure would arrive.

nodes.title: Waterfall
nodes.short: Requirements, design, code, test in a strict sequence. Winston Royce presented it as a flawed model.
nodes.long: Royce's 1970 paper showed the sequence and then argued it was risky without feedback. Later procurement rules nonetheless adopted it as a template. It works for well-understood problems and fails for uncertain ones.

nodes.title: No Silver Bullet
nodes.short: Fred Brooks's 1986 essay arguing that no single technique would deliver a tenfold gain within a decade, because software's essential difficulty is conceptual.
nodes.long: In 1986 Fred Brooks argued that no single development, in technology or management technique, promises even one order-of-magnitude improvement within a decade in productivity, reliability or simplicity. He separated the essence of software, a construct of interlocking concepts, from the accidents of how it is expressed, and named four inherent properties of the essence: complexity, conformity, changeability and invisibility. High-level languages had already removed the biggest accidental difficulty, and he predicted that Ada, object-oriented programming, AI and expert systems would not be silver bullets. The attacks he endorsed were buying instead of building, rapid prototyping, growing software incrementally and finding great designers. He added that skepticism is not pessimism: disciplined effort on many innovations could still add up to a tenfold gain.
nodes.sleeper: The essay predates the web, open source and the cloud. No single tool has delivered a tenfold gain in a decade, but forty years of accumulated change arguably has, which fits Brooks's own caveat. It is routinely invoked in debates about AI coding tools.

refs.label: Wikipedia: The Mythical Man-Month (the essay is reprinted in the 1995 edition)

nodes.title: Scrum
nodes.short: An Agile framework built on fixed-length sprints, a backlog and a daily check-in. The name comes from a 1986 article on product development.
nodes.long: The word "scrum" comes from Takeuchi and Nonaka's January 1986 Harvard Business Review paper "The New New Product Development Game", about developing products in general. In the early 1990s Ken Schwaber (Advanced Development Methods) and Jeff Sutherland (Easel Corporation) developed similar approaches for software, and they presented Scrum at the OOPSLA object-oriented programming conference in Austin in 1995. Teams work in fixed-length sprints with a product owner, a scrum master, a backlog, a daily scrum, a review and a retrospective. The Scrum Alliance (2002) and Scrum.org (2009) followed, and a public Scrum Guide has existed since 2009 or 2010; the current version is dated November 2020.
nodes.sleeper: If you remember phase-by-phase project plans, many teams now plan in sprints instead. Surveys rank Scrum the most widely used Agile framework, but they come from a tooling vendor's audience and are self-reported.

nodes.title: Open Source Software
nodes.short: Software whose source code is published for anyone to use, change and share. The term was coined in 1998; Linux, Git and Apache are its best-known successes.
nodes.long: Netscape announced on 23 January 1998 that its browser would be free with source code. A strategy meeting on 3 February in Palo Alto led Christine Peterson to suggest the term "open source", and the Open Source Initiative was founded later that month with Eric Raymond as president and Bruce Perens as vice-president. Its Open Source Definition derives from the Debian Free Software Guidelines, and its first list of approved licenses appeared in October 1999. The model won in infrastructure: Linux, Git and Apache. Fred Brooks's advice to buy rather than build is the case for reusing such components, and the downside is dependency risk, as Heartbleed showed in an under-resourced OpenSSL. Open source has succeeded commercially when a neutral body holds the code while companies compete on services.
nodes.sleeper: In 1990 the nearest idea was the Free Software Foundation's "free software". The term "open source" did not exist until 1998.

nodes.title: Extreme Programming
nodes.short: Kent Beck's 1999 method: pair programming, unit tests for everything, code review and simple design. Many practices went mainstream; the XP name did not.
nodes.long: Kent Beck became leader of Chrysler's C3 payroll project in March 1996 and refined its practices there: pair programming, extensive code review, unit tests for all code, simple design, building features only when needed, and an expectation that requirements will change. He published Extreme Programming Explained in October 1999. C3 paid about 9,000 people, covering the vast majority of monthly Chrysler salaries, but never managed another release, and DaimlerChrysler stopped the project in February 2000. A DaimlerChrysler manager told the 2000 XP conference that the company had effectively banned XP afterwards. XP's showcase project therefore ended badly, even as its ideas spread elsewhere.
nodes.sleeper: Practices that looked eccentric in 1999, such as unit tests for all code and merging to a shared build every day, are routine now. Continuous integration, refactoring and user stories went mainstream; the XP name faded.

nodes.title: Agile
nodes.short: Short iterations, working software and feedback. Born at a 2001 meeting in Snowbird, Utah.
nodes.long: The Agile Manifesto reacted against heavyweight process. Scrum and Extreme Programming are its best-known forms. Many organizations now do ritual Agile without the feedback loop that made it work.

nodes.title: The 10x Programmer Claim
nodes.short: The belief that the best programmers are ten times as productive as average ones. It traces to a tiny 1968 experiment that was not about productivity.
nodes.long: The usual origin is a 1968 paper by Sackman, Erikson and Grant in Communications of the ACM, a small experiment with about a dozen experienced programmers that was designed to compare online with offline debugging, not to measure productivity. Best-to-worst ratios as large as 28 to 1 appeared on some measures. Critics, including Lutz Prechelt's 1999 report on "the 28:1 Grant/Sackman legend" and Laurent Bossavit's book The Leprechauns of Software Engineering, point to the tiny sample, mixed languages and outliers, and note that best-versus-worst ratios overstate typical gaps; the details of those critiques could not be verified. Individual variation is real and large, but a precise "10x" is folklore.

refs.label: Bossavit, The Leprechauns of Software Engineering

nodes.title: Conway's Law
nodes.short: Any organization that designs a system will produce a design that copies its own communication structure. Melvin Conway wrote it in 1968.
nodes.long: Melvin Conway's April 1968 Datamation article "How Do Committees Invent?" held that any organization that designs a system will inevitably produce a design whose structure is a copy of the organization's communication structure. His example was two military services told by their Commander-in-Chief to develop a common weapon system; after great effort they produced a copy of their organization chart. He also argued that the communication structures of large design organizations tend to disintegrate under conventional management, and that the system then mirrors the disintegration. The law is used to reason about boundaries between teams and between microservices (small, independently deployed programs), and Team Topologies turns it into advice: shape the teams to get the architecture you want.

nodes.title: "Go To Statement Considered Harmful"
nodes.short: Dijkstra's 1968 letter arguing that unrestricted jumps make programs hard to follow. It opened the structured programming debate and launched a headline template.
nodes.long: Edsger Dijkstra submitted the piece as "A Case against the GO TO Statement"; it appeared in Communications of the ACM in March 1968 as a letter to the editor, under a title supplied by the editor, Niklaus Wirth. Dijkstra argued that human minds grasp static text far better than processes unfolding in time, and that unrestricted go to statements, which jump from one place in a program to any other, make it terribly hard to say where a running program is. Bohm and Jacopini had shown in 1966 that any program can be written with sequence, choice and loops. Donald Knuth's 1974 reply defended go to in some cases, and Dijkstra himself wrote that others were making a religion of it. The letter launched the "considered harmful" headline template, and nearly every language since builds its control flow from if, while and for.

refs.label: Dijkstra, A Case against the GO TO Statement (EWD215)
Knuth, Structured Programming with go to Statements (1974)

nodes.title: The Art of Computer Programming
nodes.short: Donald Knuth's multi-volume treatise on algorithms, begun in 1968 and still being extended. It made the analysis of algorithms a teachable subject.
nodes.long: Volume 1, Fundamental Algorithms, appeared in 1968. The series later added Volume 2 Seminumerical Algorithms, Volume 3 Sorting and Searching, Volume 4A Combinatorial Algorithms Part 1 (2011) and Volume 4B (2023). At the end of 1999 American Scientist named the set among the twelve best physical-science monographs of the century. It made the analysis of algorithms, meaning how much time and memory a procedure needs, a respectable and teachable subject, and it set a standard of rigor for describing procedures. Knuth applied the same rigor to the structured-programming debate in his 1974 paper on go to statements.
nodes.sleeper: The set was unfinished in 1990 and still is: Volume 4A appeared in 2011 and Volume 4B in 2023.

nodes.title: Lehman's Laws of Software Evolution
nodes.short: Meir Lehman and Les Belady's observations that real-world software must keep changing, and grows more complex unless effort is spent to reduce it.
nodes.long: From 1974 Meir Lehman and Les Belady formulated laws for real-world systems, called E-type systems, that operate in a changing environment. "Continuing change" says such a system must be continually adapted or become progressively less satisfactory; "increasing complexity" says its complexity grows unless work is done to reduce it. Laws added in 1996 include "declining quality", which says quality appears to decline unless rigorously maintained, and "feedback system". The laws were derived from OS/360 and later systems, and the quantitative support is reportedly mixed. They are qualitatively accepted, and they are the theory behind the metaphor of technical debt.

refs.label: Wikipedia: Lehman's laws of software evolution

nodes.title: Brooks's Law
nodes.short: Adding people to a software project that is already late makes it later. Fred Brooks drew the rule from managing IBM's OS/360.
nodes.long: Fred Brooks stated the rule in The Mythical Man-Month (1975), drawing on his experience managing IBM's OS/360: adding manpower to a software project that is behind schedule delays it further. The logic was already in Melvin Conway's 1968 paper, which called it a fallacy that two people working for a year and a hundred working for a week are resources of equal value. The evidence is one large project plus simulation studies, and no controlled experiment exists. As a rule of thumb it is widely accepted, though it depends on how far along the project is and how divisible the work is. The usual advice is to cut scope, re-plan early and keep teams small.

nodes.title: Goodhart's Law
nodes.short: When a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure. In software it corrupts lines of code, velocity, test coverage and even delivery metrics.
nodes.long: The wording "When a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure" is the anthropologist Marilyn Strathern's 1997 summary of an idea credited to the economist Charles Goodhart's 1975 article on UK monetary policy. In software it explains why lines of code, story-point velocity (units of estimated work finished per sprint) and test-coverage percentages go wrong once people are judged by them. DORA, the research group behind the best-known delivery metrics, warns about it in its own guidance: setting the metrics as goals makes teams more likely to game them, so they should drive improvement, not comparisons between teams. The Standish CHAOS figures show another form: in one organization, steering by their definition of success led managers to pad their estimates, by tenfold to a hundredfold.

nodes.title: The Mythical Man-Month
nodes.short: Fred Brooks's lessons from IBM's OS/360: adding people to a late project makes it later.
nodes.long: Brooks's essays introduced Brooks's law, the second-system effect and 'No Silver Bullet' (1986), which argued no single technique would deliver a tenfold gain. Fifty years later they still hold up.

nodes.title: The Unix Philosophy
nodes.short: Build small programs that each do one thing well and combine them, with plain text as the common interface. First written down at Bell Labs in 1978.
nodes.long: The Unix philosophy was first set down as maxims in the foreword to the July-August 1978 Bell System Technical Journal issue on Unix, by Doug McIlroy, E. N. Pinson and B. A. Tague. They said to make each program do one thing well; to expect the output of every program to become the input of another, as yet unknown, program; to design and build software to be tried early, ideally within weeks, and to throw away the clumsy parts; and to use tools in preference to unskilled help. A compact summary from 1994, usually attributed to McIlroy, says to write programs that do one thing well, write programs that work together, and write programs that handle text streams, because that is a universal interface.

code.text:
# the five most common words in a file, built from small tools joined by pipes
tr -cs 'A-Za-z' '\n' < book.txt | tr 'A-Z' 'a-z' | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head -5

refs.label: Bell System Technical Journal, UNIX Time-Sharing System: Foreword (1978)

nodes.title: Capability Maturity Model
nodes.short: A 1980s framework from Carnegie Mellon's Software Engineering Institute that rated organizations by how repeatable their processes were.
nodes.long: The Capability Maturity Model began in 1986 after a US Department of Defense-funded study of its software contractors. Watts Humphrey, who had spent 27 years at IBM, joined the Software Engineering Institute (SEI) at Carnegie Mellon University that year. The framework was published in 1988 and in his 1989 book Managing the Software Process, and it rated organizations on five maturity levels. Version 1.1 appeared in July 1993, and the integrated CMMI followed; ISACA took over CMMI in 2016 and released versions 2.0 (2021) and 3.0 (2023). The idea is that a predictable process produces predictable outcomes. The supporting evidence is reportedly before-and-after case studies from organizations that chose to take part, and no independent trial.
nodes.sleeper: In the early 1990s process maturity was a leading answer to late software. The model has reportedly lived on mainly in defense, government and outsourcing contracts, and is marginal in product companies.

nodes.title: GNU General Public License
nodes.short: Richard Stallman's license that lets anyone use and change a program but requires derivatives to stay free. This copyleft idea underlies GNU and Linux.
nodes.long: Richard Stallman announced the GNU project on 27 September 1983, began work in January 1984 after leaving MIT, and founded the Free Software Foundation in October 1985. The GNU General Public License introduced copyleft, which requires derivative works to stay free; version 1 appeared in 1989, version 2 in 1991 and version 3 in 2007. GNU produced the Emacs editor, the GCC compiler, the GDB debugger, the Bash shell and the glibc C library, and Linux supplied the missing kernel, the core of an operating system, after Linus Torvalds adopted version 2 of the GPL in 1992. Sun released Java under the GPL in 2006 and 2007 as OpenJDK. Permissive licenses such as MIT, BSD and Apache 2.0 allow closed derivatives, while copyleft licenses such as the GPL and AGPL require sharing.

nodes.title: Design Patterns
nodes.short: The "Gang of Four" book cataloguing 23 recurring object-oriented designs. Its vocabulary stuck, though many patterns are now built into languages.
nodes.long: Design Patterns: Elements of Reusable Object-Oriented Software, by Erich Gamma, Richard Helm, Ralph Johnson and John Vlissides (the "Gang of Four"), was published on 31 October 1994 with a 1995 copyright. It catalogued 23 recurring designs with names such as Observer, Factory and Singleton. Its advice to favor object composition over class inheritance has held up: in 2005 Gamma said he still thought it true after ten years. In 1996 Peter Norvig argued that 16 of the 23 patterns have qualitatively simpler implementations in Lisp or Dylan than in C++, which suggests patterns partly patch weaknesses in a language. The vocabulary survived, while many patterns are now language features such as closures and iterators.
nodes.sleeper: If you learned object-oriented design in the early 1990s, note that language features such as closures and iterators now cover several of the patterns, and composition is preferred over deep inheritance.

code.text:
# A swappable "strategy" object is just a function argument
# in a language with first-class functions.
words = ["pear", "fig", "banana"]
print(sorted(words, key=len))  # ['fig', 'pear', 'banana']

refs.label: Norvig, Design Patterns in Dynamic Languages

nodes.title: Standish CHAOS Report
nodes.short: A 1994 survey claiming only 16 percent of IT projects succeed. A 2010 analysis showed its definitions are misleading and its figures meaningless.
nodes.long: The Standish Group's first CHAOS report (1994) sorted IT projects into successful, challenged or failed. From 365 respondents representing 8,380 applications it reported 16 percent successful, 53 percent challenged and 31 percent failed. Standish defines success purely as meeting the original forecast of cost, time and functionality. In 2010 Eveleens and Verhoef of Vrije Universiteit Amsterdam applied those definitions to 5,457 forecasts for 1,211 real projects and found them misleading, one-sided because they ignore under-runs, harmful to estimating, and productive of meaningless figures. One organization that steered by the definitions padded its estimates tenfold to a hundredfold and so scored about 70 percent successes. The Standish numbers are not a measure of project health.
nodes.sleeper: Later editions put success between 26 and 35 percent from 1996 to 2009. The figures are still widely repeated, but they should be treated as discredited.

refs.label: Eveleens and Verhoef, The Rise and Fall of the Chaos Report Figures

nodes.title: The Cathedral and the Bazaar
nodes.short: Eric Raymond's 1997 essay contrasting closed, planned "cathedral" development with open, many-contributor "bazaar" development, and the slogan "many eyes".
nodes.long: Eric S. Raymond presented the essay in May 1997, and O'Reilly published it as a book in 1999. It contrasted closed, planned "cathedral" development with the open "bazaar" development of Linux, and coined "Linus's law": given enough eyeballs, all bugs are shallow. Netscape's January 1998 decision to release its browser source was reportedly influenced by the essay, and Raymond became president of the new Open Source Initiative that year. The slogan has a counter-example in Heartbleed, a flaw that sat in the widely deployed OpenSSL encryption library from December 2011 until April 2014. Many eyes help only when someone is funded and motivated to look.
nodes.sleeper: If you remember open development as a hobbyist fringe, it has since won in infrastructure: Linux, Git and Apache are all developed in the open.

nodes.title: Refactoring
nodes.short: Changing code's structure in small steps without changing what it does. Martin Fowler published a book on it in 1999, and programming tools now automate much of it.
nodes.long: Refactoring means improving the internal structure of code in small, behavior-preserving steps. Martin Fowler, later chief scientist at Thoughtworks, published his book Refactoring in 1999, the year Extreme Programming Explained appeared; refactoring is one of XP's practices and the last step of the test-driven development cycle. It is also the usual alternative to rewriting from scratch, which Joel Spolsky called the single worst strategic mistake a software company can make. A code-analytics vendor, GitClear, reported that moved code, its proxy for refactoring, fell from about 25 percent of changed lines in 2021 to under 10 percent in 2024; this correlates with the rise of AI tools but does not prove they caused it.
nodes.sleeper: Integrated development environments (IDEs), the editors programmers work in, now automate many refactorings, so small, frequent restructuring is practical. IntelliJ IDEA, released in 2001, was one of the first Java IDEs with advanced refactoring built in.

nodes.title: Site Reliability Engineering
nodes.short: Google's way of running services: software engineers do operations, guided by reliability targets and error budgets. The practice began in 2003.
nodes.long: Site reliability engineering began at Google in 2003, when Benjamin Treynor Sloss founded a team of seven production engineers; by 2016 there were more than 1,000 SREs. He described it as what happens when you ask a software engineer to design an operations team. Its signature ideas are service-level objectives, error budgets, reducing toil (repetitive manual operations work) and blameless postmortems. Google caps routine operations work at 50 percent of an SRE's time, and the SRE book says 100 percent is the wrong reliability target for basically everything; the error budget is one minus the availability target. It also says roughly 70 percent of outages are due to changes in a live system, so changes are tried on a few users first (canary releases) and rolled out gradually.
nodes.sleeper: Operations used to be a separate group from the developers. SRE staffs it with software engineers, limits routine ops work to half their time, and treats a small amount of failure as a budget to spend.

nodes.title: Kanban Method
nodes.short: A method borrowed from Toyota: show the work on a board and limit how much is in progress at once. David J. Anderson adapted it for software around 2004.
nodes.long: Kanban comes from the Toyota Production System of the 1940s and 1950s. Its two primary practices in software are to visualize the work, usually on a board, and to limit work in progress (WIP), so that new items start only when others finish. David J. Anderson adapted it for software at Microsoft around 2004 and wrote a book on it in 2010. The method is widely used, and teams often combine it with Scrum.

nodes.title: "The Free Lunch Is Over"
nodes.short: Herb Sutter's 2005 essay: processor clock speeds had stopped rising, so programs must become concurrent to keep getting faster.
nodes.long: Herb Sutter's essay appeared in Dr. Dobb's Journal in March 2005, with the text first posted in December 2004. Its thesis was that the biggest sea change in software since object-oriented programming was concurrency, meaning programs that do several things at the same time. The "free lunch" had been faster software without changing it. Sutter noted that Intel chips reached 2 GHz (two billion clock ticks per second) in August 2001, and that trends before 2003 would have put 10 GHz Pentium-family chips on the market by early 2005; they had not appeared. Heat, power consumption and current leakage were the obstacles. Transistor counts kept growing, so manufacturers turned to multicore chips, with several processors on one chip, and to hyperthreading. Two 3 GHz cores are not 6 GHz, and most multi-threaded applications will not run twice as fast on a dual-core machine.
nodes.sleeper: If you remember clock speeds climbing with every new chip, that ended around 2003. Sutter's argument was that faster programs would depend on using extra cores, and threads, async code and message passing have since become everyday tools.

nodes.title: DevOps
nodes.short: Developers and operators sharing responsibility, automating releases and monitoring.
nodes.long: The movement combined version control, CI/CD, infrastructure as code and monitoring. DORA research links its practices to faster, more reliable delivery.

nodes.title: Evidence on Static Typing
nodes.short: A 2017 study found that Flow or TypeScript would have caught about 15 percent of real JavaScript bugs: a modest effect, and among the cleanest evidence on typing.
nodes.long: Static typing means a tool checks, before a program runs, that values are used consistently, such as numbers not treated as text. Gao, Bird and Barr (ICSE 2017) took 400 real, already public JavaScript bugs that had survived testing and review, added type annotations to the buggy code, and checked whether Facebook's Flow 0.30 or Microsoft's TypeScript 2.0 would have flagged each one. Flow detected 59 and TypeScript 58, and the true share lies between 11.5 and 18.5 percent, with a mean of 15 percent. The authors say this probably understates the value of static typing, since it ignores bugs caught privately and benefits such as documentation and tooling. It also measures what the checkers could detect, not what typing costs, and the authors argue for typing. No large, replicated defect reduction from static typing has been shown, although industry adopts types anyway for tooling reasons.
nodes.sleeper: The debate used to rest on taste. Since then dynamic languages have grown optional types, and by August 2025 TypeScript was the most-used language on GitHub by contributor count.

refs.label: Gao, Bird and Barr, To Type or Not to Type (ICSE 2017)

nodes.title: Open-Source Relicensing
nodes.short: From 2018 several open-source vendors moved to licenses that restrict cloud resellers, and the cloud providers and foundations answered with forks.
nodes.long: A pattern played out from 2018: a company whose open-source product was being sold as a service by cloud providers changed its license to stop that, and the cloud vendors or a foundation forked the last open version, meaning they copied it to continue independently. MongoDB moved from the AGPL, a copyleft license, to the Server Side Public License in October 2018, which the Open Source Initiative does not consider open source. Elastic moved Elasticsearch to SSPL and the Elastic License in January 2021, AWS forked it as OpenSearch in April 2021, and Elastic offered the AGPL again in August 2024. HashiCorp moved from the Mozilla Public License to the Business Source License on 10 August 2023, prompting the OpenTofu fork. Redis relicensed in March 2024, prompting the Valkey fork, and added the AGPLv3 as an option in May 2025.
nodes.sleeper: The old worry was closed-source rivals. For these vendors the risk became large cloud providers reselling their code as a service, and forks now appear within weeks.

refs.label: HashiCorp blog on the Business Source License
Elastic blog: Elasticsearch is open source again

nodes.title: What Goes Around Comes Around
nodes.short: Stonebraker and Pavlo's 2024 survey of database history, concluding that SQL and the relational model outlasted every challenger.
nodes.long: Stonebraker and Pavlo's paper "What Goes Around Comes Around... And Around..." appeared in SIGMOD Record in June 2024. It follows a 2005 chapter by Stonebraker and Hellerstein that examined nine data-model movements and concluded the relational model with an extendable type system had dominated all comers. The 2024 survey says SQL kept absorbing the best ideas of its rivals, including JSON in 2016 and property graphs in 2023, so most systems that deviated from SQL or the relational model have not dominated. It calls document databases essentially the same as 1980s object-oriented and late-1990s XML databases, and it lists database machines, custom hardware accelerators and blockchain databases among failed bets. The authors have a stake in the relational story, so their judgments are opinion.
nodes.sleeper: Object databases, XML databases and early NoSQL were each expected to replace SQL. The survey's view is that each faded or was absorbed into SQL systems.

refs.label: Stonebraker and Pavlo, What Goes Around Comes Around... And Around... (2024)

nodes.title: Iterative and Incremental Development
nodes.short: Building a system in repeated passes rather than one. It predates waterfall: teams worked this way in the 1950s, and Royce's 1970 paper advised doing it twice.
nodes.long: Larman and Basili's 2003 history traces iterative and incremental development to Walter Shewhart's 1930s plan-do-study-act cycles, the 1950s X-15 program and NASA's Project Mercury, which ran time-boxed iterations. One veteran recalled incremental development as early as 1957 at IBM's Service Bureau Corporation. IBM built the Trident submarine command system (1972, over a million lines) in four time-boxed iterations of about six months each. Winston Royce's 1970 paper, later labeled "waterfall" although it never uses the word, called the single-pass sequence risky and said to build the system twice. The label may first appear in 1976. So strict one-pass development was never the only practice, and Agile's iterative core is not new.
nodes.sleeper: If you were taught that software gets built once, in order, from requirements to testing, the record says otherwise. Iterative delivery is now the default, and it predates the waterfall label by decades.

refs.label: Larman and Basili, history of iterative development (IEEE Computer, 2003)
Royce, Managing the Development of Large Software Systems (1970), archived copy

nodes.title: NATO Software Engineering Conference
nodes.short: A 1968 meeting at Garmisch, Germany, that deliberately adopted the name "software engineering" to say software needed the discipline of older engineering fields.
nodes.long: The NATO Science Committee sponsored a working conference at Garmisch, Germany, from 7 to 11 October 1968. Its report, edited by Peter Naur and Brian Randell, says the phrase "software engineering" was deliberately chosen as provocative, implying that software manufacture should rest on the theoretical foundations and practical disciplines of the established branches of engineering. More than fifty people from eleven countries attended. Randell believed the idea of the title came from Professor Fritz Bauer, although other claimants for the term exist. Doug McIlroy used the meeting to call for a components industry selling catalogues of routines, and a follow-up conference in Rome in 1969 was judged far less harmonious and successful.

nodes.title: Premature Optimization
nodes.short: Knuth's 1974 line that premature optimization is the root of all evil, usually quoted without the sentences around it.
nodes.long: In his 1974 paper "Structured Programming with go to Statements", Donald Knuth wrote: "We should forget about small efficiencies, say about 97% of the time: premature optimization is the root of all evil. Yet we should not pass up our opportunities in that critical 3%." The sentences around it say that the grail of efficiency leads to abuse, and that a good programmer will look carefully at the critical code, but only after that code has been identified. The advice is to measure first. The line is often quoted without its second sentence, and it is used to excuse neglect of performance in the design itself.

refs.label: Knuth, Structured Programming with go to Statements (1974)

nodes.title: Postel's Law
nodes.short: "Be conservative in what you do, be liberal in what you accept from others." Jon Postel's rule for Internet protocols, written in 1979, is now disputed.
nodes.long: Jon Postel's robustness principle reads: "Be conservative in what you do, be liberal in what you accept from others." It was first written down in the 1979 specification of the Internet Protocol (IPv4), though one source dates it to RFC 761 of 1980. In 2023 the Internet Engineering Task Force (IETF) published RFC 9413, "Maintaining Robust Protocols", which says the principle has been interpreted in a variety of ways: some help ensure the health of the Internet, while others can harm interoperability over time. Thomson and Schinazi argued that being liberal in what you accept actually reduces robustness, including security, and the RFC recommends active protocol maintenance instead. Hyrum's law helps explain the problem: once receivers tolerate sloppy input, senders come to depend on that tolerance, and the protocol hardens around it.
nodes.sleeper: If you learned the robustness principle as good practice, note that the IETF's 2023 RFC 9413 now recommends active protocol maintenance instead, and warns that liberal acceptance can damage interoperability over time.

nodes.title: Spiral Model
nodes.short: Barry Boehm's risk-driven process: each loop tackles the riskiest unknowns first, using a prototype, an increment or a waterfall step as needed.
nodes.long: Barry Boehm of TRW described the spiral model in a 1986 paper, and a 1988 IEEE Computer version reached a wider audience. Each turn of the spiral identifies the riskiest unknowns and picks whichever approach attacks them best: a prototype, an increment or an ordinary waterfall step. Boehm later called it a "process model generator" and defined six invariants and anchor-point milestones. The widely copied spiral diagram is described as conveying several misconceptions through oversimplification. The evidence for the model is case studies only. It influenced risk-first planning and the Rational Unified Process, but few teams adopt it by name.

nodes.title: Peopleware
nodes.short: Tom DeMarco and Timothy Lister's 1987 book arguing that software's major problems are human rather than technical: teams, quiet and uninterrupted time.
nodes.long: Tom DeMarco and Timothy Lister published Peopleware in 1987, with revised editions in 1999 and 2013. Its central claim is that the major problems of software work are not so much technological as sociological. It discusses how teams jell, the value of uninterrupted "flow time", quiet workplaces and the cost of staff turnover, and it argues for sustainable work rather than crunch. Their "Coding War Games" study of hundreds of developers reportedly found performance tracking workspace quiet and privacy, though the figures could not be verified. The diagnosis has aged well, yet open-plan offices spread anyway, and a 2024 randomized trial of hybrid work is a modern test of its themes.

nodes.title: Worse Is Better
nodes.short: Richard Gabriel's slogan that simpler designs often beat more elaborate ones in the marketplace, a pattern seen in Unix, TCP/IP and HTTP.
nodes.long: Richard Gabriel's "worse is better" is a slogan for the observation that simple designs tend to win over more elaborate ones. Accounts of platform and internet history draw on it to explain several outcomes: simple, inspectable, text-based formats beat elaborate ones; open specifications with free implementations beat licensed ones; backward compatibility beat clean-slate redesign, as HTML5 did over XHTML 2 and AMD64 over Itanium; and commodity hardware beat bespoke hardware. Unix, TCP/IP, HTTP and Linux are the usual examples. These are generalizations from history rather than measured laws.

nodes.title: V-Model
nodes.short: A waterfall variant pairing each design stage with a test stage, drawn as a V. Reportedly still common in automotive, aerospace and medical devices.
nodes.long: The V-model arranges development as a V: design levels descend the left side and the matching test levels, unit, integration, system and acceptance, ascend the right, so each design level has a test that checks it. It is credited to the Forsberg and Mooz systems-engineering "Vee" (1991) and the German federal V-Modell (1992), although those origins have not been verified. As a waterfall variant it assumes requirements are known up front. It is reportedly still common in automotive, aerospace and medical-device work.

nodes.title: Technical Debt
nodes.short: A metaphor for shortcuts in code: they save time now but cost extra work later, like interest. Ward Cunningham is credited with the term in 1992.
nodes.long: Ward Cunningham, who also created the wiki (a web site anyone can edit) in 1995, is credited with the "technical debt" metaphor in 1992. The comparison is to a loan: a shortcut in design or code gets something working sooner, but the extra effort of working around it later is the interest, and cleaning up is paying down the principal. The theory behind it is Lehman's laws of software evolution, which say a system must keep changing and grows more complex unless work reduces it. The term has stretched to cover neglected maintenance, tangled design and even low-value tests: Google warns that chasing a coverage number can create technical debt from tests that check little.

refs.label: Google Testing Blog: Code Coverage Best Practices

nodes.title: UML and Model-Driven Architecture
nodes.short: A standard set of diagram notations for software design, adopted in 1997, and the later push to generate code from such models. It survives mainly as sketching.
nodes.long: The Unified Modeling Language merged the diagram notations of Booch and Rumbaugh after Rational bought Jacobson's Objectory method. The Object Management Group adopted it as a standard in 1997, ISO published it in 2005, and UML 2 defines 14 diagram types. Model-Driven Architecture, the OMG's 2001 approach, aimed to generate code from abstract models. Like the computer-aided software engineering (CASE) tools of the late 1980s before it, this promise of code from diagrams did not take hold: generated code was hard to maintain and diagrams drifted from reality. UML survives mainly as a whiteboard sketching notation, and executable-model code generation is niche.
nodes.sleeper: In the late 1990s UML was expected to be the blueprint from which programs were generated. It survives as a sketching notation, and refactoring-capable IDEs took the place of round-trip code generation.

nodes.title: Rational Unified Process
nodes.short: Rational Software's 1998 iterative framework built around use cases and UML. Critics found it ceremony-heavy; Agile kept the iteration.
nodes.long: The Rational Unified Process was Rational Software's iterative framework, organized in four phases: Inception, Elaboration, Construction and Transition. It was built around use cases and UML, and was sold as the IBM Rational Method Composer. Critics saw it as heavy on ceremony, and Agile took its iterative core while dropping the paperwork. Boehm's spiral model is counted among its influences, through risk-first planning. Frameworks such as RUP, CMMI and SAFe tend to be adopted through procurement and consulting channels first and shown to work second. RUP is now regarded as legacy.

nodes.title: Pair Programming
nodes.short: Two developers share one workstation and work on the same code. An Extreme Programming practice whose evidence is mixed.
nodes.long: In pair programming two developers work together at one workstation. It was one of the practices of Extreme Programming, and the original enthusiastic papers (Cockburn and Williams, 2000; Williams, Kessler, Cunningham and Jeffries, 2000) were written by XP proponents. A later meta-analysis found that pairs consider more design alternatives, arrive at simpler and more maintainable designs and catch design defects earlier, but it flagged signs of publication bias and concluded that pair programming is not uniformly beneficial or effective. Total human hours rise even when tasks finish faster. It is best treated as a situational tool, not a universal win.

nodes.title: Clean Code
nodes.short: Robert C. Martin's 2008 book of rules for readable code, such as very short functions. Critics say its rules are taste backed by experience, not evidence.
nodes.long: Robert C. Martin, known as Uncle Bob, is an Agile Manifesto signatory and the originator of the SOLID design principles; his book Clean Code appeared in 2008. In a published written discussion, John Ousterhout, author of A Philosophy of Software Design, argued that very small methods create "shallow" interfaces, with a lot of interface for little functionality. Martin replied that he strongly recommends very short functions but that the book sets no arbitrary limits, citing 2-to-4-line functions from a 1999 exercise with Kent Beck. On a worked example they concluded that they disagree on how far to decompose code, and they also disagreed on test-driven development. No controlled study of these style rules exists. The book is still widely read and contested.

refs.label: Ousterhout and Martin: A Philosophy of Software Design vs Clean Code

nodes.title: Trunk-Based Development
nodes.short: Developers merge small changes into one shared main line at least daily instead of keeping long-lived branches. DORA's surveys link it to better delivery.
nodes.long: In trunk-based development developers collaborate on a single branch called the trunk and resist pressure to create other long-lived branches. Short-lived branches are allowed for review and continuous integration (automatic builds and tests on each merge), and feature flags, switches that keep unfinished code turned off, separate deploying code from releasing it. DORA, the DevOps research program run by Google Cloud, defines it as each developer merging small batches into trunk at least once a day, with branches lasting no more than a few hours. Its analysis of 2016 and 2017 survey data linked three or fewer active branches, daily merges and no code freezes to better delivery performance, which is correlation, not an experiment. Vincent Driessen's Git Flow post of 5 January 2010, built on long-lived branches, is the usual contrast; in 2020 he suggested simpler workflows for continuous delivery.
nodes.sleeper: If you remember CVS and Subversion branches merged after weeks, the advice for fast-moving teams is now the reverse: merge to the main line at least daily, with unfinished work hidden behind feature flags.

nodes.title: Scaled Agile Framework (SAFe)
nodes.short: Dean Leffingwell's packaged framework for Agile in large organizations, with defined roles, ceremonies and planning cycles. Widely sold and criticized.
nodes.long: The Scaled Agile Framework, by Dean Leffingwell, packages Agile for large enterprises with defined roles, ceremonies (recurring meetings) and planning cycles. Wikipedia dates its first formal description to a 2007 book, with version 1.0 following in 2011, and its article has a criticism section. Agile Manifesto signatory Dave Thomas wrote on 4 March 2014 that "agile" had been subverted to the point of being effectively meaningless, with the agile community largely an arena for consultants and vendors, and he called for retiring the word as a noun. The phrase "Agile industrial complex" is usually credited to Martin Fowler around 2018, though that attribution is unverified. No reliable adoption figures were found.

refs.label: Dave Thomas, essay on retiring the word agile (4 March 2014)

nodes.title: Blameless Postmortems
nodes.short: After an outage, write up what happened and why without hunting for someone to blame, so the team can learn. Standard in SRE and DevOps cultures.
nodes.long: Google's SRE book defines a postmortem as a written record of an incident, its impact, the actions taken to mitigate or resolve it, the root causes and the follow-up actions to prevent a recurrence. The blameless version, set out by John Allspaw in an Etsy essay around 2012, views mistakes, errors, slips and lapses from a perspective of learning rather than fault. The idea is said to borrow from "just culture" thinking in aviation and healthcare. Published analyses such as CrowdStrike's root-cause report, the Ariane 5 inquiry and NASA's Mars Climate Orbiter board report follow the style. The Post Office Horizon scandal shows the opposite: an institution that would not believe its own system could be wrong.

refs.label: Allspaw, Blameless PostMortems and a Just Culture (archived copy)

nodes.title: Language and Defects Studies
nodes.short: A 2014 GitHub study linked some programming languages to more bugs than others. A 2019 reproduction found that almost all of the effect disappears.
nodes.long: Ray, Posnett, Filkov and Devanbu (FSE 2014) analyzed 729 GitHub projects covering 80 million lines, 29,000 authors and 1.5 million commits in 17 languages. They reported that some languages are associated with more defects than others, although the effect is small, with functional languages associated with fewer. Berger, Hollenbeck, Maj, Vitek and Vitek reproduced the study in 2019 and found the repetition only partially successful. Their reanalysis found flaws that undermine the conclusions: only four languages had a statistically significant association with defects, and the effect size was exceedingly small. Ten developers relabeled 400 commits and estimated a 36 percent false-positive rate in the original's automated bug-fix labels. The claim that language choice measurably changes defect rates at repository scale is unsupported.

refs.label: Ray, Posnett, Filkov and Devanbu, FSE 2014
Berger et al., reproduction of the study (2019)

nodes.title: Hyrum's Law
nodes.short: With enough users of an API, every observable behavior of your system will be depended on by somebody, whatever the documentation promises.
nodes.long: Hyrum's Law reads: with a sufficient number of users of an API (the interface one program offers to others), it does not matter what you promise in the contract, because all observable behaviors of your system will be depended on by somebody. Hyrum Wright stated it from large-scale infrastructure migrations at Google, and Titus Winters named it after him; it is also called the Law of Implicit Interfaces. It explains why changing "undefined" behavior breaks other people's programs, and why Postel-style tolerance tends to freeze a protocol in place. It is widely cited in API and versioning design. No exact first-publication date was confirmed; it dates from the 2010s.

nodes.title: Over-Abstraction
nodes.short: Building a general abstraction too early costs more than copying code. Sandi Metz's maxim: duplication is far cheaper than the wrong abstraction.
nodes.long: Sandi Metz gave the line "duplication is far cheaper than the wrong abstraction" at the RailsConf conference in 2014 and wrote it up on her blog on 20 January 2016. The concern is premature generalization: pulling similar-looking code into one shared abstraction before the real shape of the problem is clear. John Ousterhout's objection to very small methods that create "shallow" interfaces, with a lot of interface for little functionality, is the same worry from another direction. Taking the "don't repeat yourself" rule to extremes is a common source. No controlled evidence exists either way, and the accepted heuristic is to wait for the third use before abstracting.

refs.label: Ousterhout and Martin: A Philosophy of Software Design vs Clean Code

nodes.title: Shape Up
nodes.short: Basecamp's free book describing six-week cycles, an "appetite" for each problem and a betting table that replaces the ever-growing backlog.
nodes.long: Shape Up is a free book from the software company Basecamp, credited to Ryan Singer and dated 2019. It describes work in six-week cycles. Before a project is designed, leaders set its "appetite": how much time the problem deserves. At a "betting table" they then choose which projects to take on, instead of maintaining an ever-growing backlog of requests. The method is admired but niche, and the only evidence for it is one company's experience.

nodes.title: Team Topologies
nodes.short: A 2019 book by Matthew Skelton and Manuel Pais on shaping team structure so that it produces the software architecture you want.
nodes.long: Matthew Skelton and Manuel Pais propose four team types: stream-aligned, enabling, complicated-subsystem and platform teams. Teams relate to one another in three ways: collaboration, X-as-a-Service and facilitating. The book applies Conway's Law deliberately, shaping team boundaries to get the architecture you want, which is sometimes called the inverse Conway maneuver. It also limits what any one team must hold in its head, a limit it calls cognitive load. The approach is popular in architecture and platform-engineering circles, and its support comes from experience reports rather than controlled studies.

nodes.title: COBOL Usage Claims
nodes.short: Popular figures such as "95 percent of ATM transactions run on COBOL" come from vendors and journalists. No audited count exists.
nodes.long: COBOL does run inside banks and governments, but no audited figure exists for its share. IBM's website says COBOL supports 80 percent of in-person credit card transactions and handles 95 percent of all ATM transactions, with no method given. A 2020 Wealthsimple Magazine article repeats them and adds that Bank of New York Mellon found in 2012 it had 112,500 COBOL programs and almost 350 million lines, and that estimates run as high as 240 billion lines in all. A 1997 Gartner figure of 200 billion lines is also cited everywhere, though the actual report is hard to find. "Uses COBOL somewhere in the chain" is not "COBOL executes the transaction", lines of code are not transactions, and the figures repeat one another rather than confirming each other.
nodes.sleeper: COBOL ranked 20th in the TIOBE index of language popularity in September 2026, and 1 percent of respondents to the 2025 Stack Overflow survey used it.

nodes.title: Dead Ends & Cautionary Tales
nodes.short: Ideas that promised to end programming's hard parts and did not, plus the famous disasters.
nodes.long: Each wave (4GLs, CASE tools, UML code generation, low-code, now AI) raised the abstraction level without eliminating programmers. Disasters from the Therac-25 to CrowdStrike show what unchecked software costs.

nodes.title: Fifth Generation Computer Systems
nodes.short: Japan's ten-year national project to build parallel logic-programming computers. It cost about 57 billion yen, left no commercial legacy and ended in 1994.
nodes.long: In 1982 Japan's Ministry of International Trade and Industry (MITI) launched a ten-year initiative to build computers based on massively parallel processing and logic programming. It ran from 1982 to 1994, spent a little under 57 billion yen (about 320 million US dollars) and built five Parallel Inference Machines. It ended in commercial failure, though it contributed to concurrent logic programming, and MITI then stopped funding large computer research projects. One contested account, from a single secondary source, says the specialized hardware was overtaken by cheaper machines such as Sun workstations and Intel x86 systems, that the choice of concurrent logic programming undermined the logic it was meant to bridge, and that the project missed outside innovations such as graphical interfaces and the Internet.
nodes.sleeper: In 1982 many expected Japan's logic-programming machines to define the next generation of computing. Ordinary microprocessors and workstations improved fast enough to overcome the barriers experts had expected.

nodes.title: CASE Tools
nodes.short: Computer-aided software engineering: draw the design, generate the code. Mostly abandoned.
nodes.long: In the late 1980s CASE tools promised automatic code from diagrams. Generated code was hard to maintain and diagrams drifted from reality. UML code generation had the same fate.

nodes.title: Therac-25
nodes.short: A computer-controlled radiation machine gave massive overdoses in at least six accidents from 1985 to 1987 after hardware interlocks were removed.
nodes.long: The Therac-25, a radiation-therapy machine from the Canadian company AECL, delivered massive overdoses in at least six accidents between 1985 and 1987. Doses were about 100 times the intended amount, in what has been called the worst series of radiation accidents in the 35-year history of medical accelerators; the commonly cited death toll is three, though sources differ. Causes included a race condition, in which an operator who changed the mode within about eight seconds left the machine in an unsafe state, and a flag that was incremented instead of set, so that integer overflow let the beam fire without its target. AECL had removed the hardware interlocks of earlier models and reused Therac-20 software. A commission blamed generally poor software design and development practices. Lessons include re-validating reused software and never relying on software alone for safety.

nodes.title: Heartbleed
nodes.short: A missing length check in OpenSSL's heartbeat feature let anyone read 64 KB chunks of server memory, including private keys. Disclosed on 7 April 2014.
nodes.long: Heartbleed, CVE-2014-0160, was a missing bounds check in OpenSSL's version of the TLS heartbeat, a keep-alive message. The receiver trusted a 16-bit length field in the request, so a short request claiming a long length got back up to 64 KB of server memory, such as private keys, passwords and session cookies. The flawed code shipped in OpenSSL 1.0.1 in March 2012 and was fixed in 1.0.1g. Neel Mehta of Google reported it privately on 1 April 2014, Codenomicon found it independently, and about 17 percent of the Internet's certified secure web servers, roughly half a million, were believed vulnerable. The author of the change said he missed validating a length variable. Commentary pointed to memory-unsafe C, a critical library kept up by very few people and the weakness of the 'many eyes' argument; the Linux Foundation's Core Infrastructure Initiative and the LibreSSL fork followed.
nodes.sleeper: The Internet's encryption rests on open-source libraries maintained by very few people. Heartbleed led to mass replacement of certificates and to new funding for open-source infrastructure.

nodes.title: Log4Shell
nodes.short: A flaw in the widely embedded Log4j logging library let attackers run code on servers by getting a crafted string logged. Public on 9 and 10 December 2021.
nodes.long: Log4Shell, CVE-2021-44228, was a flaw in Apache Log4j, a Java logging library embedded in countless products. Versions from 2.0-beta9 to 2.14.1 performed lookups on logged text, so an attacker who got a crafted string logged, such as a web header or a chat message, could make the server load attacker code. An engineer at Alibaba Cloud reported it to the Apache Software Foundation on 24 November 2021, the flaw became public on 9 and 10 December, and version 2.15.0 was released on 10 December. It scored the maximum 10.0 for severity. The US Cyber Safety Review Board called it an endemic vulnerability that could remain in systems for a decade or longer, and found that none of the organizations it surveyed had used software bills of materials to find vulnerable systems. Volunteers maintained the library, and the feature dated from 2013.
nodes.sleeper: Applications now inherit hundreds of libraries, some several layers down. Log4Shell showed organizations often did not know whether they ran Log4j, which is why dependency inventories and SBOMs, lists of a product's components, became policy topics.

refs.label: Cyber Safety Review Board, Review of the December 2021 Log4j Event

nodes.title: xz-utils Backdoor
nodes.short: A patient attacker took over the xz-utils compression project and hid a backdoor aimed at SSH logins on Linux servers. A slow login exposed it.
nodes.long: In March 2024 Andres Freund noticed that SSH logins on a Debian development system were using extra processor time, and traced it to a backdoor, CVE-2024-3094, in the xz compression library. Russ Cox's reconstruction shows a persona called Jia Tan contributing from October 2021 while other accounts pressed the sole maintainer, Lasse Collin, to hand over work. Jia Tan became a maintainer in 2022 and built the 5.6.0 and 5.6.1 releases, which carried the backdoor in February and March 2024. The exploit hid in build files present only in the release tarball and in disguised test files, and reached the SSH server indirectly through libsystemd and liblzma. Those versions had reached mostly pre-release distribution builds. Lessons: a tired volunteer maintainer is a target, release tarballs can differ from the source repository, and trust passes through indirect links.
nodes.sleeper: Open-source libraries are often kept alive by one volunteer. The xz case shows that taking over such a project is a workable attack, and that the source you read may differ from the tarball you build.

nodes.title: UNCOL
nodes.short: A 1958 proposal for one universal intermediate language, so N languages and M machines need only N plus M translators. Never built, but the idea won later.
nodes.long: In 1958 a committee of the SHARE user group proposed UNCOL, the Universal Computer Oriented Language. Every compiler would translate its source language into UNCOL once, and one translator per machine would turn UNCOL into machine code, so N languages and M machines would need N plus M translators instead of N times M. It was never fully specified or implemented. A later white paper by Stavros Macrakis says it failed because language and compiler technology were not yet mature, and that compiler-compilers in the 1970s ended up solving the problem in another way. The same arithmetic now drives LLVM's intermediate representation and bytecode virtual machines such as the Java Virtual Machine.
nodes.sleeper: What failed as a single standard in 1958 became ordinary practice: LLVM and the Java Virtual Machine both put a shared intermediate form between many languages and many processors.

refs.label: Lattner, LLVM chapter in The Architecture of Open Source Applications

nodes.title: Lines of Code as a Metric
nodes.short: Measuring productivity by volume rewards bloat. Decades of evidence say don't.
nodes.long: Counting lines punishes concise solutions and rewards copy-paste. Researchers and practitioners have recommended against it for fifty years, yet it keeps returning in new forms.

nodes.title: AI Winters
nodes.short: Two stretches of cut funding and lost faith in AI, about 1974 to 1980 and 1987 to 2000. Promises ran ahead of results, and the Lisp machine market collapsed.
nodes.long: An AI winter is a period of reduced funding and interest after hopes for artificial intelligence outrun results. Wikipedia counts two major ones, roughly 1974 to 1980 and 1987 to 2000, though sources differ. The first followed the 1973 Lighthill report for the British Science Research Council, which said that in no part of the field had the discoveries made so far produced the major impact that was then promised.
